- List of Sustainable Development Goals (unverified) - - List of all the protected zones (unverified) -
Protected Area Type Purpose Key Features
Biodiversity Hotspots To identify and conserve regions with exceptionally high levels of plant endemism and habitat loss, serving as global priorities for biodiversity protection. Globally recognized areas meeting criteria of at least 1,500 endemic vascular plant species and 70% loss of primary vegetation; India has 4: Western Ghats & Sri Lanka, Himalayas, Indo-Burma, Sundaland; Focus on threat mitigation through research and policy.
Tiger Reserves To conserve Bengal tigers and their prey in viable populations while maintaining ecological balance. 53 reserves covering core (national park/sanctuary) and buffer zones; Governed by Project Tiger (1973) under National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA); Total area ~75,000 km²; Habitat management, anti-poaching, and community involvement.
Elephant Reserves To protect Asian elephants, their habitats, and migration corridors to reduce human-elephant conflict. 33 reserves covering ~65,000 km²; Established under Project Elephant (1992); Includes 10 km buffer around national parks/sanctuaries; Focus on corridor restoration, conflict mitigation, and veterinary care for elephants.
National Parks To protect ecological, faunal, floral, geomorphological, or natural significance for wildlife propagation and development. 110 parks covering ~44,403 km² (1.35% of India's area); Highest protection level (IUCN Category II); No human activities except tourism/research; Rights extinguished; Can upgrade from sanctuaries but not vice versa; Includes several marine/coastal parks like Gulf of Mannar.
Wildlife Sanctuaries To protect, propagate, and develop wildlife and their environments in areas of ecological or zoological importance. 574 sanctuaries covering ~127,241 km² (3.73% of India's area); IUCN Category IV; Regulated human activities with chief wildlife warden permission; Can include grazing/logging if sustainable; Buffer for national parks; Many coastal examples like Thane Creek Flamingo Sanctuary.
Biosphere Reserves To conserve biodiversity, promote sustainable development, and foster harmonious human-nature relationships in large ecosystems. 18 reserves (12 UNESCO-recognized) covering core, buffer, and transition zones; Often include national parks/sanctuaries; Total area ~85,000 km²; Research, education, and local community livelihoods integrated; IUCN Category V; Includes coastal ones like Gulf of Mannar and Sundarbans.
Conservation Reserves To protect landscapes, seascapes, flora, fauna, and habitats, acting as buffers or corridors between protected areas. Declared on government land adjacent to parks/sanctuaries; 115 reserves covering ~5,549 km² (0.17% of area); Managed with local community involvement; No extinguishment of existing rights; Sustainable resource use allowed; Some coastal applications for mangroves/seashores.
Community Reserves To encourage voluntary conservation of wildlife and habitats by individuals or communities on private/community lands. Declared on non-government land outside parks/sanctuaries; 220 reserves covering ~1,446 km² (0.043% of area); Local management via panchayats; Connectors for migration; Rights of residents unaffected; Potential for coastal community-led initiatives.
Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) To regulate human activities in ocean/estuarine zones for conserving marine biodiversity, fisheries, and ecosystems. 132 MPAs covering ~8,214 km² (0.4% of EEZ); Defined under IUCN guidelines; Includes no-take zones; Examples: Gulf of Kachchh Marine National Park (Gujarat, corals/mangroves), Gulf of Mannar (Tamil Nadu, dugongs/turtles); Focus on anti-poaching, research, and sustainable fishing; Often overlap with national parks/sanctuaries.
Coastal Regulation Zones (CRZ) To protect coastal ecosystems from unregulated development while balancing economic needs through zoning. Covers 7,500+ km coastline under CRZ Notification 2019; Four zones (CRZ-I: ecologically sensitive/no development; CRZ-II: urban/developed; CRZ-III: rural; CRZ-IV: territorial waters); Regulates industries, tourism, and construction; Includes mangroves, coral reefs, and sand dunes.
Ramsar Wetlands To conserve wetlands of international importance, especially as waterfowl habitats, under the Ramsar Convention. 93 sites covering ~1.36 million ha; Many coastal/estuarine (e.g., Sundarbans, Chilika Lake); Focus on wise use, flood control, and fisheries; Overlaps with national parks/sanctuaries; IUCN Category varies; Added 4 new sites in 2025: Menar Wetland Complex, Khichan Wetland, Gokul Jalashay, Udaipur Jheel.
Important Coastal and Marine Biodiversity Areas (ICMBAs) To identify priority sites for enhanced protection to meet global biodiversity targets like Aichi Target 11. 106 sites identified by Wildlife Institute of India; Includes mangroves, coral reefs, seagrasses; Supports expansion of PA network; Focus on research, monitoring, and threat reduction in high-biodiversity coastal/marine hotspots.
Eco-Sensitive Zones (ESZs) To safeguard fragile ecosystems around protected areas by regulating development and acting as buffers to prevent biodiversity fragmentation. Notified under Environment (Protection) Act, 1986; Typically 10 km around national parks/sanctuaries (variable width); 92 ESZs and 2 Ecologically Sensitive Areas in 13 Himalayan states; Prohibited/regulated activities like mining, large industries; Promotes sustainable land use and connectivity.
Biodiversity Heritage Sites To conserve unique biological resources, traditional knowledge, and cultural practices at community/local levels under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002. Declared by State Biodiversity Boards; 35 sites as of 2023 (e.g., Ganda-Bachao Andolan in Uttarakhand); Focus on community stewardship, education, and sustainable use; Protects sacred groves, medicinal plants, and endemic species.
Reserved Forests To preserve and sustainably manage forest resources with higher protection levels, restricting activities like logging without permission. Under Indian Forest Act, 1927 (IUCN Category IV/VI); Cover ~30% of forest area; Government-owned; Higher protection than protected forests; Essential for timber, wildlife habitat, and watershed protection.
Protected Forests To manage forests for conservation and limited resource use, allowing certain activities unless prohibited. Under Indian Forest Act, 1927; Cover significant forest land; Government-owned; Permits grazing, limited extraction; Acts as buffer for stricter PAs; Focus on soil conservation and local livelihoods.
Village and Panchayat Forests To empower local communities in sustainable forest management, promoting conservation and development. Under state laws (e.g., Van Panchayats in Uttarakhand); IUCN Category VI; Community-managed with government oversight; ~1.5 lakh ha; Enhances livelihoods through NTFP collection and eco-restoration.
Private Protected Areas To protect habitats on private lands from exploitation, supporting voluntary conservation efforts. Under Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act, 2002; Includes wildlife land/land tenures; No government enforcement but legal recognition; Examples: private sanctuaries for birds/endangered species; Growing via eco-tourism.
UNESCO Global Geoparks To promote conservation of geological heritage, sustainable development, and education in geodiverse areas. 2 sites: Lonar (Maharashtra, meteor crater) and Gulf of Mannar (Tamil Nadu, marine geology); UNESCO-recognized since 2020-2022; Integrates geo-tourism, research, and community involvement; Highlights volcanic, sedimentary, and tectonic features.
- Timeline related to wildlife protection in India (unverified)
Period Key Events/Initiatives Details
Pre-Independence (1800s–1947) Indian Forest Act (1865, 1927) Introduced by British for forest management; focused on timber revenue, minimal wildlife protection; 1927 version formalized reserved/protected forests.
Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act (1890) Early British law targeting animal welfare; limited focus on wild species, set precedent for 1960 act.
Hailey National Park (1936) India’s first national park (now Jim Corbett, Uttarakhand); established to protect Bengal tigers and habitats.
Post-Independence (1947–1970) Indian Board for Wildlife (IBWL) (1952) Advisory body under MoEF; formulated early wildlife policies, precursor to NTCA.
Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act (1960) Updated 1890 law; regulates animal welfare, limited wildlife focus; enforced by Animal Welfare Board of India.
Vedanthangal Bird Sanctuary (1936, formalized 1962) One of India’s oldest sanctuaries (Tamil Nadu); protected as a key bird habitat.
Import and Export (Control) Act (1947, amended 1960s) Regulates trade in wildlife products; early step to curb illegal trade.
1970s Wildlife (Protection) Act (1972) Landmark legislation; prohibits hunting, establishes national parks, sanctuaries, and schedules (I–VI); 5 initial national parks (~44,403 km² by 2025).
Project Tiger (1973) Launched with 9 reserves (58 by 2025, ~75,000 km²); conserves Bengal tigers via habitat management, anti-poaching; population ~3,682 (2022).
Forest (Conservation) Act (1980) Restricts forest land diversion; requires central approval for non-forest use, protecting wildlife habitats.
Central Zoo Authority (CZA) (1979, formalized 1992) Regulates zoos; promotes captive breeding for endangered species conservation.
Constitutional Amendment (1976) 42nd Amendment; added Article 48A (environmental protection duty) and Article 51A(g) (citizen duty to protect wildlife, forests).
1980s Environment (Protection) Act (1986) Umbrella law for environmental protection; empowers central government to safeguard wildlife habitats.
National Forest Policy (1988) Targets 33% forest cover; prioritizes conservation, ecological balance over commercial use.
Social Forestry (1980s) Community-based afforestation; enhances wildlife corridors, supports rural livelihoods via plantations.
Bombay Natural History Society (BNHS) Activities (1883, active 1980s) Non-governmental; conducts wildlife research, conservation advocacy; key for bird and habitat studies.
1990s Project Elephant (1992) Protects Asian elephants, habitats, corridors; 33 reserves (~65,000 km²) by 2025; mitigates human-elephant conflict.
Joint Forest Management (JFM) (1990) Community-driven forest management; integrates conservation with local livelihoods.
National Afforestation and Eco-Development Board (NAEB) (1992) Promotes afforestation, habitat restoration; supports biodiversity via community projects.
Project Snow Leopard (1999, formalized 2009) Conserves high-altitude ecosystems, snow leopards; community-based in Himalayas (Ladakh, Himachal).
Wildlife Trust of India (1998) NGO focused on wildlife rescue, rehabilitation; supports endangered species like rhinos, elephants.
2000s Biological Diversity Act (2002) Regulates access to biological resources; establishes National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) and State Biodiversity Boards.
Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act (2002) Introduces conservation and community reserves; strengthens penalties for wildlife crimes.
National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) (2005) Statutory body under WPA; oversees Project Tiger, reserve management, anti-poaching.
Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act (2006) Grants forest rights to tribal communities; balances conservation with livelihoods.
Wildlife Crime Control Bureau (WCCB) (2006) Combats illegal wildlife trade; coordinates enforcement across states, aligns with CITES.
National Ganga River Basin Authority (NGRBA) (2009) Protects Ganges ecosystem, including aquatic species like Ganges River Dolphin.
Vulture Conservation Action Plan (2006) Bans diclofenac; promotes breeding programs for critically endangered vultures (e.g., Gyps species).
National Bamboo Mission (2006, restructured 2018) Promotes bamboo cultivation for habitat restoration, carbon sequestration, and livelihoods.
Mining and Mineral Development (Regulation) Act (1957, amended 2000s) Regulates mining in forest areas; ensures minimal impact on wildlife habitats.
2010s Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) Notification (2011) Protects coastal ecosystems (mangroves, corals); regulates development in CRZ-I to IV zones; updated in 2019.
Island Protection Zone Notification (2011) Safeguards biodiversity in Andaman & Nicobar and Lakshadweep islands; protects marine and terrestrial species.
Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules (2010, revised 2017) Protects wetlands as critical wildlife habitats; regulates activities to preserve biodiversity (e.g., Chilika Lake).
Biodiversity Conservation & Rural Livelihood Improvement Project (BCRLIP) (2011) World Bank-supported; integrates biodiversity conservation with rural livelihoods in key ecosystems.
M-STrIPES (2010) Monitoring System for Tigers; tech-based tool for tracking tigers, prey, and poaching in reserves.
National Green Tribunal (NGT) Act (2010) Establishes NGT for environmental and wildlife disputes; enforces compliance with conservation laws.
National Wildlife Action Plan (NWAP III, 2017–2031) Emphasizes habitat restoration, climate resilience, anti-poaching, and community involvement.
Green Highways Policy (2015) Promotes afforestation along highways; enhances wildlife corridors, ecological connectivity.
Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management and Planning Authority (CAMPA) (2016) Manages funds for afforestation to compensate forest loss; supports wildlife habitat restoration.
Nagoya Protocol Adoption (2014) Implements fair sharing of genetic resources; aligns with CBD for biodiversity conservation.
2020s Project Lion (2020) Conserves Asiatic lions; expands habitats in Gir (Gujarat) and surrounding areas.
Project Dolphin (2021) Conserves Ganges River Dolphin; focuses on riverine habitat restoration, pollution control.
Project Cheetah (2022) Reintroduces cheetahs to India (Kuno National Park, Madhya Pradesh); restores savanna ecosystems.
Project Gaur (2023) Conserves Indian bison (gaur); focuses on Central Indian forests, habitat protection.
Project Vulture (2020–2025, ongoing) Continues diclofenac ban; expands breeding centers for vulture recovery (e.g., Pinjore, Haryana).
National Lake Conservation Plan (NLCP, merged into 2020s programs) Restores lakes as wildlife habitats; integrated into National Plan for Conservation of Aquatic Ecosystems.
Constitutional Strengthening (2023) Reinforces Article 48A; emphasizes state responsibility for wildlife and environmental protection.
- Timeline related to India's environmental initiatives (unverified)
Period Key Events/Initiatives Details
Pre-Independence (1800s–1947) Indian Penal Code (1860) Section 268 addresses public nuisance, including pollution; early legal basis for environmental control.
Factories Act (1948, roots in 1881) Regulates industrial waste and emissions; mandates safe disposal of effluents to prevent pollution.
1950s–1960s Merchant Shipping Act (1958) Prevents marine pollution from ships; regulates oil and waste discharge in coastal waters.
River Boards Act (1956) Establishes boards for river water quality; early focus on preventing water pollution.
Atomic Energy Act (1962) Regulates radioactive waste; ensures safe disposal to prevent environmental contamination.
1970s Water (Prevention & Control of Pollution) Act (1974) First major pollution law; establishes Central/State Pollution Control Boards (CPCB/SPCBs); regulates industrial effluents.
Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) Established (1974) Apex body under Water Act; sets pollution standards, coordinates with SPCBs for enforcement.
Water (Prevention & Control of Pollution) Cess Act (1977) Imposes cess on water use by industries; funds pollution control; amended 2003 for wider coverage.
42nd Constitutional Amendment (1976) Adds Article 48A (state duty to protect environment) and Article 51A(g) (citizen duty to prevent pollution).
1980s Air (Prevention & Control of Pollution) Act (1981) Regulates air emissions; includes noise pollution (1987 amendment); mandates industry consents.
Environment (Protection) Act (EPA) (1986) Umbrella law post-Bhopal disaster; empowers central government to regulate all pollution types; basis for waste rules.
National Environment Awareness Campaign (NEAC) (1986) Annual MoEFCC campaign; funds NGOs/schools for pollution awareness; focuses on air, water, waste issues.
Environment Education, Awareness & Training (EEAT) Scheme (1983) Promotes pollution education; trains stakeholders; supports environmental literacy programs.
Hazardous Waste (Management & Handling) Rules (1989) Regulates hazardous waste generation, transport, disposal; precursor to 2016 rules; amended 2000, 2008.
1990s Public Liability Insurance Act (1991) Mandates insurance for hazardous substance accidents; ensures compensation for pollution victims.
National Environment Tribunal Act (1995) Handles pollution-related damage claims; precursor to National Green Tribunal; repealed 2010.
Bio-Medical Waste (Management & Handling) Rules (1998) Regulates hospital waste; mandates segregation, treatment; precursor to 2016 rules.
Municipal Solid Waste (Management & Handling) Rules (2000) Sets norms for urban waste collection, segregation, disposal; replaced by 2016 SWM Rules.
Eco-Clubs (National Green Corps) (1990s, formalized 2001) School-based program under EEAT; educates youth on pollution prevention; ~1.5 lakh clubs by 2025.
2000s Ozone Depleting Substances (Regulation & Control) Rules (2000) Phases out CFCs/HCFCs under Montreal Protocol; HCFC-141b phased out by 2020; amended 2014, 2019.
Batteries (Management & Handling) Rules (2001) Regulates lead-acid battery recycling; introduces EPR for producers; amended 2016, 2022.
Noise Pollution (Regulation & Control) Rules (2000) Sets ambient noise standards; regulates sources like firecrackers, industries; enforces silent zones.
E-Waste (Management & Handling) Rules (2008) Introduces EPR for electronics; sets collection/recycling targets; updated in 2016, 2023.
Comprehensive Environmental Pollution Index (CEPI) (2009) Assesses pollution in 88 industrial clusters; identifies 43 critically polluted areas; moratorium on expansions.
National Ganga River Basin Authority (NGRBA) (2009) Addresses river pollution; integrates waste management, sewage treatment for Ganges.
National Clean Energy Fund (2010) Coal cess-funded; supports clean tech, waste-to-energy projects to reduce pollution.
2010s National Green Tribunal (NGT) Act (2010) Establishes NGT for environmental/pollution disputes; enforces EPA, Air/Water Acts; applies polluter-pays principle.
Green India Mission (2014) Part of NAPCC; afforestation to sequester carbon, reduce soil erosion, and control dust pollution.
Swachh Bharat Mission (2014) Urban/rural waste management; promotes segregation, processing; reduces open dumping pollution.
Solid Waste Management (SWM) Rules (2016) Mandates source segregation; EPR for bulk generators; urban bodies manage landfills, composting.
Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management & Transboundary Movement) Rules (2016) Simplifies hazardous waste procedures; regulates import/export; EPR for producers.
Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules (2016) Segregation into 4 categories; mandatory treatment at Common Bio-Medical Waste Treatment Facilities; annual reporting.
Construction and Demolition Waste Management Rules (2016) Mandates segregation, recycling; bans landfill disposal; urban areas to set up C&D waste plants.
E-Waste (Management) Rules (2016) EPR for producers; covers 21 e-waste types; collection targets; SPCB registration mandatory.
Plastic Waste Management (PWM) Rules (2016) Bans single-use plastics; EPR for producers; minimum thickness norms; amended 2021, 2022 for traceability.
National Clean Air Programme (NCAP) (2019) Targets 20–30% PM reduction in 131 cities by 2024; extended to 2026; addresses industrial, vehicular, waste burning emissions.
Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) Guidelines (2016–2018) Mandatory for plastic/e-waste; sets recycling targets; centralized EPR portal launched 2022.
Net Metering Policies (2010s) State-level policies; credits solar energy to grid; reduces fossil fuel emissions; adopted in 25+ states by 2019.
2020s National Mission for Clean Air (2020) Expands NCAP; targets 40% PM reduction by 2026; funds air quality monitoring, waste burning controls.
Plastic Waste Management Amendment Rules (2021–2022) Introduces QR codes for traceability; EPR for multi-layered plastics; bans specific single-use plastics (2022).
Battery Waste Management Rules (2022) EPR for battery producers; collection/recycling targets; covers all battery types.
Hazardous Waste Management Amendments (2022) EPR for waste tyres; extended liability for producers; aligns with Basel Convention.
E-Waste (Management) Rules Amendment (2023) Strengthens EPR; increases recycling targets to 60% by 2023; covers solar panels, IT equipment.
Environment Protection (EPR for Packaging) Rules (2024) Covers paper, glass, metal, sanitary products; promotes circular economy; reduces packaging waste.
CEPI Reassessment (2021–2025) Updates pollution index; 38 critically polluted areas; enforces action plans for industrial clusters.
National Action Plan on Plastic Waste (2024) Integrates PWM rules; targets 100% recycling of PET plastics; promotes alternatives like biodegradable materials.
- Timeline related to India's renewable energy initiatives (unverified)
Period Key Events/Initiatives Details
Pre-Independence & Early Post-Independence (1947–1970) Early Hydropower Development (1950s) Bhakra Nangal Dam (1950s); foundational for non-fossil energy; early focus on hydro as renewable source.
Atomic Energy Act (1962) Includes non-conventional energy research; precursors to renewables like solar/wind.
1970s Department of Non-Conventional Energy Sources (1981, roots 1970s) Early R&D in solar, wind, bioenergy; small hydro projects initiated.
42nd Constitutional Amendment (1976) Adds Article 48A for environmental protection; supports renewable integration.
National Wind Energy Programme (1976) Early wind R&D; leads to first wind farms in 1980s.
1980s Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) Established (1992, roots 1981) Department of Non-Conventional Energy Sources becomes full ministry; coordinates RE policies.
Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency (IREDA) (1987) Financing arm for RE projects; supports solar, wind, bioenergy deployment.
Solar Photovoltaic Programme (1980s) Early solar lantern and pump initiatives; rural electrification focus.
National Solar Cooker Programme (1987) Promotes solar thermal; community-level adoption.
1990s Grid-Connected Renewable Power Policy (1993) Buy-back tariffs for wind/solar; accelerates grid integration.
National Programme on Improved Cookstoves (1991) Biomass efficiency; reduces fuelwood use, supports bioenergy.
Remote Village Electrification Programme (1990s) Solar/diesel hybrids for off-grid areas; reaches 100+ villages.
Wind Power Policy (1999) Incentives for wind farms; capacity reaches 1 GW by 2000.
Biogas Programme (1980s–1990s) Family biogas plants; 3 million+ installations by 2000.
2000s National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC, 2008) 8 missions including Solar, Enhanced Energy Efficiency; sets RE foundation.
National Solar Mission (NSM, 2010) Targets 20 GW solar by 2022 (achieved 100+ GW by 2025); grid/off-grid focus.
National Wind Mission (2010) Aims 15 GW wind addition; offshore wind guidelines.
Lighting a Billion Lives (LaBL, 2008) TERI initiative; solar lanterns for rural access; reaches 1M+ households by 2025.
Eco Mark Scheme (1991, active 2000s) BIS certification for eco-friendly products; includes RE appliances like solar cookers.
Jawaharlal Nehru National Solar Mission (JNNSM, 2010) Phased targets: 1 GW Phase I (2013), scales to 100 GW ambition.
2010s National Clean Energy Fund (NCEF, 2010) Coal cess-funded; Rs. 10,000 Cr corpus; supports RE R&D, clean coal; renamed NCEEF 2017.
Urban Services Environmental Rating System (USERS, 2010s) UNDP/TERI/MoEFCC project; rates urban services (water, waste) for sustainability; RE integration in cities.
National Offshore Wind Energy Policy (2015) Targets 5 GW offshore wind by 2022; pilot projects in Gujarat/Tamil Nadu.
Green Energy Corridor (2015) Rs. 10,000 Cr; transmits 10 GW RE; intra/inter-state lines for solar/wind.
National Mission for Electric Mobility (NMEM, 2013) Targets 6-7M EVs by 2020; leads to FAME schemes; 30% EV penetration by 2030.
FAME India Phase I (2015) Rs. 795 Cr; subsidies for 2-wheelers/3-wheelers; 1.4 lakh EVs supported.
Solar Park Scheme (2015) 50 parks, 38 GW by 2025-26; Bhadla (2.2 GW) operational.
International Solar Alliance (ISA, 2015) India-France initiative; 121 countries; mobilizes $1T for solar by 2030.
Perform, Achieve, Trade (PAT, 2012) Energy efficiency in industries; saves 20M tonnes oil equivalent annually.
KUSUM (2018) Decentralized solar pumps; 30,000 MW solar agri by 2022; expanded 2025.
2020s FAME India Phase II (2021) Rs. 10,000 Cr; 8,000 EV charging stations; 1.5M EVs supported by 2025.
National Hydrogen Mission (2021) 5M tonnes green H2 by 2030; electrolyser 5 GW; $2.4B incentives.
PLI Scheme for Solar PV Modules (2021) 48 GW domestic manufacturing; Tranche II: 39 GW by 2026; $1.7B investment.
PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana (2024) 1 Cr rooftop solar households; Rs. 75,000 Cr; free 300 units/month.
National Bio Energy Mission (2022) 5 GW biomass; compressed biogas plants; ethanol blending 20% by 2025.
ISTS Waiver Extension (2022) Waives transmission charges for RE projects till June 2025; boosts solar/wind.
Smart Meter Rollout (2020s) 250M meters by 2025; 7M installed by 2023; enables RE integration.
Production Linked Incentive for Batteries (2021) 50 GWh capacity; supports EV/RE storage; $2.4B allocation.
SATAT Initiative (2018, expanded 2020s) 5,000 CBG plants; 15M tonnes CBG/year by 2025; vehicle fuel.
Budget 2025-26 Allocation (2025) Rs. 25,649 Cr for MNRE (39% increase); focuses on solar, green H2.
Net-Zero Pledge (2021) Net-zero by 2070; 50% non-fossil by 2030; RE at 220 GW (2025).
50% Non-Fossil Milestone (2025) Achieved July 2025; 5 years ahead of 2030 target; RE 217 GW (Jan 2025).
- Timeline of world climate change initiatives (unverified) -
Period Key Events/Initiatives Details
Pre-1970s Greenhouse Effect Theory (1824–1896) Joseph Fourier identifies greenhouse effect; Eunice Newton Foote and John Tyndall show CO2 traps heat; Svante Arrhenius predicts 5–6°C warming from CO2 doubling.
Keeling Curve (1958) Charles Keeling measures CO2 at Mauna Loa; shows rise from ~315 ppm, foundational for climate monitoring.
UN Conference on Human Environment (Stockholm, 1972) First global environmental conference; establishes UNEP; sparks climate awareness.
1970s–1980s First Earth Day (1970) Global environmental movement; 20M+ participants; influences climate activism.
World Climate Conference (1979) WMO’s first climate conference; warns of CO2-driven warming; calls for global research.
Vienna Convention (1985) Framework for ozone protection; precursor to Montreal Protocol; addresses climate-relevant gases.
Montreal Protocol (1987) Phases out ozone-depleting substances (CFCs); reduces climate-warming HFCs via later amendments.
IPCC Established (1988) UNEP/WMO forms Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change; first report (1990) confirms human-driven warming.
1990s UNFCCC Adopted (1992) United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (Rio Summit); 154 signatories; stabilizes GHGs; launches COPs.
Agenda 21 (1992) Rio Summit outcome; sustainable development blueprint; integrates climate action with development.
UNCCD (1994) UN Convention to Combat Desertification; addresses land degradation, climate resilience.
Kyoto Protocol (COP3, 1997) Binding targets for developed countries (5% GHG cut below 1990 by 2008–2012); CDM, emissions trading; effective 2005.
Greenhouse Gas Protocol (1998) WRI/WBCSD standard for corporate GHG accounting; adopted globally for emissions reporting.
National Greenhouse Gas Inventories Programme (NGGIP, 1995) IPCC program; standardizes GHG inventories for UNFCCC reporting; supports transparency.
COP4 (Buenos Aires, 1998) Buenos Aires Action Plan; advances Kyoto implementation, adaptation for developing nations.
2000s Stockholm Convention on POPs (2001) Bans persistent organic pollutants; reduces toxic emissions impacting climate systems.
Basel Convention (1989, active 2000s) Controls hazardous waste movement; prevents pollution affecting climate (e.g., e-waste).
Rotterdam Convention (1998, effective 2004) Regulates trade in hazardous chemicals/pesticides; reduces environmental pollution linked to climate.
International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources (ITPGRFA, 2004) Ensures crop diversity for food security; supports climate-resilient agriculture.
COP13 (Bali, 2007) Bali Roadmap; long-term action plan; aims for 50% GHG cut by 2050; includes REDD framework.
REDD & REDD+ (2007) Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and Degradation; REDD+ adds conservation, sustainable forest management; funds via GEF.
Global Environment Facility (GEF, 1992, active 2000s) Funds climate projects; $20B+ for mitigation/adaptation; supports REDD+, renewables.
Earth Hour (2007) WWF-led global campaign; annual lights-off event; raises climate awareness.
2010s COP15 (Copenhagen, 2009) Copenhagen Accord; voluntary pledges; $100B/year climate finance by 2020; introduces INDCs.
TEEB (The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity, 2010) UNEP-led; values ecosystems for climate policy; informs adaptation/mitigation strategies.
COP16 (Cancun, 2010) Cancun Agreements; establishes Green Climate Fund, technology mechanism; formalizes adaptation.
Forest Carbon Partnership Facility (FCPF, 2008, active 2010s) World Bank initiative; supports REDD+; $1.1B for forest conservation in 47 countries.
Climate and Clean Air Coalition (CCAC, 2012) Reduces short-lived climate pollutants (methane, black carbon); 160+ partners.
COP20 (Lima, 2014) Lima Call for Climate Action; INDCs submitted for Paris; $100B finance mobilized.
COP21 (Paris, 2015) Paris Agreement; limits warming to <2°C, aims for 1.5°C; NDCs, ratchet mechanism; effective 2016.
International Solar Alliance (ISA, 2015) India-France initiative; 121 countries; $1T for solar by 2030; scales renewables.
Kigali Amendment (2016) Montreal Protocol amendment; phases down HFCs; prevents 0.5°C warming by 2100.
COP22 (Marrakech, 2016) Marrakech Partnership; accelerates Paris implementation; adaptation focus.
2020s Minamata Convention (2013, effective 2017) Reduces mercury emissions; protects ecosystems, indirectly supports climate goals.
BioCarbon Fund Initiative for Sustainable Forest Landscapes (2013, active 2020s) World Bank; $350M for REDD+; promotes sustainable land use in 6 countries.
COP23 (Bonn, 2017) Fiji-led; Talanoa Dialogue for ambition; advances Paris rulebook, adaptation.
Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs, 2015, active 2020s) UN’s 17 goals; SDG 13 (climate action) drives mitigation, adaptation, resilience.
Partnership for Action on Green Economy (PAGE, 2013, active 2020s) UN initiative; 22 countries; supports green economy policies for low-carbon growth.
Momentum for Change: Climate Neutral Now (2015, active 2020s) UNFCCC initiative; encourages organizations/individuals to measure, reduce, offset emissions.
COP26 (Glasgow, 2021) Glasgow Climate Pact; phases down coal; methane pledge (30% cut by 2030); $100B finance met.
COP27 (Sharm El-Sheikh, 2022) Loss and damage fund established; fossil fuel transition emphasized; adaptation doubled.
COP28 (Dubai, 2023) UAE Consensus; transitions from fossil fuels; global stocktake; $700M for loss/damage.
Climate Action Tracker (2009, active 2023) Independent tool; tracks NDC ambition; warns of 2.4–3.5°C warming under current policies.
2024–2025 (Current Status) COP29 (Baku, 2024) New climate finance goal ($300B/year); strengthens carbon markets; NDCs due 2025.
Emissions Gap Report (2024) UNEP: 57.1 GtCO2e (2023); 42% cut needed by 2030 for 1.5°C; NDCs insufficient.
State of Global Climate (2024) WMO: 2024 warmest year at 1.55°C above pre-industrial; urgent emission cuts needed.
ICJ Advisory Opinion (July 2025) States legally obligated to act on climate; enables 2,500+ global lawsuits; boosts accountability.
COP30 (Belém, 2025) Brazil hosts; new NDCs; $300B+ finance; Amazon focus; aims for 1.5°C pathway.

Name IUCN Status (2025) Location in India Habitat Diet/Food Gestation Period Lifespan Special Behaviors/Features
Important Animals
Asiatic Lion Endangered Gir National Park, Gujarat Dry deciduous forests, grasslands Chital, sambar, wild boar, livestock 100–119 days 10–14 years Panthera leo persica; smaller prides (2–5 females) than African lions; males often solitary; ~709 individuals (2023); WPA Schedule I; roars audible up to 8 km; territorial scent-marking; threatened by human conflict, inbreeding; conservation via Gir translocation plans.
Bengal Tiger Endangered Sundarbans, Ranthambore, Corbett NPs Mangroves, forests, grasslands Sambar, chital, wild boar, buffalo 93–112 days 8–10 years National animal; solitary hunters with 20–100 km² territories; ~3,167 individuals (2022); WPA Schedule I; swims in Sundarbans; camouflaged stripes; Project Tiger success; threatened by poaching, habitat loss; uses scent and vocalization for communication.
Chiru (Tibetan Antelope) Near Threatened Changthang Plateau, Ladakh High-altitude plains (4,000–5,500 m) Grasses, sedges, forbs 6 months 8–10 years Shahtoosh wool source (banned); migratory herds (up to 200 km); ~1,500 in India; WPA Schedule I; males have long, curved horns; high-altitude stamina; threatened by fencing, grazing; conservation via Changthang Sanctuary.
Double-humped Camel Critically Endangered Nubra Valley, Ladakh Cold deserts, 3,000–4,500 m Grasses, shrubs, saltbush 12–14 months 30–40 years Bactrian camel; two humps store fat; <1,000 in India (wild/domestic); WPA Schedule I; nomadic grazing; survives -40°C; threatened by tourism, habitat loss; used by pastoralists for transport; conservation via breeding programs.
Dugong Vulnerable Gulf of Mannar, Palk Bay, Andaman Coastal waters, seagrass beds Seagrass, algae (10–15 kg/day) 13–15 months Up to 70 years Marine mammal ("sea cow"); ~250 individuals; WPA Schedule I; slow swimmers, dive up to 30m; social groups of 2–6; threatened by fishing nets, seagrass loss; conservation via Gulf of Mannar Biosphere Reserve.
Ganges River Dolphin Endangered Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghna (UP, Bihar, Assam) Freshwater rivers, deep pools Fish (carp, catfish), crustaceans 9–10 months Up to 30 years Blind, uses echolocation; national aquatic animal; ~1,800 individuals; WPA Schedule I; side-swims in murky waters; threatened by dams, pollution; conservation via Vikramshila Sanctuary.
Indian Elephant Endangered Western Ghats, Northeast, Odisha Forests, grasslands, scrub Grasses, leaves, bark (150 kg/day) 18–22 months 60–70 years Keystone species; matriarchal herds; ~27,000 individuals; WPA Schedule I; migrates 10–20 km daily; Project Elephant (1992); threatened by habitat loss, rail collisions; mud-bathing, trunk versatility.
Indian Flying Fox Least Concern Across India, urban/rural Forests, mangroves, orchards Fruits (mango, fig), nectar, pollen 4–5 months 10–20 years Largest Indian bat (1.5m wingspan); roosts in colonies (100–1,000); key pollinator, seed disperser; declining due to tree felling; nocturnal foraging up to 15 km.
Indian Squirrel (Giant Squirrel) Near Threatened Western Ghats, Central India Evergreen forests, canopies Nuts, fruits, bark, insects 28–35 days 5–10 years Ratufa indica; state animal of Maharashtra; arboreal, leaps 6m; WPA Schedule II; colorful fur (purple, orange); threatened by deforestation; builds multiple nests (dreys).
Indian Wild Ass Near Threatened Little Rann of Kutch, Gujarat Desert, salt marshes Grasses, shrubs, crops 11–12 months 20–25 years Equus hemionus khur; ~5,700 individuals (2023); WPA Schedule I; runs 50 km/h; migratory herds; adapted to saline water; threatened by water scarcity; conservation via Wild Ass Sanctuary.
Kharai Camel Vulnerable (domestic breed) Kutch, Gujarat Coastal mangroves, salt flats Halophytic plants, mangroves 12–13 months 20–30 years Swims 3–5 km to graze mangroves; ~20,000 individuals; vital for pastoralists; threatened by overgrazing, salinity rise; conservation via breed recognition (2015).
Lion-tailed Macaque Endangered Western Ghats (Kerala, Karnataka) Rainforests, evergreen forests Fruits (80%), insects, small vertebrates 5–6 months 20–25 years Silver mane, arboreal; ~4,000 individuals; WPA Schedule I; troops of 10–20; threatened by tea plantations; vocalizes with loud whoops; conservation via Silent Valley NP.
Malabar Civet Endangered Western Ghats (Kerala, Karnataka) Evergreen forests, coastal areas Small mammals, birds, fruits 2–3 months 8–10 years Nocturnal, spotted coat; <50 individuals; WPA Schedule I; possibly extinct in wild; solitary; scent-marking; threatened by poaching, habitat loss; conservation via surveys.
Musk Deer Endangered Himalayas (Uttarakhand, Sikkim) Alpine forests, 2,500–4,000 m Grasses, leaves, moss, lichens 6–7 months 10–15 years Fang-like tusks, musk gland; ~5,000 individuals; WPA Schedule I; solitary, crepuscular; poached for musk (perfume); leaps 6m; conservation via Kedarnath Sanctuary.
Nilgiri Tahr Endangered Western Ghats (Kerala, Tamil Nadu) Shola grasslands, cliffs (1,200–2,600 m) Grasses, herbs 6 months 10–12 years State animal of Tamil Nadu; ~3,000 individuals; WPA Schedule I; agile climbers; males have curved horns; threatened by grazing, tourism; conservation via Eravikulam NP.
One-horned Rhinoceros Vulnerable Kaziranga, Manas NPs, Assam Tall grasslands, swamps Grasses, aquatic plants (200 kg/day) 15–16 months 35–45 years Single horn; ~3,700 individuals (2024); WPA Schedule I; wallows in mud; conservation success (from 200 in 1908); territorial; threatened by poaching; Kaziranga key habitat.
Pygmy Hog Critically Endangered Manas NP, Assam Tall grasslands, riverbanks Grasses, roots, insects 100–120 days 5–10 years Smallest wild pig (25 cm); <250 individuals; WPA Schedule I; builds grass nests; nocturnal foraging; threatened by grassland loss; captive breeding in Assam.
Sambar Deer Vulnerable Across India, forests Forests, grasslands, wetlands Grasses, leaves, fruits 8–9 months 15–20 years Largest Indian deer; three-tined antlers; tiger prey; WPA Schedule III; nocturnal; barks when alarmed; declining due to poaching, habitat loss; widespread but fragmented.
Sloth Bear Vulnerable Central India, Western Ghats Forests, scrublands Termites, fruits, honey 6–7 months 20–30 years Long snout for termite sucking; ~20,000 individuals; WPA Schedule I; nocturnal, climbs trees; threatened by habitat loss, human conflict; conservation via Daroji Sanctuary.
Swamp Deer (Barasingha) Vulnerable Kaziranga, Dudhwa NPs (Assam, UP) Swamps, grasslands Grasses, aquatic plants 8–9 months 15–20 years 12-point antlers; ~5,000 individuals; WPA Schedule I; state animal of Assam; forms herds; recovered from 100 in 1970s; threatened by wetland loss; conservation via Kanha NP.
Wild Buffalo Endangered Kaziranga, Manas NPs, Assam Grasslands, wetlands Grasses, sedges (100 kg/day) 10–11 months 25–30 years Largest bovine; ~2,000 purebred; WPA Schedule I; wallows in water; threatened by hybridization, habitat loss; conservation via Kaziranga; migratory in floodplains.
Important Birds
Black-necked Crane Vulnerable Changthang, Ladakh High-altitude wetlands (4,000 m) Grasses, insects, roots 30–35 days (incubation) 20–30 years State bird of Ladakh; migratory from Tibet; ~100 in India; WPA Schedule I; elaborate mating dance; threatened by wetland loss; conservation via Tso Kar Sanctuary.
Ceylon Frogmouth Least Concern Western Ghats (Kerala, Tamil Nadu) Rainforests, understory Insects, small vertebrates 25–30 days (incubation) 5–8 years Nocturnal; leaf-like camouflage; monogamous; WPA Schedule IV; perches motionless to mimic branches; declining due to forest fragmentation.
Coppersmith Barbet Least Concern Across India, urban areas Woodlands, gardens Insects, fruits, nectar 20–25 days (incubation) 10 years Red forehead, "tuk-tuk" call; cavity nester in dead trees; WPA Schedule IV; pollinates fruit trees; adapts to urban areas but faces nest competition.
Great Indian Bustard Critically Endangered Rajasthan, Gujarat, Maharashtra Arid grasslands, scrub Insects, seeds, small vertebrates 25–30 days (incubation) 12–15 years Largest flying bird; <150 individuals; WPA Schedule I; lekking behavior (male display); threatened by power lines, agriculture; conservation via Desert NP.
Gray-chinned Minivet Least Concern Himalayas (Arunachal, Uttarakhand) Mixed forests, 1,000–2,000 m Insects, berries 14–16 days (incubation) 5–7 years Male red/black, female gray; migratory flocks; WPA Schedule IV; forages in canopy; indicator of forest health; declining in fragmented areas.
Indian Peafowl Least Concern Across India, rural areas Forests, farmlands Seeds, insects, small reptiles 28–30 days (incubation) 15–20 years National bird; male’s vibrant tail display; WPA Schedule I; roosts in trees; omnivorous; faces local hunting but adapts to human areas.
Jerdon’s Courser Critically Endangered Eastern Ghats (Andhra Pradesh) Scrub forests, rocky terrain Insects, spiders 25–28 days (incubation) 5–10 years Nocturnal, rediscovered 1986; <50 individuals; WPA Schedule I; ground-nesting; threatened by mining, agriculture; conservation via Sri Lankamalleswara Sanctuary.
Sarus Crane Vulnerable UP, Bihar, Gujarat Wetlands, marshes Plants, insects, fish 26–35 days (incubation) 20–30 years Tallest flying bird; monogamous, lifelong pairs; ~15,000 individuals; WPA Schedule IV; unison calling dance; threatened by wetland drainage.
Siberian Crane Critically Endangered Keoladeo NP, Rajasthan (rare) Wetlands, marshes Aquatic plants, fish 29–31 days (incubation) 15–30 years Migratory from Siberia; nearly extinct in India (last sighted 2002); WPA Schedule I; white plumage, red face; threatened by wetland loss.
Spoon-billed Sandpiper Critically Endangered East coast (Odisha, Tamil Nadu) Coastal wetlands, mudflats Insects, crustaceans 21–24 days (incubation) 10–15 years Spoon-shaped bill; migratory from Russia; <100 in India; WPA Schedule I; threatened by coastal development; conservation via Chilika Lake.
Vulturine Kingfisher Near Threatened Western Ghats, Sundarbans Mangroves, rivers Fish, crustaceans 19–22 days (incubation) 7–10 years Blue-green plumage; dives for prey; WPA Schedule IV; nests in riverbank burrows; threatened by mangrove loss, pollution.
White-throated Redstart Least Concern Himalayas (Sikkim, Himachal) Forest understory, streams Insects, spiders 14–16 days (incubation) 5–8 years Red tail, white throat; tail-fanning display; WPA Schedule IV; migratory; declining in fragmented forests due to habitat loss.
Reptiles/Amphibians
Ganges Softshell Turtle Endangered Ganges, Brahmaputra rivers Freshwater rivers, muddy banks Fish, crustaceans, plants 60–70 days (incubation) 30–50 years Large (1m shell); ~1,000 individuals; WPA Schedule I; buries in mud to ambush prey; threatened by sand mining, fishing; conservation via hatcheries.
Gharial Critically Endangered Chambal River (Rajasthan, MP, UP) Freshwater rivers, sandbanks Fish (almost exclusively) 60–90 days (incubation) Up to 60 years Long, narrow snout; ~650 adults (2023); WPA Schedule I; males have ghara (nasal bulb); nests in sandbanks; conservation via Chambal breeding program.
Indian Rock Python Near Threatened Across India, forests, wetlands Forests, marshes, rocky areas Mammals, birds, reptiles 60–80 days (incubation) 20–30 years Non-venomous constrictor; ~6m long; WPA Schedule I; coils around prey; threatened by skin trade; thermoregulates by basking.
Indian Star Tortoise Vulnerable Gujarat, Rajasthan, Andhra Pradesh Dry scrub, grasslands Grasses, fruits, flowers 90–150 days (incubation) 50–80 years Star-patterned shell; ~10,000 individuals; WPA Schedule IV; retracts into shell; poached for pet trade; drought-tolerant; conservation via breeding bans.
King Cobra Vulnerable Western Ghats, Northeast, Andaman Rainforests, bamboo thickets Other snakes, lizards 60–70 days (incubation) 20–25 years Longest venomous snake (5.5m); builds nests; WPA Schedule II; hood display when threatened; threatened by deforestation, snake charming.
Leatherback Turtle Vulnerable Bay of Bengal (Odisha, Andaman) Open ocean, nesting beaches Jellyfish, soft invertebrates 60–70 days (incubation) Up to 45 years Largest turtle (900 kg); leathery shell; ~1,000 nesting females; WPA Schedule I; migrates 10,000 km; threatened by plastic ingestion.
Marsh Crocodile (Mugger) Vulnerable Across India, wetlands, rivers Lakes, marshes, rivers Fish, birds, mammals 55–75 days (incubation) 40–60 years Medium-sized (4m); WPA Schedule I; nests in burrows; adaptable to human areas; threatened by habitat loss; conservation via crocodile farms.
Monitor Lizard (Bengal Monitor) Least Concern Across India, forests, deserts Forests, water bodies, scrub Insects, eggs, small mammals 6–8 months (incubation) 10–15 years Venomous bite; tongue-flicking scent detection; WPA Schedule II; climbs trees, swims; hunted for meat; widespread but locally threatened.
Olive Ridley Turtle Vulnerable Odisha (Gahirmatha), Tamil Nadu Ocean, nesting beaches Jellyfish, crabs, shrimp 45–60 days (incubation) Up to 40 years Arribada mass nesting (100,000 females/year); WPA Schedule I; smallest sea turtle; migrates 4,000 km; threatened by trawling; conservation via hatcheries.
Purple Frog Endangered Western Ghats (Kerala, Tamil Nadu) Moist forests, streams Termites, ants 2–3 weeks (incubation) 10–15 years Underground amphibian; discovered 2003; WPA Schedule I; breeds in monsoon streams; threatened by dams, soil erosion; balloon-like body.
Saltwater Crocodile Least Concern Sundarbans, Bhitarkanika, Andaman Estuaries, mangroves Fish, mammals, birds 80–90 days (incubation) Up to 100 years Largest reptile (7m); ~2,000 individuals; WPA Schedule I; ambushes prey; recovered via breeding; threatened by mangrove loss, human conflict.
Siamese Crocodile Critically Endangered Assam (introduced), Northeast Freshwater wetlands, rivers Fish, small mammals 60–80 days (incubation) 50–70 years Smaller crocodilian (3m); WPA Schedule I; reintroduced in India; shy, nocturnal; threatened by habitat loss; conservation via captive breeding.
Important Insects
Bengal Tiger Butterfly Endangered Western Ghats (Kerala, Tamil Nadu) Shola forests, hill slopes Nectar (lantana, milkweed) 10–14 days (egg to adult) Adult: 1–2 weeks Tiger-like stripes; indicator of forest health; migrates locally; threatened by pesticides, habitat loss; conservation via protected forests.
Great Hornbill Beetle Vulnerable Western Ghats, Northeast India Rainforests, dead wood Fungi, wood sap 3–4 months (larvae) 1–2 years Large horns for mating; decomposer; nocturnal; threatened by logging; key for nutrient cycling in forests; conservation via biodiversity parks.
Honey Bee (Apis dorsata) Least Concern Across India, forests, fields Forests, agricultural areas Nectar, pollen 3–4 weeks (egg to adult) Worker: 6 weeks Giant honey bee; pollinates 80% crops; builds large combs (1m); migratory; threatened by pesticides; vital for agriculture; conservation via beekeeping programs.
Indian Apollo Butterfly Endangered Himalayas (Uttarakhand, Sikkim) Alpine meadows, 2,000–4,000 m Nectar (sedum, saxifrage) 10–14 days (egg to adult) Adult: 1 week White wings, red spots; high-altitude specialist; migrates locally; threatened by climate change, grazing; conservation via Himalayan sanctuaries.
Kaiser-i-Hind Butterfly Near Threatened Northeast (Arunachal, Assam) Subtropical forests, 1,500–3,000 m Nectar (rhododendron) 10–14 days (egg to adult) Adult: 1–2 weeks Green wings; state butterfly of Arunachal; WPA Schedule II; flies at dawn; threatened by collection, deforestation; conservation via Namdapha NP.
Peacock Tarantula Critically Endangered Eastern Ghats (Andhra Pradesh) Scrub forests, rocky areas Insects, small vertebrates 2–3 months (egg sac) 7–10 years Blue metallic legs; burrows in soil; nocturnal hunter; <100 individuals; threatened by habitat loss, pet trade; conservation via surveys.
Red Helen Butterfly Near Threatened Northeast, Western Ghats Tropical forests, gardens Nectar (hibiscus, lantana) 10–14 days (egg to adult) Adult: 1–2 weeks Red and black wings; fast flier; WPA Schedule II; pollinator; threatened by pesticide use; conservation via butterfly parks.
Silk Moth (Antheraea assamensis) Least Concern Assam, Northeast Tropical forests, plantations Leaves (castor, som) 3–4 weeks (egg to adult) Adult: 1–2 weeks Produces muga silk; nocturnal; vital for Assam’s economy; declining due to habitat loss; conservation via sericulture programs.
Important Plants
Bamboo (various species) Least Concern Northeast, Western Ghats Forests, riverbanks N/A N/A (clonal, flowers 20–100 years) 20–100 years Fast-growing (1m/day); 125 species in India; carbon sink (30 t CO2/ha); supports livelihoods; National Bamboo Mission; threatened by overharvesting.
Cluster Bean (Guar) Least Concern Rajasthan, Haryana, Gujarat Arid, semi-arid soils N/A N/A (annual) Annual Legume crop; guar gum for industry; ~8M tonnes produced; drought-tolerant; fixes nitrogen; vital for Rajasthan’s economy; not threatened.
Lotus (Nelumbo nucifera) Least Concern Across India, wetlands Lakes, ponds N/A N/A (perennial) Perennial (10+ years) National flower; aquatic; seeds viable for centuries; supports wetland biodiversity; cultural significance; resilient to pollution.
Mangroves (Sundari - Heritiera fomes) Vulnerable (ecosystem) Sundarbans, Godavari Delta Coastal estuaries, tidal zones N/A N/A (perennial) 50–100 years Carbon sink (400 t CO2/ha); 4,000 km² in India; cyclone buffer; pneumatophores for oxygen; threatened by sea-level rise, pollution.
Pitcher Plant (Nepenthes khasiana) Endangered Meghalaya, Assam Hilly forests, 1,000–2,000 m Insects (carnivorous) N/A (perennial) 10–20 years Carnivorous; traps insects in pitchers; <1,000 individuals; CITES Appendix I; threatened by mining, tourism; conservation via Nokrek Biosphere.
Red Sanders Endangered Seshachalam Hills, Andhra Pradesh Dry deciduous forests N/A N/A (perennial) 50–100 years Red wood for dyes, medicine; CITES Appendix II; ~7,000 ha; poached for export; WPA Schedule IV; conservation via protected forests.
Sandalwood Vulnerable Western Ghats, Karnataka Dry forests, rocky slopes N/A N/A (perennial) 60–80 years Hemiparasitic; aromatic oil for perfumes; CITES Appendix II; threatened by illegal logging; WPA Schedule IV; slow-growing, culturally significant.
Shola Trees (e.g., Rhododendron) Vulnerable Western Ghats, Nilgiris Shola forests, 1,500–2,400 m N/A N/A (perennial) 50+ years Keystone species; vibrant flowers; water retention for streams; threatened by invasive species, climate change; conservation via shola restoration.
- All major soil types in India (unverified) -
Soil Type Regions/Locations Characteristics Crops Grown Other Notes
Alluvial Soil Indo-Gangetic Plains (Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal), Brahmaputra Valley (Assam), deltas of Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri Fine to coarse texture (sandy loam to silty clay); light grey/ash grey; rich in potash, phosphoric acid, lime; deficient in nitrogen, organic matter; pH 6.5–8.5; high water retention (150–200 mm/m); fertile due to annual silt deposition Rice, wheat, sugarcane, maize, pulses (lentils, chickpeas), oilseeds (mustard, groundnut), jute, cotton, tobacco, vegetables (potato, onion), fruits (mango, banana) Most extensive (46% of India, ~143 Mha); formed by river sedimentation (Himalayan rivers, peninsular deltas); Khadar (new, finer) and Bhangar (older, coarser); supports 50% of food production; challenges: waterlogging, alkalinity in over-irrigated areas; managed via crop rotation, green manuring
Arid/Desert Soil Thar Desert (Rajasthan, parts of Gujarat, Haryana, Punjab), Kutch region Sandy texture (90% sand); low organic matter (<0.5%); high soluble salts, calcium carbonate; poor water retention (50–100 mm/m); high pH 8.5–9.0; low nitrogen, phosphorus Bajra, pulses (moth bean), guar, fodder crops; wheat, cotton, mustard with irrigation Covers 4% of India (~12 Mha); formed in low rainfall (<50 cm/year); contains kankar (calcium nodules); challenges: wind erosion, salinity; managed via drip irrigation, shelterbelts; supports drought-resistant crops like guar (cluster bean)
Black Soil (Regur) Deccan Plateau (Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Tamil Nadu), Malwa, Vidarbha, Saurashtra Clayey (60–70% clay); black due to titaniferous magnetite, iron oxides; high moisture retention (200–250 mm/m); self-ploughing (cracks in dry season); low nitrogen, phosphorus; pH 6.8–8.5 Cotton, sugarcane, tobacco, millets (jowar, bajra), wheat, oilseeds (groundnut, soybean), pulses, citrus fruits, sunflower Covers 16% of India (~50 Mha); formed from weathered basalt (Deccan Traps); known as ‘black cotton soil’; retains fertility for centuries; challenges: poor drainage, low organic content; managed via contour bunding, organic fertilizers
Forest/Hill Soil Himalayan foothills (Jammu & Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim), Western/Eastern Ghats (Karnataka, Kerala, Odisha) Loamy to silty; high humus (2–5%); acidic (pH 4.5–6.5); thin topsoil, prone to erosion; variable texture due to slope/vegetation Maize, barley, wheat, temperate fruits (apple, pear, peach), tea, coffee, spices (cardamom, ginger) Covers 9% of India (~28 Mha); formed under dense forest cover; fertile but erosion-prone; challenges: landslides, deforestation; managed via terracing, agroforestry; supports plantation crops in Ghats
Karewa Soil (Loess) Kashmir Valley, Bhadarwah Valley (Jammu & Kashmir) Silty clay with boulder gravel; fossil-rich (Pliocene lacustrine deposits); well-drained; moderate fertility; pH 6.0–7.5 Saffron, almonds, apple, walnut, orchard fruits (cherry, apricot) Covers <0.5% of India (~1 Mha); formed by ancient lake sedimentation; supports Kashmir’s saffron (GI tag); challenges: limited area, frost; managed via irrigation, protected cultivation
Laterite Soil Western/Eastern Ghats (Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Odisha, Assam hills), parts of Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand Porous, leached; high iron/aluminum oxides; red/brown; acidic (pH 5.0–6.5); low humus, nitrogen, phosphorus; hardens on exposure Tea, coffee, rubber, cashew, coconut, rice, ragi, sugarcane, spices (cardamom, pepper) Covers 7% of India (~22 Mha); formed in high rainfall (2,000–4,000 mm/year); used for bricks; challenges: low fertility, leaching; managed via manuring, contour ploughing; supports plantation crops
Mountain Soil Himalayas (Jammu & Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Arunachal Pradesh), above 2,000 m Thin, rocky; high organic matter at lower altitudes; acidic (pH 5.0–6.5); low fertility due to steep slopes; skeletal with gravel Orchard fruits (apple, apricot), potatoes, barley, buckwheat; limited agriculture Covers ~3% of India (~9 Mha); formed by weathering of crystalline rocks; challenges: erosion, inaccessibility; managed via step farming, afforestation; supports pastoralism, horticulture
Peaty/Marshy Soil Coastal Kerala, Odisha, Tamil Nadu, Bihar, West Bengal (Sundarbans), Uttar Pradesh wetlands Dark, organic-rich (humus 20–40%); waterlogged; acidic (pH 4.5–6.0); high sulfur, saline in coastal areas Rice, jute, vegetables; limited due to salinity/acidity Covers 0.2% of India (~0.6 Mha); formed in waterlogged, anaerobic conditions; high fertility but saline; challenges: drainage issues, salinity; managed via reclamation, raised beds
Red Soil Eastern/Southern Deccan (Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand), parts of Northeast Sandy to loamy; red/yellow due to iron oxides; poor in nitrogen, phosphorus, lime; porous, low water retention (100–150 mm/m); pH 5.5–7.5 Millets (ragi, bajra), groundnut, cotton, pulses (lentils, chickpeas), tobacco, potato, vegetables Covers 10% of India (~31 Mha); formed from granite/gneiss weathering; improves with irrigation; challenges: low fertility, erosion; managed via tank irrigation, mulching
Saline/Alkaline Soil Coastal areas (Gujarat, West Bengal, Tamil Nadu), Indo-Gangetic plains, arid regions (Rajasthan, Haryana) High sodium salts (NaCl, Na2SO4); white crust; poor drainage; low permeability; high pH (>8.5); low organic matter Salt-tolerant crops: barley, cotton, wheat, millets, date palm; rice with amendments Covers 6.7% of India (~21 Mha); formed by evaporation, capillary action; challenges: infertility, crusting; managed via gypsum application, leaching; reclamation under PMKSY
- India's different cropping seasons and their crops (unverified) -
Cropping Season Sowing Period Harvesting Period Major Crops Minor Crops Regions and Notes
Kharif June–July (onset of monsoon) September–October (post-monsoon) Rice, maize, millets (jowar, bajra, ragi), cotton, sugarcane, groundnut, soybean, pulses (pigeon pea, moong, urad) Jute, sesame, sunflower, tobacco, guar, vegetables (okra, brinjal) Monsoon-dependent (80% rainfall June–September); grown in Indo-Gangetic Plains (UP, Bihar, Punjab), Deccan Plateau (Maharashtra, Telangana), coastal deltas (Andhra Pradesh, Odisha); rice dominates (45% of foodgrain production); challenges: erratic monsoon, flooding; supports 55% of cropped area (~125 Mha)
Rabi October–November (post-monsoon) March–April (summer onset) Wheat, barley, pulses (chickpea, lentil), mustard, rapeseed, linseed Oats, cumin, coriander, fennel, vegetables (cauliflower, cabbage, potato), peas Winter season; relies on irrigation (canals, tubewells), residual soil moisture; dominant in Punjab, Haryana, UP, Madhya Pradesh; wheat accounts for 35% of foodgrain production; challenges: water scarcity, frost in North; covers 40% of cropped area (~90 Mha)
Zaid March–April (post-Rabi) June–July (pre-Kharif) Watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, vegetables (bitter gourd, pumpkin), fodder crops Moong, summer rice, groundnut, sunflower, hybrid maize Short summer season; grown in irrigated areas (Punjab, Haryana, UP, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka); suited to alluvial, black soils; high-value crops (fruits, vegetables); covers 5% of cropped area (~10 Mha); challenges: heat stress, irrigation dependency
- List of major pollutants (unverified) -
Industry Pollutant Source Reason of Origin Contamination Medium Impact Control Measures (India Context)
Asbestos and Asbestos Products Asbestos Fibers Processing, manufacturing Friable asbestos in insulation, roofing Air Lung cancer, asbestosis, mesothelioma; 10,000 deaths/year globally Asbestos ban (2011); CPCB hazardous waste rules; wet handling to reduce dust
PM (TSPM/RPM) Grinding, cutting Dust from raw asbestos Air Respiratory issues, pneumoconiosis; soil deposition Bag filters, electrostatic precipitators (ESPs)
SO2 Processing fuels Sulfur in fuel combustion Air Acid rain, respiratory irritation Low-sulfur fuels, scrubbers
Heavy Metals (Cr, Ni) Raw material impurities Trace metals in asbestos Soil, water Carcinogenic, bioaccumulation Hazardous waste management, zero-liquid discharge (ZLD)
VOCs Adhesive use Solvent evaporation Air Ozone formation, neurological effects Vapor recovery, low-VOC adhesives
Cement Industry Heavy Metals (Cr, Ni) Raw material dust, fly ash Trace metals in limestone Air, soil, water Carcinogenic, soil infertility; bioaccumulation Hazardous waste rules 2016, ZLD
NOx High-temperature kilns Thermal NOx formation Air Ozone/smog, respiratory issues; 5% of industrial premature deaths Low-NOx burners, selective catalytic reduction (SCR)
PM (TSPM/RPM) Kiln emissions, crushing Limestone/clinker dust Air, soil Silicosis, crop yield reduction; 10% of industrial PM Bag filters, ESPs; NCAP targets for 43 polluted cities
SO2 Coal/limestone burning Sulfur in fuels/raw materials Air Acid rain, asthma; contributes to 15% urban PM Flue gas desulfurization (FGD), low-sulfur fuels
Chemical Fertilizer Industry Ammonia (NH3) Ammonia synthesis Leakage during production Air, water Eutrophication, respiratory irritation; 20% PM2.5 secondary formation Leak detection, scrubbers; CPCB standards
Fluoride Phosphoric acid production HF gas emissions Air, water Fluorosis, bone deformities; crop damage Defluoridation units, emission controls
NOx Nitric acid production Oxidation of ammonia Air Ozone, smog; lung irritation SCR, process optimization
Phosphates (PO4) Phosphogypsum waste Runoff from waste piles Water, soil Algal blooms, heavy metal leaching Phosphogypsum stacks, ZLD
PM (TSPM/RPM) Granulation, drying Urea/ammonium dust Air Respiratory issues, visibility reduction Dust extraction, cyclone separators
Chlor-Alkali Industry Chlorine (Cl2) Electrolysis of brine Gas leaks during production Air, water Airway inflammation, pulmonary edema Leak detection, scrubbers; CPCB emission norms
HCl Vapors Byproduct reactions Acid formation in processes Air Ocular, airway irritation; corrosion Neutralization systems, scrubbers
Hydrogen (H2) Electrolysis Byproduct gas release Air Explosion risk, minor health impact Ventilation, gas recovery

- Important Ramsar wetland sites in India (unverified) - - India has 93 Ramsar sites as of September 2025, the highest in Asia and third globally, covering over 1.36 million hectares. These wetlands are crucial for biodiversity, flood control, carbon sequestration, and livelihoods, but face threats like pollution, encroachment, and climate change. The list below focuses on the most important ones that are frequently in the news (e.g., recent designations, conservation efforts) or have special features (e.g., biodiversity hotspots, migratory bird havens, cultural significance). -
Name Location/State Area (ha) Special Features Highlighted Feature
Chilika Lake Odisha 116,500 Largest brackish water lagoon in Asia; supports Irrawaddy dolphins, 1M+ migratory birds (e.g., flamingos, pelicans); 150+ fish species; Ramsar since 1981 Dolphin population recovery (194 in 2024); UNESCO Biosphere Reserve
Sundarbans Mangrove Forest West Bengal 423,000 Largest mangrove forest; UNESCO World Heritage Site; Bengal tiger, saltwater crocodile habitat; absorbs 4M tonnes CO2/year; Ramsar since 1992 Tiger translocation efforts in 2025; sea-level rise threat

- All Tiger Reserves of India (unverified) - India has 58 Tiger Reserves spread across 18 states, covering approximately 82,836 km² (2.5% of India's land area). These reserves are managed under Project Tiger (launched in 1973) by the National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA). The latest addition is Madhav Tiger Reserve in Madhya Pradesh (notified March 2025). The tiger population stands at 3,682 (2022 census, with 2025 estimates projecting growth to ~4,000). Reserves have core and buffer zones for habitat protection. -

- All Elephant Reserves of India (unverified) - India has 33 Elephant Reserves spread across 14 states, covering approximately 65,000 km² (2% of India's land area). These reserves are managed under Project Elephant (launched in 1992) by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC). The elephant population is ~27,000 (2017 census, with 2025 estimates ~29,000). The latest addition is the Terai Elephant Reserve in Uttar Pradesh (notified 2023). Reserves focus on habitat protection, migration corridors, and human-elephant conflict mitigation. -

- All Mike Sites in India (unverified) - The Monitoring the Illegal Killing of Elephants (MIKE) programme is a CITES-mandated initiative launched in 2003 in South Asia to track elephant poaching trends, build enforcement capacity, and inform conservation decisions. India has 10 MIKE sites, strategically selected in high-risk elephant habitats across 6 states, covering ~20,000 km². These sites monitor carcasses, poaching incidents, and law enforcement, contributing to Project Elephant. Data from MIKE sites showed a 70% decline in poaching between 2007 and 2017, but challenges persist with ~400 elephant deaths annually (2024 data). The sites are managed by state forest departments under NTCA/MoEFCC. -

These sites, spread across 9 states and 3 union territories, are critical habitats for species like Bengal tigers, saltwater crocodiles, and migratory birds. Some are Ramsar sites, UNESCO World Heritage Sites, or part of biosphere reserves, managed under state forest departments and the MoEFCC. The total mangrove cover in India is ~4,975 km² (Forest Survey of India, 2021), with notable growth in Gujarat and Odisha (2023-2025 reports). -
