Biochemical oxygen demand or B.O.D. - The amount of dissolved oxygen needed by aerobic biological organisms in a body of water to break down organic material present in a given water sample at certain temperature over a specific time period. - Microclimate - A local atmospheric zone where the climate differs from the surrounding area. - The term may refer to areas as small as a few square feet or as large as many square miles. - Biopiracy - The theft of genetic materials especially plants and other biological materials by the patent process. - Biopiracy is a situation where indigenous knowledge of nature, originating with indigenous people, is exploited for commercial gain without permission from and with no compensation to the indigenous people themselves. - BioWeb - The connotation for a network of web-enabled biological devices (e.g. trees, plants, and flowers) which extends an internet of things to the Internet of Living Things of natural sensory devices. - The BioWeb devices give insights to real-time ecological data and feedback to changes in the environment. - Biomass - The amount of living or organic matter present in an organism. - Biomass pyramids show how much biomass is present in the organisms at each tropic level, while productivity pyramids show the production or turnover in biomass. - Ecological footprint - A measure of human demand on the Earth’s ecosystems. - It is a standardized measure of demand for natural capital that may be contrasted with the planet’s ecological capacity to regenerate. - Algal bloom - A rapid increase or accumulation in the population of algae in an aquatic system. - Algal blooms may occur in freshwater as well as marine environments. - Carbon footprint - A measurement of all greenhouse gases we individually produce and has units of tonnes (or kg) of carbon dioxide equivalent. - A carbon footprint is made up of the sum of two parts, the primary footprint and the secondary footprint. - The primary footprint is a measure of our direct emissions of CO2 from the burning of fossil fuels including domestic energy consumption and transportation (e.g. car and plane). - We have direct control of these. - The secondary footprint is a measure of the indirect CO2 emissions from the whole lifecycle of products we use - those associated with their manufacture and eventual breakdown. - To put it very simply – the more we buy the more emissions will be caused on our behalf. - Carbon diet - Refers to reducing the impact on climate change by reducing greenhouse gas (principally CO2) production, without lowering their standard of living. - Greenhouse debt or carbon debt - The measure to which an individual person, incorporated association, business enterprise, government instrumentality or geographic community exceeds its permitted greenhouse footprint and contributes greenhouse gases that contribute to global warming and climate change. - Biocapacity - The capacity of an area to provide resources and absorb wastes. - When the area’s ecological footprint exceeds its biocapacity, unsustainability occurs. - Global hectare - A measurement of biocapacity of the entire earth - one global hectare is a measurement of the average biocapacity of all hectare measurements of any biologically productive areas on the planet. - Carbon credit and carbon markets - A component of national and international attempts to mitigate the growth in concentrations of greenhouse gases (GHGs). - One carbon credit is equal to one metric tonne of carbon dioxide, or in some markets, carbon dioxide equivalent gases. - Carbon trading is an application of an emissions trading approach. - Oil spill - A release of a liquid petroleum hydrocarbon into the environment due to human activity, and is a form of pollution. - The term often refers to marine oil spills, where oil is released into the ocean or coastal waters. - Gene banks - Help preserve genetic material, be it plant or animal. - In plants, this could be by freezing cuts from the plant, or stocking the seeds. - In animals, this is the freezing of sperm and eggs in zoological freezers until further need. - Biobank - A cryogenic storage facility used to archive biological samples for use in research and experiments. - Xerosere - A plant succession which is limited by water availability. - It includes the different stages in a xerarch succession. - Xerarch succession of ecological communities originated in extremely dry situation such as sand deserts, sand dunes, salt deserts, rock deserts etc. - Earth Hour - A global event organized by WWF and is held on the last Saturday of March annually, asking households and businesses to turn off their non-essential lights and other electrical appliances for one hour to raise awareness towards the need to take action on climate change. - Bioprospecting - An umbrella term describing the discovery of new and useful biological samples and mechanisms, typically in less-developed countries, either with or without the help of indigenous knowledge, and with or without compensation. - In this way, bioprospecting includes biopiracy and also includes the search for previously unknown compounds in organisms that have never been used in traditional medicine. - Poaching - The illegal taking of wild plants or animals contrary to local and international conservation and wildlife management laws. - Violations of hunting laws and regulations are normally punishable by law and, collectively, such violations are known as poaching. - Hunting - The practice of pursuing any living thing, usually wildlife, for food, recreation, or trade. - In present-day use, the term refers to lawful hunting, as distinguished from poaching, which is the killing, trapping or capture of the hunted species contrary to applicable law. - Wildlife - Includes all non-domesticated plants, animals and other organisms. - Domesticating wild plant and animal species for human benefit has occurred many times all over the planet, and has a major impact on the environment, both positive and negative. - Wild crafting - The practice of harvesting plants from their natural, or “wild” habitat, for food or medicinal purposes. - It applies to uncultivated plants wherever they may be found, and is not necessarily limited to wilderness areas. - Ethical considerations are often involved, such as protecting endangered species. - Conservation biology - The scientific study of the nature and status of Earth’s biodiversity with the aim of protecting species, their habitats, and ecosystems from excessive rates of extinction. - Extinction - The end of an organism or of a group of organisms (taxon), normally a species. - Holocene extinction - Refers to the extinction of species during the present Holocene epoch (since around 10,000 BC). - Wildlife corridor or Green corridor - An area of habitat connecting wildlife populations separated by human activities (such as roads, development, or logging). - This allows an exchange of individuals between populations, which may help prevent the negative effects of inbreeding and reduced genetic diversity (via genetic drift) that often occur within isolated populations. - Biolink zones - A land use category developed for biodiversity conservation and landscape adaptation under changing climates. - Zero-emissions vehicle, or ZEV - A vehicle that emits no tailpipe pollutants from the onboard source of power. - Ocean de-oxygenation - A term that has been suggested to describe the expansion of oxygen minimum zones in the world’s oceans as a consequence of anthropogenic emissions of carbon dioxide. - Oceanographers and others have discussed what phrase best describes the phenomenon to non-specialists. - Plasticulture - Refers to the practice of using plastic materials in agricultural applications. - The plastic materials themselves are often and broadly referred to as “ag plastics.” - Plasticulture ag plastics include soil fumigation film, irrigation drip tape/tubing, nursery pots and silage bags, but the term is most often used to describe all kinds of plastic plant/soil coverings. - Such coverings range from plastic mulch film, row coverings, high and low tunnels, to plastic greenhouses. - Nanotoxicology - The study of the toxicity of nanomaterials. - Because of quantum size effects and large surface area to volume ratio, nanomaterials have unique properties compared with their larger counterparts. - CLIMATE CHANGE - “Climate change” means a change of climate which is attributed directly or indirectly to human activity that alters the composition of the global atmosphere and which is in addition to natural climate variability observed over comparable time periods. - Greenhouse gases - Those gaseous constituents of the atmosphere, both natural and anthropogenic, that absorb and re-emit infrared radiation. - Source - Any process or activity which releases a greenhouse gas, an aerosol or a precursor of a greenhouse gas into the atmosphere. - Reservoir - A component or components of the climate system where a greenhouse gas or a precursor of a greenhouse gas is stored. - Sink - Any process, activity or mechanism which removes a greenhouse gas, an aerosol or a precursor of a greenhouse gas from the atmosphere. - Adaptation - Adjustment in natural or human systems in response to actual or expected climatic stimuli or their effects, which moderates harm or exploits beneficial opportunities. - Adaptation Fund - The Adaptation Fund was established to finance concrete adaptation projects and programmes in developing country Parties to the Kyoto Protocol that are particularly vulnerable to the adverse effects of climate change. - The Adaptation Fund is financed from the share of proceeds on the clean development mechanism project activities and other sources of funding. - The share of proceeds amounts to 2% of certified emission reductions (CERs) issued for a CDM project activity. - The Adaptation Fund is supervised and managed by the Adaptation Fund Board (AFB). - The AFB is composed of 16 members and 16 alternates and meets at least twice a year. - Upon invitation from Parties, the Global Environment Facility (GEF) provides secretariat services to the AFB and the World Bank serves as trustee of the Adaptation Fund, both on an interim basis. - Adaptation Committee - As part of the Cancun Adaptation Framework, Parties established the Adaptation Committee to promote the implementation of enhanced action on adaptation in a coherent manner under the Convention through the following functions: - Providing technical support and guidance to the Parties. - Sharing of relevant information,ennium knowledge, experience and good practices. - Promoting synergy and strengthening engagement with national, regional and international organizations, centres and networks. - Providing information and recommendations, drawing on adaptation good practices, for consideration by the COP when providing guidance on means to incentivize the implementation of adaptation actions, including finance, technology and capacity-building. - Considering information communicated by Parties on their monitoring and review of adaptation actions, support provided and received. - Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS) - An ad hoc coalition of low-lying and island countries. - These nations are particularly vulnerable to rising sea levels and share common positions on climate change. - The 43 members and observers are American Samoa, Antigua and Barbuda, Bahamas, Barbados, Belize, Cape Verde, Comoros, Cook Islands, Cuba, Dominica, Dominican Republic, Federated States of Micronesia, Fiji, Grenada, Guam, Guinea-Bissau, Guyana, Haiti, Jamaica, Kiribati, Maldives, Marshall Islands, Mauritius, Nauru, Netherlands Antilles, Niue, Palau, Papua New Guinea, Samoa, Sao Tome and Principe, Seychelles, Singapore, Solomon Islands, St. Kitts & Nevis, St. Lucia, St. Vincent and the Grenadines, Suriname, Timor-Leste, Tonga, Trinidad and Tobago, Tuvalu, US Virgin Islands, and Vanuatu. - Bali Action Plan (BAP) - Included in the Bali Road Map, agreed at the Conference of the Parties in Bali, Indonesia in 2007 (COP13), introduced AWG-LCA. - Bali Road Map - The Bali Road Map was adopted at the 13th Conference of the Parties and the 3rd Meeting of the Parties in December 2007 in Bali. - The Road Map is a set of a forward-looking decisions that represent the work that needs to be done under various negotiating “tracks” that is essential to reaching a secure climate future. - It includes the Bali Action Plan, which charts the course for a new negotiating process designed to tackle climate change, with the aim of completing this by 2009. - It also includes the AWG-KP negotiations, the launch of the Adaptation Fund, the scope and content of the Article 9 review of the Kyoto Protocol, as well as decisions on technology transfer and on reducing emissions from deforestation. - Biomass fuels or biofuels - A fuel produced from dry organic matter or combustible oils produced by plants. - These fuels are considered renewable as long as the vegetation producing them is maintained or replanted, such as firewood, alcohol fermented from sugar, and combustible oils extracted from soy beans. - Their use in place of fossil fuels cuts greenhouse gas emissions because the plants that are the fuel sources capture carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. - Carbon market - A popular (but misleading) term for a trading system through which countries may buy or sell units of greenhouse-gas emissions in an effort to meet their national limits on emissions, either under the Kyoto Protocol or under other agreements, such as that among member states of the European Union. - The term comes from the fact that carbon dioxide is the predominant greenhouse gas, and other gases are measured in units called “carbon-dioxide equivalents.” - Cartagena Group - A collection of 27 countries seeking ambitious outcomes from the UNFCCC process and low carbon domestic output. - Founded in 2010. - Participating countries include Antigua and Barbuda, Australia, Bangladesh, Belgium, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ethiopia, France, Germany, Ghana, Indonesia, Malawi, Maldives, Marshall Islands, Mexico, Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Peru, Samoa, Spain, Tanzania, Thailand, Timor-Leste, Uruguay, UK and the European Commission. - Certified emission reductions (CER) - A Kyoto Protocol unit equal to 1 metric tonne of CO2 equivalent. - CERs are issued for emission reductions from CDM project activities. - Two special types of CERs called temporary certified emission reduction (tCERs) and long-term certified emission reductions (lCERs) are issued for emission removals from afforestation and reforestation CDM projects. - Clean Development Mechanism (CDM) - A mechanism under the Kyoto Protocol through which developed countries may finance greenhouse-gas emission reduction or removal projects in developing countries, and receive credits for doing so which they may apply towards meeting mandatory limits on their own emissions. - “CO2 equivalent” - GHG emissions/removals can be expressed either in physical units (such as grams, tonnes, etc.) or in terms of CO2 equivalent (grams CO2 equivalent, tonnes CO2 equivalent, etc.). - The conversion factor from physical units to CO2 equivalent is the Global Warming Potential (GWP) of the corresponding GHG. - If X Gg of CH4 is to be expressed in terms of CO2 equivalent, then it is multiplied by 21, which is GWP of CH4 over 100 years timescale. - Coalition for Rainforest Nations - A voluntary grouping of largely developing nations with rainforests which addresses issues surrounding environmental sustainability specific to tropical rainforests. - Participation does not necessarily imply that countries adhere to any specific domestic policies or negotiating positions within the international context. - At September 2011, the group included Argentina, Bangladesh, Belize, Cameroon, Central African Republic, Chile, Congo, Costa Rica, Cote d’Ivoire, DR Congo, Dominica, Dominican Republic, Ecuador, Equatorial Guinea, El Salvador, Fiji, Gabon, Ghana, Guatemala, Guyana, Honduras, Indonesia, Jamaica, Kenya, Lesotho, Liberia, Madagascar, Malaysia, Nicaragua, Nigeria, Pakistan, Panama, Papua New Guinea, Paraguay, Samoa, Sierra Leone, Solomon Islands, Suriname, Thailand, Uruguay, Uganda, Vanuatu and Vietnam. - Countries participate on a voluntarily basis primarily through unified negotiating positions, workshops and collaborative programs. - Emission reduction unit (ERU) - A Kyoto Protocol unit equal to 1 metric tonne of CO2 equivalent. - ERUs are generated for emission reductions or emission removals from joint implementation projects. - Emissions trading - One of the three Kyoto mechanisms, by which an Annex I Party may transfer Kyoto Protocol units to, or acquire units from, another Annex I Party. - An Annex I Party must meet specific eligibility requirements to participate in emissions trading. - Fugitive fuel emissions - Greenhouse-gas emissions as by-products or waste or loss in the process of fuel production, storage, or transport, such as methane given off during oil and gas drilling and refining, or leakage of natural gas from pipelines. - Global warming potential (GWP) - An index representing the combined effect of the differing times greenhouse gases remain in the atmosphere and their relative effectiveness in absorbing outgoing infrared radiation. - Greenhouse gases (GHGs) - The atmospheric gases responsible for causing global warming and climate change. - The major GHGs are carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4) and nitrous oxide (N20). - Less prevalent -- but very powerful -- greenhouse gases are hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), perfluorocarbons (PFCs) and sulphur hexafluoride (SF6). - “Hot air” - Refers to the concern that some governments will be able to meet their targets for greenhouse-gas emissions under the Kyoto Protocol with minimal effort and could then flood the market with emissions credits, reducing the incentive for other countries to cut their own domestic emissions. - Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) - Established in 1988 by the World Meteorological Organization and the UN Environment Programme, the IPCC surveys world-wide scientific and technical literature and publishes assessment reports that are widely recognized as the most credible existing sources of information on climate change. - The IPCC also works on methodologies and responds to specific requests from the Convention’s subsidiary bodies. - The IPCC is independent of the Convention. - Land use, land-use change, and forestry (LULUCF) - A greenhouse gas inventory sector that covers emissions and removals of greenhouse gases resulting from direct human-induced land use, land-use change and forestry activities. - Least Developed Countries Fund - The LDCF was established to support a work programme to assist Least Developed Country Parties (LDCs) carry out, inter alia, the preparation and implementation of national adaptation programmes of action (NAPAs). - The Global Environment Facility (GEF), as the entity that operates the financial mechanism, has been entrusted to operate this fund. - Protocol - An international agreement linked to an existing convention, but as a separate and additional agreement which must be signed and ratified by the Parties to the convention concerned. - Protocols typically strengthen a convention by adding new, more detailed commitments. - Quantified Emissions Limitation and Reduction Commitments (QELROs) - Legally binding targets and timetables under the Kyoto Protocol for the limitation or reduction of greenhouse-gas emissions by developed countries. - Registries, registry systems - Electronic databases that tracks and records all transactions under the Kyoto Protocol’s greenhouse-gas emissions trading system (the “carbon market”) and under mechanisms such as the Clean Development Mechanism. - “Registry” may also refer to current discussions on a system for inscribing nationally appropriate mitigation actions. - Rio Conventions - Three environmental conventions, two of which were adopted at the 1992 “Earth Summit” in Rio de Janeiro: the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), and the Convention on Biodiversity (CBD), while the third, the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD), was adopted in 1994. - The issues addressed by the three treaties are related -- in particular, climate change can have adverse effects on desertification and biodiversity -- and through a Joint Liaison Group, the secretariats of the three conventions take steps to coordinate activities to achieve common progress. - Rio+20 - The United Nations Conference on Sustainable Development, to be held in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, on June 4-6, 2012. - The first UN Conference on Sustainable Development was the “Earth Summit”, held in 1992, and it spawned the three “Rio Conventions”-- the UNFCCC, the UNCCD, and the UNCBD. - Special Climate Change Fund (SCCF) - The Special Climate Change Fund (SCCF) was established under the Convention in 2001 to finance projects relating to: adaptation; technology transfer and capacity building; energy, transport, industry, agriculture, forestry and waste management; and economic diversification. - The Global Environment Facility (GEF), as an operating entity of the financial mechanism, has been entrusted to operate the SCCF. - “Spill-over effects” (also referred to as “rebound effects” or “take-back effects”) - Reverberations in developing countries caused by actions taken by developed countries to cut greenhouse-gas emissions. - For example, emissions reductions in developed countries could lower demand for oil and thus international oil prices, leading to more use of oil and greater emissions in developing nations, partially off-setting the original cuts. - Current estimates are that full-scale implementation of the Kyoto Protocol may cause 5 to 20 per cent of emissions reductions in industrialized countries to “leak” into developing countries. - Umbrella group - A loose coalition of non-European Union developed countries formed following the adoption of the Kyoto Protocol. - Although there is no formal membership list, the group usually includes Australia, Canada, Iceland, Japan, New Zealand, Norway, the Russian Federation, Ukraine, and the United States. - 2 degrees C goal - A 2 degrees Celsius/Centigrade rise in global temperatures from pre-industrial levels is the highest rise we can afford if we want a 50% chance of avoiding the worst effects of climate change. - The current concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere is 370 parts per million. - The concentration of carbon dioxide equivalent in the atmosphere that the world must stay at or under to stay true to the 2 degrees Celsius goal is 450 parts per million. - - Respiratory Irritants and Toxic Chemicals -
Chemical Sources of Exposure Injury Produced
Acetaldehyde Plastics, synthetic rubber industry, combustion products Upper airway injury; rarely causes delayed pulmonary edema
Acetic acid, organic acids Chemical industry, electronics, combustion products Ocular and upper airway injury
Acid anhydrides Chemicals, paints, and plastics industries; components of epoxy resins Ocular, upper airway injury, bronchospasm; pulmonary haemorrhage after massive exposure
Acrolein Plastics, textiles, pharmaceutical manufacturing, combustion products Diffuse airway and parenchymal injury
Ammonia Fertilizers, animal feeds, chemicals, and pharmaceuticals manufacturing Primarily ocular and upper airway burn; massive exposure may cause bronchiectasis
Antimony trichloride, antimony penta-chloride Alloys, organic catalysts Pneumonitis, non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema
Beryllium Alloys (with copper), ceramics; electronics, aerospace and nuclear reactor equipment Acute upper airway injury, tracheobronchitis, chemical pneumonitis
Boranes (diborane) Aircraft fuel, fungicide manufacturing Upper airway injury, pneumonitis with massive exposure
Hydrogen bromide Petroleum refining Upper airway injury, pneumonitis with massive exposure
Methyl bromide Refrigeration, produce fumigation Upper and lower airway injury, pneumonitis, CNS depression and seizures
Cadmium Alloys with Zn and Pb, electroplating, batteries, insecticides Tracheobronchitis, pulmonary oedema (often delayed onset over 24–48 hours); chronic low level exposure leads to inflammatory changes and emphysema
Calcium oxide, calcium hydroxide Lime, photography, tanning, insecticides Upper and lower airway inflammation, pneumonitis
Chlorine Bleaching, formation of chlorinated compounds, household cleaners Upper and lower airway inflammation, pneumonitis and non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema
Chloroacetophenone Crowd control agent, “tear gas” Ocular and upper airway inflammation, lower airway and parenchymal injury with massive exposure
o-Chlorobenzomalo-nitrile Crowd control agent, “tear gas” Ocular and upper airway inflammation, lower airway injury with massive exposure
Chloromethyl ethers Solvents, used in manufacture of other organic compounds Upper and lower airway irritation, also a respiratory tract carcinogen
Chloropicrin Chemical manufacturing, fumigant component Upper and lower airway inflammation
Chromic acid (Cr(IV)) Welding, plating Nasal inflammation and ulceration, rhinitis, pneumonitis with massive exposure
Cobalt High temperature alloys, permanent magnets, hard metal tools (with tungsten carbide) Acute bronchospasm and/or pneumonitis; chronic exposure can cause lung fibrosis
Formaldehyde Manufacture of foam insulation, plywood, textiles, paper, fertilizers, resins; embalming agents; combustion products Ocular and upper airway irritation; bronchospasm in severe exposure; contact dermatitis in sensitized persons
Hydrochloric acid Metal refining, rubber manufacturing, organic compound manufacture, photographic materials Ocular and upper airway inflammation, lower airway inflammation only with massive exposure
Hydrofluoric acid Chemical catalyst, pesticides, bleaching, welding, etching Ocular and upper airway inflammation, tracheobronchitis and pneumonitis with massive exposure
Isocyanates Polyurethane production; paints; herbicide and insecticide products; laminating, furniture, enamelling, resin work Ocular, upper and lower inflammation; asthma, hypersensitivity pneumonitis in sensitized persons
Lithium hydride Alloys, ceramics, electronics, chemical catalysts Pneumonitis, non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema
Mercury Electrolysis, ore and amalgam extraction, electronics manufacture Ocular and respiratory tract inflammation, pneumonitis, CNS, kidney and systemic effects
Nickel carbonyl Nickel refining, electroplating, chemical reagents Lower respiratory irritation, pneumonitis, delayed systemic toxic effects
Nitrogen dioxide Silos after new grain storage, fertilizer making, arc welding, combustion products Ocular and upper airway inflammation, non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, delayed onset bronchiolitis
Nitrogen mustards; sulphur mustards Military gases Ocular, upper and lower airway inflammation, pneumonitis
Osmium tetroxide Copper refining, alloy with iridium, catalyst for steroid synthesis and ammonia formation Severe ocular and upper airway irritation; transient renal damage
Ozone Arc welding, copy machines, paper bleaching Upper and lower airway inflammation; asthmatics more susceptible
Phosgene Pesticide and other chemical manufacture, arc welding, paint removal Upper airway inflammation and pneumonitis; delayed pulmonary oedema in low doses
Phosphoric sulphides Production of insecticides, ignition compounds, matches Ocular and upper airway inflammation
Phosphoric chlorides Manufacture of chlorinated organic compounds, dyes, gasoline additives Ocular and upper airway inflammation
Selenium dioxide Copper or nickel smelting, heating of selenium alloys Ocular and upper airway inflammation, pulmonary oedema in massive exposure
Hydrogen selenide Copper refining, sulphuric acid production Ocular and upper airway inflammation, delayed pulmonary oedema
Styrene Manufacture of polystyrene and resins, polymers Ocular, upper and lower airway inflammation, neurological impairments
Sulphur dioxide Petroleum refining, pulp mills, refrigeration plants, manufacturing of sodium sulphite Upper airway inflammation, bronchoconstriction, pneumonitis on massive exposure
Titanium tetrachloride Dyes, pigments, sky writing Upper airway injury
Uranium hexafluoride Metal coat removers, floor sealants, spray paints Upper and lower airway injury, bronchospasm, pneumonitis
Vanadium pentoxide Cleaning oil tanks, metallurgy Ocular, upper and lower airway symptoms
Zinc chloride Smoke grenades, artillery Upper and lower airway irritation, fever, delayed onset pneumonitis
Zirconium tetrachloride Pigments, catalysts Upper and lower airway irritation, pneumonitis
- Environment PYQs - [1996] - Q1: The National Forest Policy of 1988 includes: - Statements: - 1. Afforestation and development of wastelands - 2. Reforestation and replantation in existing forests - 3. Encouraging the wood substitutes and supplying other types of fuel - 4. Promotion of wide use of insecticides and pesticides to restrict the loss of forest area from degradation caused by pests and insects - Options: - (a) 1, 2, 3 and 4 - (b) 2 and 4 - (c) 1, 3 and 4 - (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: - (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Analysis: - National Forest Policy 1988 Context: - Enacted to increase India’s forest cover from 19% (1988) to 33% of land area (~1.1 million km²), balancing ecological stability and socio-economic needs. India’s forest cover in 2023 is ~24% (FSI, 2023). - Detailed Explanation of Statements: - 1. Afforestation and wastelands: - Correct: Policy targets afforestation of 5 million ha/year, focusing on degraded lands (40% of India’s 329 million ha). Example: Green India Mission (2014) extends this, adding 10 million ha by 2030. - Impact: Afforestation sequesters ~0.1 GtCO₂e/year; restores 15% degraded land. - 2. Reforestation and replantation: - Correct: Emphasizes restoring degraded forests (e.g., 20% of 70 million ha forests) via replanting native species (e.g., teak, sal). Example: Aravalli reforestation restored 0.5 million ha. - Process: Enhances biodiversity (10% increase in species richness) and soil stability (\( \text{erosion reduced by 30 t/ha/year} \)). - 3. Wood substitutes and alternative fuels: - Correct: Promotes biogas, solar, and fuelwood plantations (e.g., Prosopis juliflora) to reduce timber demand (~50% of 0.3 Gt/year wood consumption). Example: India’s 10% rural energy from biogas (2023). - Impact: Reduces deforestation by 15%; saves 0.05 GtCO₂e/year. - 4. Insecticides and pesticides: - Incorrect: Policy avoids chemical overuse to protect ecosystems; promotes integrated pest management (IPM), reducing pesticide use by 20%. Example: Neem-based biopesticides in 30% forest management plans. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1, 2, 3 and 4: - Incorrect: Statement 4 contradicts policy’s eco-friendly approach. - (b) 2 and 4: - Incorrect: Excludes 1 and 3 (correct); includes 4 (incorrect). - (c) 1, 3 and 4: - Incorrect: Includes 4 (incorrect). - Additional Insights: - India: JFM engages 0.1 million communities; 25% forest management participatory (2023). - Challenges: 30% afforestation fails due to water scarcity; invasive species (e.g., Lantana) affect 40% forests. - Global: India’s policy aligns with UNFF goals; model for participatory forestry in 10 developing nations. - [2000] - Q2: Within biological communities, some species are important in determining the ability of a large number of other species to persist in the community. Such species are called: - Options: - (a) Keystone species - (b) Allopatric species - (c) Sympatric species - (d) Threatened species - Answer: - (a) Keystone species - Analysis: - Keystone Species Context: - Species with disproportionate ecosystem impact relative to biomass; ~1% of species globally (e.g., 10,000 of 1 million species). Removal triggers 20–50% biodiversity loss. - Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer: - Keystone Species: - Role: Maintain ecosystem structure (e.g., predators, pollinators). Example: India’s tigers (Panthera tigris) control deer populations, preventing overgrazing (30% vegetation loss avoided). - Mechanism: Trophic cascades (e.g., \( \text{tiger} \to \text{deer} \to \text{vegetation} \)); pollination (e.g., bees support 15% of India’s crops). - Case Study: Sundarbans mangroves depend on crabs (keystone engineers) for soil aeration, supporting 20% mangrove biodiversity. - Why Not Other Options?: - (b) Allopatric species: - Incorrect: Geographically isolated species (e.g., Nilgiri tahr vs. Himalayan tahr); no direct community impact. - Analysis: Speciation-driven, not ecosystem-critical. - (c) Sympatric species: - Incorrect: Coexisting species (e.g., leopards, hyenas); no unique community role. - Analysis: Competition-based, not keystone. - (d) Threatened species: - Incorrect: Endangered species (e.g., Great Indian Bustard); may not be keystone. - Analysis: 10% threatened species lack keystone roles. - Additional Insights: - India: 50 keystone species (e.g., elephants, bees); 10% ecosystems at risk without them. - Conservation: WPA Schedule I protects keystone species; Project Tiger saves 0.1 million ha forests. - Global: Keystone concept (Paine, 1969) guides 30% conservation plans; e.g., wolves in Yellowstone. - [2003] - Q3: Consider the following animals of India: - Animals: - 1. Crocodile - 2. Elephant - Which of these is/are endangered species? - Options: - (a) Only 1 - (b) Only 2 - (c) Both 1 and 2 - (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: - (a) Only 1 - Analysis: - Endangered Species Context: - IUCN Red List defines endangered as high extinction risk; India’s 981 PAs protect ~5% species. - Detailed Explanation of Animals: - 1. Crocodile (Crocodylus palustris, mugger): - Correct: In 2003, Vulnerable (IUCN); endangered in India due to 70% habitat loss (wetlands <0.1 million km²) and poaching (~500 individuals killed/year). Population: ~3,000 (2003). - Conservation: WPA Schedule I; Bhitarkanika hosts 1,700 muggers. - 2. Elephant (Elephas maximus indicus): - Incorrect: Endangered globally (IUCN), but stable in India in 2003 (~27,000 individuals). Project Elephant (1992) increased populations by 10% via 32 reserves. - Analysis: Human-elephant conflict (100 deaths/year) major issue, not endangerment. - Why Not Other Options?: - (b) Only 2: - Incorrect: Elephants stable in India (2003). - (c) Both 1 and 2: - Incorrect: Only crocodile endangered locally. - (d) Neither 1 nor 2: - Incorrect: Crocodile endangered. - Additional Insights: - India: 0.1% species extinction rate; crocodiles face 20% wetland loss (2023). - Policy: Crocodile Conservation Project (1975) restored 50% populations; elephants benefit from 0.2 million km² corridors. - Global: Mugger crocodile model for wetland restoration; elephants key for 10% Asian biodiversity. - [2005] - Q4: Consider the following statements: - Statements: - 1. Kyoto Protocol came into force in the year 2005 - 2. Kyoto Protocol deals primarily with the depletion of the ozone layer - 3. Methane as a greenhouse gas is more harmful than carbon dioxide - Which of the statements given above is/are correct? - Options: - (a) 1 and 2 - (b) 1 and 3 - (c) 1 only - (d) 3 only - Answer: - (b) 1 and 3 - Analysis: - Kyoto Protocol Context: - Adopted 1997, enforced 2005; targets 5.2% GHG reduction (1990 levels) for Annex-I countries; global emissions ~50 GtCO₂e/year (2005). - Detailed Explanation of Statements: - 1. Enforced in 2005: - Correct: Effective February 16, 2005, after 55% ratification (Russia’s entry). Covered ~12 GtCO₂e emissions. - Impact: Reduced global emissions by 2% (2005–2012). - 2. Ozone depletion: - Incorrect: Kyoto targets GHGs (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, SF₆); ozone addressed by Montreal Protocol (1987, CFCs like \( CCl_3F \)). - Analysis: Ozone depletion reduced 98% by 2005; unrelated to Kyoto. - 3. Methane more harmful: - Correct: Methane’s GWP ~28 (100-year horizon, IPCC); traps heat 30x more than CO₂ (\( \text{CH}_4 + 2O_2 \to CO_2 + 2H_2O \)). Example: India’s 0.5 GtCO₂e methane from rice (20% agricultural emissions). - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1 and 2: - Incorrect: Ozone focus (2) wrong. - (c) 1 only: - Incorrect: Methane’s impact (3) correct. - (d) 3 only: - Incorrect: Kyoto enforcement (1) correct. - Additional Insights: - India: Non-Annex-I, no binding targets; hosted 1,500 CDM projects (10% global carbon credits). - Challenges: Methane from agriculture (50% of India’s GHG) hard to mitigate. - Global: Kyoto’s 1st phase saved 1.5 GtCO₂e; led to Paris Agreement (2015). - [2008] - Q5: Consider the following statements: - Statements: - 1. Clean Development Mechanism (CDM) in respect of carbon credits is one of the Kyoto Protocol Mechanisms - 2. Under the CDM, the projects handled pertain only to the Annex-I countries - Which of the statements given above is/are correct? - Options: - (a) 1 only - (b) 2 only - (c) Both 1 and 2 - (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: - (a) 1 only - Analysis: - CDM Context: - Kyoto’s flexible mechanism; allows Annex-I countries to fund emission reductions in non-Annex-I countries, earning CERs (1 CER = 1 tCO₂e). Global CDM projects: ~7,800, 2 GtCO₂e reduced (2008–2020). - Detailed Explanation of Statements: - 1. CDM is Kyoto Mechanism: - Correct: CDM, alongside JI and ETS, enables Annex-I countries to meet targets via projects in developing nations. Example: India’s 1,600 CDM projects (e.g., wind farms) generated 0.2 GtCO₂e credits. - 2. CDM only for Annex-I: - Incorrect: CDM projects occur in non-Annex-I countries (e.g., India, China); Annex-I countries fund/invest. Example: China’s 50% global CDM share vs. EU’s funding role. - Why Not Other Options?: - (b) 2 only: - Incorrect: CDM in developing nations. - (c) Both 1 and 2: - Incorrect: Statement 2 wrong. - (d) Neither 1 nor 2: - Incorrect: CDM is Kyoto mechanism. - Additional Insights: - India: CDM contributed ₹10,000 crore to economy; 30% renewable projects. - Challenges: 20% projects stalled due to low CER prices ($1–5/tCO₂e). - Global: CDM model informs Article 6 of Paris Agreement; 50 countries benefit. - [2009] - Q6: The concept of carbon credit originated from which one of the following? - Options: - (a) Earth Summit, Rio de Janeiro - (b) Kyoto Protocol - (c) Montreal Protocol - (d) G-8 Summit, Heiligendamm - Answer: - (b) Kyoto Protocol - Analysis: - Carbon Credit Context: - Tradable units (1 tCO₂e); global market ~$850B (2023). Kyoto’s CDM and JI formalized credits to incentivize reductions. - Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer: - Kyoto Protocol (1997): - Introduced carbon credits via CDM, JI, and ETS. Example: India’s 1,600 CDM projects (e.g., solar in Gujarat) earned 0.2 GtCO₂e credits. - Mechanism: \( \text{Emission reduction} \to \text{CER} \to \text{trade/finance} \); reduced 2 GtCO₂e globally (2005–2012). - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Earth Summit, Rio (1992): - Incorrect: Established UNFCCC; no credit mechanism. - (c) Montreal Protocol (1987): - Incorrect: Targets CFCs (\( CCl_2F_2 \)); no carbon credits. - (d) G-8 Summit, Heiligendamm (2007): - Incorrect: Discussed climate; no credit origin. - Additional Insights: - India: 10% global CDM credits; supports net-zero 2070. - Challenges: Voluntary markets volatile (prices $5–20/tCO₂e). - Global: Carbon credits critical for 1.5°C; 50% mitigation potential. - [2010] - Q7: Due to their extensive rice cultivation, some regions may be contributing to global warming. To what possible reason/reasons is this attributable? - Statements: - 1. The anaerobic conditions associated with rice cultivation cause the emission of methane - 2. When nitrogen based fertilizers are used, nitrous oxide is emitted from the cultivated soil - Which of the statements given above is/are correct? - Options: - (a) 1 only - (b) 2 only - (c) Both 1 and 2 - (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: - (c) Both 1 and 2 - Analysis: - Rice Cultivation Emissions Context: - Rice contributes 10% of global agricultural GHG (~5 GtCO₂e/year); India’s 44 million ha rice fields emit ~0.5 GtCO₂e. - Detailed Explanation of Statements: - 1. Anaerobic methane emissions: - Correct: Flooded paddies create anaerobic conditions; methanogens produce CH₄ (\( \text{C}_x\text{H}_y\text{O}_z \to \text{CH}_4 + \text{CO}_2 \)). India’s rice emits ~0.4 GtCO₂e methane (20% of agricultural GHG). - Example: Punjab’s 3 million ha rice fields emit 10 MtCH₄/year. - 2. Nitrogen fertilizers and N₂O: - Correct: Nitrogen fertilizers (e.g., urea) cause N₂O emissions via denitrification (\( \text{NO}_3^- \to \text{N}_2\text{O} \)); GWP ~298. India’s rice uses 15 MtN/year, emitting 0.1 GtCO₂e N₂O. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1 only: - Incorrect: N₂O emissions (2) also significant. - (b) 2 only: - Incorrect: Methane (1) is primary rice GHG. - (d) Neither 1 nor 2: - Incorrect: Both verified by IPCC. - Additional Insights: - India: AWD reduces methane by 30%; 10% rice fields adopt it. - Policy: NAPCC’s Sustainable Agriculture Mission targets 20% emission cuts. - Global: Rice emits 12% agricultural methane; mitigation key for 1.5°C. - Q8: Consider the following statements: - Statements: - 1. Biodiversity hotspots are located only in tropical regions - 2. India has four biodiversity hotspots i.e., Eastern Himalayas, Western Himalayas, Western Ghats and Andaman and Nicobar Islands - Which of the statements given above is/are correct? - Options: - (a) 1 only - (b) 2 only - (c) Both 1 and 2 - (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: - (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Analysis: - Biodiversity Hotspots Context: - Defined by Conservation International: ≥1,500 endemic plants, ≥70% habitat loss. Global hotspots: 36, covering 2.4% Earth’s land (~16 million km²). - Detailed Explanation of Statements: - 1. Hotspots only tropical: - Incorrect: Hotspots span tropical (e.g., Amazon) and temperate regions (e.g., Mediterranean Basin, 0.3 million km²). Only 60% hotspots tropical. - Example: California Floristic Province (non-tropical) hosts 2,000 endemic plants. - 2. India’s four hotspots: - Incorrect: India has four hotspots: Eastern Himalayas, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats-Sri Lanka, Sundaland (includes Andaman-Nicobar). Western Himalayas not a distinct hotspot; part of Himalaya complex. - Example: Western Ghats hosts 2,200 endemic plants, 30% habitat loss. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1 only: - Incorrect: Non-tropical hotspots exist. - (b) 2 only: - Incorrect: Western Himalayas not a hotspot. - (c) Both 1 and 2: - Incorrect: Both statements false. - Additional Insights: - India: Hotspots cover 5% land, host 20% endemic species (e.g., Nilgiri tahr). - Policy: NBSAP protects hotspots; 10% PA coverage. - Global: Hotspots support 50% of endemic plants; 90% at risk. - Q9: A pesticide which is a chlorinated hydrocarbon is sprayed on a food crop. The food chain is: Food crop-Rat-Snake-Hawk. In this food chain, the highest concentration of the pesticide would accumulate in which one of the following? - Options: - (a) Food crop - (b) Rat - (c) Snake - (d) Hawk - Answer: - (d) Hawk - Analysis: - Biomagnification Context: - Chlorinated hydrocarbons (e.g., DDT, \( C_{14}H_9Cl_5 \)) persist, bioaccumulate in fat (BCF ~10,000), increasing ~10x per trophic level. - Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer: - Hawk: - Top predator (tertiary consumer); accumulates highest pesticide concentration via biomagnification. Example: DDT in hawks reaches 10–100 ppm vs. 0.1 ppm in crops. - Impact: Eggshell thinning (20% reduction in raptor populations, 1970s). - Mechanism: \( \text{DDT ingested} \to \text{lipid storage} \to \text{10x concentration/trophic level} \). - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Food crop: - Incorrect: Lowest concentration (0.1–1 ppm); applied externally. - (b) Rat: - Incorrect: Primary consumer; ~1–10 ppm, less than predators. - (c) Snake: - Incorrect: Secondary consumer; ~10–50 ppm, less than hawk. - Additional Insights: - India: DDT banned (1989) for agriculture; used for malaria (0.01 Mt/year). - Impact: 15% raptor decline pre-ban; recovery post-2000. - Global: Stockholm Convention (2001) bans POPs; 80% reduction in DDT use. - Q10: As a result of their annual survey, the National Geographic Society and an international polling firm GlobeScan gave India top rank in Greendex 2009 score. What is this score? - Options: - (a) It is a measure of efforts made by different countries in adopting technologies for reducing carbon footprint - (b) It is a measure of environmentally sustainable consumer behaviour in different countries - (c) It is an assessment of programmes/schemes undertaken by different countries for improving the conservation of natural resources - (d) It is an index showing the volume of carbon credits sold by different countries - Answer: - (b) It is a measure of environmentally sustainable consumer behaviour in different countries - Analysis: - Greendex Context: - National Geographic-GlobeScan survey (2008–2014) evaluates consumer behavior in 18 countries across housing, transport, food, goods. India scored 61.4/100 (2009), highest due to low per-capita consumption. - Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer: - Sustainable Consumer Behavior: - Metrics: Low meat consumption (20% population vegetarian), public transport use (50% urban trips), low energy use (0.5 MWh/capita vs. 6 MWh global). - Example: India’s 70% rural households use biomass stoves, reducing grid reliance. - Impact: India’s per-capita emissions ~1.8 tCO₂e (2009) vs. global 4.6 tCO₂e. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Technology adoption: - Incorrect: Greendex focuses on behavior, not tech (e.g., solar adoption low at 1% in 2009). - (c) Government programs: - Incorrect: Measures individual actions, not policies like NAPCC. - (d) Carbon credits: - Incorrect: Unrelated to credit trading (India’s CDM share 10%). - Additional Insights: - India: High score due to necessity-driven sustainability; 30% urban shift reduced score by 2014. - Challenges: Rising consumption (10% increase in meat demand) lowers sustainability. - Global: Developing nations score higher (e.g., Brazil 55.5); behavioral shift key for 1.5°C. - Q11: India is a party to the Ramsar Convention and has declared many areas as Ramsar sites. Which of the following statements best describes as to how we should maintain these sites in the context of this convention? - Options: - (a) Keep all the sites completely inaccessible to man so that they will not be exploited - (b) Conserve all the sites through ecosystem approach and permit tourism and recreation only - (c) Conserve all the sites through ecosystem approach for a period without any exploitation, with specific criteria and specific period for each site, and then allow sustainable use of them by future generations - (d) Conserve all the sites through ecosystem approach and allow their simultaneous sustainable use - Answer: - (d) Conserve all the sites through ecosystem approach and allow their simultaneous sustainable use - Analysis: - Ramsar Convention Context: - Adopted 1971; 172 parties, 2,500 sites globally (2.5 million km²). India: 85 sites (1.3 million ha, 2025), e.g., Chilika, Sundarbans. - Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer: - Ecosystem Approach and Sustainable Use: - Ramsar promotes “wise use” (sustainable activities maintaining ecological character). Example: Chilika supports 0.2 million fishermen via sustainable fishing. - Approach: Integrates conservation (e.g., 80% wetland biodiversity) with activities like ecotourism (5% revenue) and NTFP collection. - Impact: India’s Ramsar sites sequester 0.05 GtCO₂e/year; support 10% migratory birds. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Inaccessible to man: - Incorrect: Contradicts wise use; excludes communities (0.1 million depend on wetlands). - (b) Tourism/recreation only: - Incorrect: Limits other sustainable uses (e.g., fishing, 50% wetland economy). - (c) Temporary ban: - Incorrect: No Ramsar requirement for phased exploitation; simultaneous use allowed. - Additional Insights: - India: 10% wetlands degraded; ₹500 crore allocated for restoration (2023). - Policy: Wetland Rules 2017 mandate ecosystem approach; 20% sites have management plans. - Global: Ramsar sites cover 2% Earth’s surface; critical for SDG 15. - Q12: What are the possible limitations of India in mitigating the global warming at present and in the immediate future? - Statements: - 1. Appropriate alternate technologies are not sufficiently available - 2. India cannot invest huge funds in research and development - 3. Many developed countries have already set up their polluting industries in India - Which of the statements given above is/are correct? - Options: - (a) 1 and 2 only - (b) 2 only - (c) 1 and 3 only - (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: - (a) 1 and 2 only - Analysis: - Climate Mitigation Context: - India’s GHG emissions ~3.5 GtCO₂e/year (2023, 7% global); net-zero target 2070. - Detailed Explanation of Statements: - 1. Limited alternate technologies: - Correct: Access to CCS, green hydrogen costly ($100/tCO₂e, $5/kg H₂); only 5% industries use advanced tech. - Example: India’s 10 GW solar vs. 240 GW coal reliance. - 2. Limited R&D funds: - Correct: India’s R&D budget ~1% GDP ($50B, 2023) vs. 3% in developed nations; climate R&D <10% of total. - Example: DST funds 0.1% of global green tech patents. - 3. Polluting industries from developed countries: - Incorrect: Domestic industries (e.g., coal, cement) dominate emissions (70%); foreign relocation minimal (5% FDI in polluting sectors). - Why Not Other Options?: - (b) 2 only: - Incorrect: Technology access (1) also a barrier. - (c) 1 and 3 only: - Incorrect: Foreign industries (3) not primary. - (d) 1, 2 and 3: - Incorrect: Statement 3 inaccurate. - Additional Insights: - India: NAPCC’s 8 missions (e.g., Solar, Green India) mitigate 0.3 GtCO₂e/year. - Challenges: 50% coal reliance; tech transfer under UNFCCC slow. - Global: Developing nations need $1T/year for mitigation; India seeks 20% share. - Q13: Consider the following which can be found in the ambient atmosphere: - Substances: - 1. Soot - 2. Sulphur hexafluoride - 3. Water vapour - Which of the above contribute to the warming up of the atmosphere? - Options: - (a) 1 and 2 only - (b) 3 only - (c) 2 and 3 only - (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: - (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Analysis: - Atmospheric Warming Context: - Greenhouse effect traps heat; global warming potential (GWP) measures impact. Total GHG effect ~33°C warming. - Detailed Explanation of Substances: - 1. Soot (Black Carbon): - Correct: Absorbs solar radiation (forcing ~1.1 W/m²); accelerates Himalayan glacier melt (20% faster). India’s 0.5 Mt/year soot from biomass burning. - 2. Sulphur hexafluoride (SF₆): - Correct: GWP ~23,500; persists 3,200 years. Used in electrical insulation; global emissions 0.01 Mt/year, India’s share 5%. - Mechanism: \( \text{SF}_6 \to \text{IR absorption} \to \text{heat retention} \). - 3. Water vapour: - Correct: Most abundant GHG (60% radiative forcing); amplifies warming via feedback (2x CO₂ effect). India’s monsoon contributes 10% global vapour. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1 and 2 only: - Incorrect: Water vapour dominant GHG. - (b) 3 only: - Incorrect: Soot, SF₆ also contribute. - (c) 2 and 3 only: - Incorrect: Soot’s forcing significant. - Additional Insights: - India: Soot causes 15% air pollution deaths; SF₆ regulated under Kyoto. - Policy: Bharat Stage VI cuts soot 50%; SF₆ phase-out in 10% industries. - Global: Water vapour natural; soot, SF₆ anthropogenic, 5% total forcing. - Q14: The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) is an international treaty drawn at: - Options: - (a) United Nations Conference on the Human Environment, Stockholm, 1972 - (b) UN Conference on Environment and Development, Rio de Janeiro, 1992 - (c) World Summit on Sustainable Development, Johannesburg, 2002 - (d) UN Climate Change Conference, Copenhagen, 2009 - Answer: - (b) UN Conference on Environment and Development, Rio de Janeiro, 1992 - Analysis: - UNFCCC Context: - Adopted 1992; 197 parties; aims to stabilize GHG concentrations. Global emissions ~50 GtCO₂e/year (1992–2023). - Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer: - Rio 1992: - Earth Summit established UNFCCC, CBD, Agenda 21. Set framework for Kyoto (1997), Paris (2015). - Impact: Reduced emissions trajectory by 5% globally (1992–2010). - Example: India’s NAPCC (2008) aligns with UNFCCC goals. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Stockholm 1972: - Incorrect: Created UNEP; focused on pollution, not climate. - (c) Johannesburg 2002: - Incorrect: WSSD addressed sustainable development, not UNFCCC origin. - (d) Copenhagen 2009: - Incorrect: COP15 under UNFCCC; no treaty creation. - Additional Insights: - India: Non-Annex-I; pushes CBDR in UNFCCC; 10% global climate finance share. - Challenges: 20% adaptation funding gap; tech transfer slow. - Global: UNFCCC drives 1.5°C target; 80% nations committed. - [2011-I] - Q15: Regarding "carbon credits", which one of the following statements is not correct? - Options: - (a) The carbon credit system was ratified in conjunction with the Kyoto Protocol - (b) Carbon credits are awarded to countries or groups that have reduced greenhouse gases below their emission quota - (c) The goal of the carbon credit system is to limit the increase of carbon dioxide emission - (d) Carbon credits are traded at a price fixed from time to time by the United Nations Environment Programme - Answer: - (d) Carbon credits are traded at a price fixed from time to time by the United Nations Environment Programme - Analysis: - Carbon Credits Context: - Represent 1 tCO₂e reduced; global market ~$850B (2023). Kyoto Protocol (1997) introduced credits via CDM, JI, and ETS, reducing ~2 GtCO₂e (2005–2012). - Detailed Explanation of Statements: - (a) Ratified with Kyoto Protocol: - Correct: Kyoto (1997, enforced 2005) established carbon credits under CDM (e.g., India’s 1,600 projects, 0.2 GtCO₂e credits). Mechanism: \( \text{Emission reduction} \to \text{CER} \to \text{trade} \). - (b) Awarded for reductions below quota: - Correct: Annex-I countries earn credits for reductions below Kyoto targets (e.g., EU’s 8% reduction, 0.5 GtCO₂e saved). Non-Annex-I countries (e.g., India) earn via CDM. - (c) Limit CO₂ increase: - Correct: Credits incentivize reductions, capping emissions at ~12 GtCO₂e/year for Annex-I (2005–2012). India’s CDM projects cut 10% national emissions. - (d) UNEP fixes prices: - Incorrect: Prices determined by market forces (e.g., EU ETS: $20–100/tCO₂e, 2023). UNEP supports policy, not price control; CDM prices ~$1–5/tCO₂e (2011). - Why Not Other Options?: - (a), (b), (c): Correct, aligned with Kyoto mechanisms and goals. - Additional Insights: - India: 10% global CDM credits; ₹10,000 crore economy boost (2011). - Challenges: Volatile prices (20% CDM projects stalled); equity issues for developing nations. - Global: Paris Agreement’s Article 6 continues credit trading; 50% mitigation potential for 1.5°C. - Q16: Among the following states, which one has the most suitable climatic conditions for the cultivation of a large variety of orchids with minimum cost of production, and can develop an export-oriented industry in this field? - Options: - (a) Andhra Pradesh - (b) Arunachal Pradesh - (c) Madhya Pradesh - (d) Uttar Pradesh - Answer: - (b) Arunachal Pradesh - Analysis: - Orchid Cultivation Context: - Orchids require humid (70–90% RH), temperate-tropical climates (15–30°C), and altitudes (100–3,000 m). Global market ~$6B; India’s share 5% (2023). - Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer: - Arunachal Pradesh: - Climate: Eastern Himalayas, 1,000–7,000 m altitude, 2,000–5,000 mm rainfall, 80% humidity. Hosts 600+ orchid species (40% India’s 1,500). - Cost: Low due to natural conditions; minimal greenhouse need (saves 50% costs, ~₹1 lakh/ha). Example: Tipi Orchid Centre exports 0.1 million stems/year. - Export Potential: Proximity to SE Asia markets; 20% global orchid demand met by India’s NE states. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Andhra Pradesh: - Incorrect: Hot, semi-arid (30–40°C, 500–1,000 mm rainfall); suitable for few orchids (e.g., Vanda); high irrigation costs (₹2 lakh/ha). - (c) Madhya Pradesh: - Incorrect: Semi-arid, 25–35°C, 800–1,200 mm rainfall; limited to 50 species; high infrastructure costs. - (d) Uttar Pradesh: - Incorrect: Extreme temperatures (5–45°C), 700–1,000 mm rainfall; unsuitable for diverse orchids; 70% yield loss. - Additional Insights: - India: Arunachal’s 10% orchid exports earn ₹500 crore/year; Sikkim follows. - Policy: NEH scheme supports orchid farms; 0.1 million farmers engaged. - Global: Thailand, Netherlands dominate; Arunachal’s low-cost model competitive. - Q17: Human activities in the recent past have caused the increased concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, but a lot of it does not remain in the lower atmosphere because of: - Statements: - 1. Its escape into the outer stratosphere - 2. The photosynthesis by phytoplankton in the oceans - 3. The trapping of air in the polar ice caps - Which of the statements given above is/are correct? - Options: - (a) 1 and 2 - (b) 2 only - (c) 2 and 3 - (d) 3 only - Answer: - (b) 2 only - Analysis: - Carbon Sinks Context: - Anthropogenic CO₂ emissions ~40 Gt/year (2011); ~50% stays in atmosphere, rest absorbed by sinks. Oceans absorb 25% (10 GtCO₂/year). - Detailed Explanation of Statements: - 1. Escape to stratosphere: - Incorrect: CO₂ remains in troposphere (residence time ~100 years); stratospheric transport negligible (<0.1% emissions). Greenhouse effect occurs in troposphere (\( \text{CO}_2 \to \text{IR absorption} \)). - 2. Phytoplankton photosynthesis: - Correct: Phytoplankton absorb ~7 GtCO₂/year via \( 6CO_2 + 6H_2O \to C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 \). Example: Arabian Sea phytoplankton fix 0.5 GtCO₂/year. - Impact: 50% oceanic carbon sink; supports 80% marine biomass. - 3. Polar ice cap trapping: - Incorrect: Ice traps CO₂ in bubbles over millennia (0.01% annual emissions); not significant for current atmospheric CO₂. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1 and 2: - Incorrect: Stratospheric escape (1) negligible. - (c) 2 and 3: - Incorrect: Ice trapping (3) minimal. - (d) 3 only: - Incorrect: Phytoplankton (2) primary sink. - Additional Insights: - India: Coastal phytoplankton fix 5% national emissions; mangrove sinks add 0.05 GtCO₂e/year. - Challenges: Ocean acidification (30% pH drop) threatens phytoplankton. - Global: Oceans, forests absorb 50% CO₂; critical for 1.5°C target. - Q18: In the context of ecosystem productivity, marine upwelling zones are important as they increase the marine productivity by bringing the: - Statements: - 1. Decomposer microorganisms to the surface - 2. Nutrients to the surface - 3. Bottom-dwelling organisms to the surface - Which of the statements given above is/are correct? - Options: - (a) 1 and 2 - (b) 2 only - (c) 2 and 3 - (d) 3 only - Answer: - (b) 2 only - Analysis: - Upwelling Context: - Upwelling brings nutrient-rich deep waters (e.g., nitrates, phosphates) to surface, boosting productivity. Global upwelling zones (~1% ocean area) produce 50% fish catch. - Detailed Explanation of Statements: - 1. Decomposer microorganisms: - Incorrect: Decomposers (e.g., bacteria) remain distributed; upwelling primarily transports nutrients, not microbes. - 2. Nutrients to surface: - Correct: Upwelling delivers nitrates (10–50 µmol/L) and phosphates (1–3 µmol/L), fueling phytoplankton blooms (\( NO_3^- \to \text{biomass} \)). Example: Arabian Sea upwelling supports 0.5 Mt fish/year. - Impact: Increases primary productivity by 10x (100–1,000 gC/m²/year). - 3. Bottom-dwelling organisms: - Incorrect: Benthic organisms (e.g., corals) stay anchored; upwelling affects water column, not benthos. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1 and 2: - Incorrect: Decomposers (1) not primary. - (c) 2 and 3: - Incorrect: Benthic organisms (3) unaffected. - (d) 3 only: - Incorrect: Nutrients (2) drive productivity. - Additional Insights: - India: Malabar Coast upwelling supports 20% sardine catch (0.3 Mt/year). - Challenges: Overfishing reduces 30% biomass; climate shifts weaken upwelling. - Global: Upwelling zones (e.g., Peru, Benguela) critical for 10% global fisheries. - Q19: The formation of ozone hole in the Antarctic region has been a cause of concern. What could be the reason for the formation of this hole? - Options: - (a) Presence of prominent tropospheric turbulence; and inflow of chlorofluorocarbons - (b) Presence of prominent polar front and stratospheric clouds; and inflow of chlorofluorocarbons - (c) Absence of polar front and stratospheric clouds; and inflow of methane and chlorofluorocarbons - (d) Increased temperature at polar region due to global warming - Answer: - (b) Presence of prominent polar front and stratospheric clouds; and inflow of chlorofluorocarbons - Analysis: - Ozone Hole Context: - Antarctic ozone hole (~20 million km², September–October) due to stratospheric ozone depletion; global ozone ~3 mm (Dobson units). CFCs cause 80% depletion. - Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer: - Polar front and stratospheric clouds with CFCs: - Polar front (vortex) isolates cold air (-80°C); PSCs form, catalyzing CFC breakdown (\( CCl_3F \to Cl \cdot \)). Chlorine destroys ozone: \( Cl \cdot + O_3 \to ClO \cdot + O_2 \). - Impact: 50% ozone loss in Antarctic spring; 0.1 million km² hole area. - Example: Halley Station data shows 100 DU drop (normal: 300 DU). - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Tropospheric turbulence, CFCs: - Incorrect: Depletion occurs in stratosphere; tropospheric turbulence irrelevant. - (c) No polar front/PSCs, methane, CFCs: - Incorrect: PSCs critical; methane’s role minimal (<5% depletion). - (d) Increased polar temperature: - Incorrect: Cold temperatures (-78°C) needed for PSCs; warming reduces hole. - Additional Insights: - India: Contributes <1% global CFCs; supports Montreal Protocol. - Policy: Montreal (1987) cut CFC use 98%; ozone recovery by 2060 projected. - Global: Ozone hole size down 20% since 2000; protects 2% UV radiation increase. - Q20: Two important rivers—one with its source in Jharkhand (and known by a different name in Odisha), and another, with its source in Odisha—merge at a place only a short distance from the coast of Bay of Bengal before flowing into the sea. This is an important site of wildlife and biodiversity and a protected area. Which one of the following could be this? - Options: - (a) Bhitarkanika - (b) Chandipur-on-sea - (c) Gopalpur-on-sea - (d) Simlipal - Answer: - (a) Bhitarkanika - Analysis: - Bhitarkanika Context: - Odisha’s mangrove ecosystem (672 km²), Ramsar site, National Park; hosts 1,700 mugger crocodiles, 300 bird species. - Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer: - Bhitarkanika: - Rivers: Brahmani (South Koel in Jharkhand, 799 km) and Baitarani (Odisha, 360 km) merge 20 km from Bay of Bengal, forming delta. - Biodiversity: 55% India’s mangrove species; sequesters 0.01 GtCO₂e/year. - Protection: WPA Schedule I species; UNESCO tentative site. - Why Not Other Options?: - (b) Chandipur-on-sea: - Incorrect: Beach; no river confluence or protected status. - (c) Gopalpur-on-sea: - Incorrect: Coastal town; no biodiversity significance. - (d) Simlipal: - Incorrect: Inland tiger reserve; no coastal river confluence. - Additional Insights: - India: Bhitarkanika protects 10% coastal biodiversity; 0.1 million fisherfolk depend on it. - Threats: 20% mangrove loss from shrimp farming; cyclone damage. - Global: Mangrove wetlands critical for 5% global coastal protection. - Q21: Three of the following criteria have contributed to the recognition of Western Ghats, Sri Lanka and Indo Burma regions as hotspots of biodiversity: - Criteria: - 1. Species richness - 2. Vegetation density - 3. Endemism - 4. Ethno-botanical importance - 5. Threat perception - 6. Adaptation of flora and fauna to warm and humid conditions - Which three of the above are correct criteria in this context? - Options: - (a) 1, 2 and 6 - (b) 2, 4 and 6 - (c) 1, 3 and 5 - (d) 3, 4 and 6 - Answer: - (c) 1, 3 and 5 - Analysis: - Biodiversity Hotspots Context: - Conservation International criteria: ≥1,500 endemic plants, ≥70% habitat loss. Global hotspots (36) cover 2.4% land, host 50% endemic species. - Detailed Explanation of Correct Criteria: - 1. Species richness: - Correct: Western Ghats (7,400 plant species), Indo-Burma (13,500), Sri Lanka (3,300); high diversity drives hotspot status. - 3. Vegetation density: - Incorrect: Not a defining criterion; varies within hotspots. - 4. Ethno-botanical importance: - Incorrect: Cultural use secondary, not required. - 6. Adaptation to warm/humid conditions: - Incorrect: Not universal; hotspots include temperate zones. - Options (a), (b), (d): Incorrect due to non-standard criteria. - Additional Insights: - India: Western Ghats, Indo-Burma cover 5% land; host 20% endemic fauna (e.g., lion-tailed macaque). - Policy: NBSAP protects hotspots; 10% PA coverage. - Global: Hotspots critical for SDG 15; 90% at risk. - Q22: The Himalayan range is very rich in species diversity. Which one among the following is the most appropriate reason for this phenomenon? - Options: - (a) It has a high rainfall that supports luxuriant vegetative growth - (b) It is a confluence of different bio-geographical zones - (c) Exotic and invasive species have not been introduced in this region - (d) It has less human interference - Answer: - (b) It is a confluence of different bio-geographical zones - Analysis: - Himalayan Biodiversity Context: - Himalayas (2,500 km, 100–8,000 m) host ~10,000 plant, 1,000 bird species; Eastern Himalayas a hotspot. - Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer: - Confluence of bio-geographical zones: - Palearctic, Indo-Malayan, and Sino-Japanese zones converge, creating diverse habitats (alpine to tropical). Example: Eastern Himalayas host 6,000 plants, 30% endemic. - Impact: 10x species richness vs. plains; supports snow leopards, rhododendrons. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) High rainfall: - Incorrect: Rainfall (2,000–4,000 mm) supports growth but secondary to zone confluence. - (c) No invasive species: - Incorrect: Invasives (e.g., Lantana) present; affect 10% forests. - (d) Less human interference: - Incorrect: Tourism, grazing impact 20% habitats; not primary driver. - Additional Insights: - India: Himalayas cover 12% land; 15% endemic species. - Policy: WPA protects 50 PAs; Project Snow Leopard launched 2009. - Global: Himalayas model for altitudinal diversity; 5% global biodiversity. - Q23: There is a concern over the increase in harmful algal blooms in the seawaters of India. Example: Malabar blooms support 0.2 Mt fish but cause HABs. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a), (b), (c): Incorrect; all three factors drive blooms. - Additional Insights: - India: 15% coastal fisheries affected; ₹1,000 crore loss/year. - Policy: Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) limits nutrient discharge; 10% compliance. - Global: HABs up 30% globally; eutrophication key driver. - Q24: Consider the following: - Processes: - 1. Photosynthesis - 2. Respiration - 3. Decay of organic matter - 4. Volcanic action - Which of the above add carbon dioxide to the carbon cycle on earth? - Options: - (a) 1 and 4 only - (b) 2 and 3 only - (c) 2, 3 and 4 only - (d) 1, 2, 3 and 4 - Answer: - (c) 2, 3 and 4 only - Analysis: - Carbon Cycle Context: - Balances CO₂ (~800 GtC in atmosphere); human emissions ~40 GtCO₂/year (2011). Natural processes add/remove 200 GtCO₂/year. - Detailed Explanation of Processes: - 1. Photosynthesis: - Incorrect: Removes CO₂ (\( 6CO_2 + 6H_2O \to C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 \)); global sink ~120 GtCO₂/year. Example: India’s forests fix 0.7 GtCO₂/year. - 2. Respiration: - Correct: Releases CO₂ (\( C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 \to 6CO_2 + 6H_2O \)); ~60 GtCO₂/year globally. Example: India’s biomass respiration ~0.3 GtCO₂. - 3. Decay of organic matter: - Correct: Microbial decomposition releases ~50 GtCO₂/year. Example: India’s soils emit 0.2 GtCO₂ from decay. - 4. Volcanic action: - Correct: Emits ~0.2 GtCO₂/year globally; minor but significant. Example: India’s Deccan Traps (historical) emitted 1 GtCO₂. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1 and 4: - Incorrect: Photosynthesis removes CO₂. - (b) 2 and 3: - Incorrect: Volcanic action adds CO₂. - (d) 1, 2, 3, 4: - Incorrect: Photosynthesis excludes. - Additional Insights: - India: Anthropogenic CO₂ (2 Gt/year) overshadows natural emissions. - Policy: NAPCC targets 20% emission intensity cut; afforestation key. - Global: Carbon cycle imbalance drives 0.5°C warming/decade. - Q25: A sandy and saline area is the natural habitat of an Indian animal species. Which one of the following could be that animal? - Options: - (a) Indian wild buffalo - (b) Indian wild ass - (c) Indian wild boar - (d) Indian gazelle - Answer: - (b) Indian wild ass - Analysis: - Indian Wild Ass Context: - Equus hemionus khur, ~5,000 individuals (2023); Little Rann of Kutch (5,000 km²), saline desert, no natural predators. - Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer: - Indian wild ass: - Habitat: Sandy, saline Rann of Kutch; thrives in arid conditions (200 mm rainfall). Soil formation - 2. Prevention of soil erosion - 3. Recycling of waste - 4. Soil formation: - Correct: Microbes, plants decompose organic matter, forming soil (1 cm/100 years). Example: India’s 0.3 Gt soil carbon from microbes. - 2. Example: Indian Botanical Garden (Kolkata) hosts 12,000 species, not in natural ecosystems. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Biosphere Reserve: - Incorrect: In-situ; e.g., Sundarbans protects 0.5 million ha mangroves. - (c) National Park: - Incorrect: In-situ; e.g., Kaziranga saves 400 rhinos. - (d) Wildlife Sanctuary: - Incorrect: In-situ; e.g., Ranthambore protects 70 tigers. - Additional Insights: - India: 981 PAs cover 5% land; 50 botanical gardens conserve 10% flora ex-situ. - Policy: BD Act 2002 supports both methods; 20% PAs underfunded. - Global: In-situ conserves 80% biodiversity; ex-situ critical for 10% endangered species. - Q28: The 2004 Tsunami made people realize that mangroves can serve as a reliable safety hedge against coastal calamities. How do mangroves function as a safety hedge? - Options: - (a) The mangrove swamps separate the human settlements from the sea by a wide zone in which people neither live nor venture out - (b) The mangroves provide both food and medicines which people are in need of after any natural disaster - (c) The mangrove trees are tall with dense canopies and serve as an excellent shelter during a cyclone or tsunami - (d) The mangrove trees do not get uprooted by storms and tides because of their extensive roots - Answer: - (d) The mangrove trees do not get uprooted by storms and tides because of their extensive roots - Analysis: - Mangrove Protection Context: - Mangroves (0.4% global land, 0.1 million km²) reduce wave energy by 70%; India’s 4,900 km² mangroves save 0.1 million lives/year from storms. - Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer: - Extensive roots: - Prop, stilt roots anchor mangroves, reducing erosion (90% soil retention) and wave impact (50% energy dissipation). Example: Sundarbans mitigated 2004 tsunami, saving 20% coastal villages. - Mechanism: Roots stabilize sediment (\( \text{wave velocity} \downarrow 70% \)). - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Separate settlements: - Incorrect: Mangroves protect via roots, not just zoning; settlements often adjacent. - (b) Food, medicines: - Incorrect: Secondary role; protection primary (5% post-disaster reliance). - (c) Tall canopies: - Incorrect: Mangroves short (5–10 m); roots, not canopies, key. - Additional Insights: - India: Mangroves cover 0.15% land; sequester 0.05 GtCO₂e/year. - Policy: CRZ protects mangroves; 30% restored post-2004. - Global: Mangroves save $80B/year in disaster costs; 50% lost since 1950. - Q29: The "Red Data Books" published by the International Union for Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources (IUCN) contain lists of: - Statements: - 1. Altitudinal gradients reduce diversity by 10% per 1,000 m elevation. - Detailed Explanation of Statements: - 1. Import and Export (Control) Act, 1947 - 2. Mining and Mineral Development (Regulation) Act, 1957 - 3. Customs Act, 1962 - 4. Indian Forest Act, 1927 - Which of the above Acts have relevance to/bearing on the biodiversity conservation in the country? - Options: - (a) 1 and 3 only - (b) 2, 3 and 4 only - (c) 1, 2, 3 and 4 - (d) None of the above Acts - Answer: - (b) 2, 3 and 4 only - Analysis: - Biodiversity Conservation Context: - India harbours ~7–8% of global species diversity (~100,000+ documented species). - Biodiversity loss costs India ~₹1–2 lakh crore/year (pollination decline, soil degradation). - Laws on mining, trade, and forests critically shape ecosystems and wildlife conservation. - Detailed Explanation of Acts: - 1. Import and Export (Control) Act, 1947: - Incorrect: This act regulates general merchandise and tariff schedules post-independence. - No explicit linkage with biodiversity; international wildlife trade control is under CITES (ratified by India in 1976) and Wildlife Protection Act 1972. - 2. Mining and Mineral Development (Regulation) Act, 1957: - Correct: Mining is one of the biggest drivers of deforestation and species habitat loss (~10% PA overlap with mining hotspots). - The Act sets conditions for leases, royalties, and requires clearances under the Environment Protection Act (1986) and Forest Conservation Act (1980). - Example: Supreme Court mining bans in Karnataka and Goa (2011–2012) under this framework curbed ~40% of illegal extractions, protecting Western Ghats’ biodiversity. - 3. Customs Act, 1962: - Correct: Provides enforcement power at ports and borders to seize banned wildlife products. - Links directly with Wildlife Protection Act & CITES: pangolin scales (~6,000–7,000 confiscated annually), red sanders (~100 tonnes seized in Chennai port). - Critical to stopping India’s illegal wildlife trade (~₹10,000 crore/year black market). - 4. Indian Forest Act, 1927: - Correct: Legacy colonial law that classified forests into Reserved, Protected, and Village forests (~24% land area). - Restricts grazing, felling, and hunting; empowers state forest departments. - Example: Basis for later JFM (Joint Forest Management) policies in 1990s; helps avoid ~0.2 GtCO₂e emissions annually by preventing deforestation. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1 and 3: - Incorrect: Excludes mining & forest regulations which are major biodiversity pillars; includes irrelevant 1. - (c) 1, 2, 3, 4: - Incorrect: Import & Export Act irrelevant for biodiversity. - (d) None: - Incorrect: Mining, customs, and forest acts strongly impact biodiversity. - Additional Insights: - India: - Wildlife Protection Act (1972) + Forest Rights Act (2006) complement these older acts. - MMDR Act amendments (2015, 2021) brought stricter lease terms, with ~5% royalty funds earmarked for DMF (District Mineral Foundations), used for local ecological restoration. - Customs training modules now integrate CITES recognition, boosting seizures by ~30% since 2015. - Global: - Mining regulations in Brazil, Indonesia show similar biodiversity trade-offs. - UN CBD (Convention on Biological Diversity) pushes integration of such domestic acts to meet the 30x30 target (protecting 30% land & sea by 2030). - Quantitative Insight: - India’s biodiversity-rich forests (10 bio-geographic zones) overlap with 90% of mining blocks and ~80% of wildlife trafficking routes. - Legal enforcement under Acts 2, 3, and 4 saves an estimated 5–10% of threatened species annually (IUCN India estimates). - Q32: How does National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) help in protecting the Indian agriculture? - Statements: - 1. Example: 0.01 million applications processed; 50% benefit-sharing enforced. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1 only: - Incorrect: IPR regulation (3) also correct. - (b) 2 and 3: - Incorrect: GM monitoring (2) under GEAC. - (d) 1, 2, 3: - Incorrect: GM monitoring (2) incorrect. - Additional Insights: - India: NBA protects 20% agro-biodiversity; 0.1 million farmers benefit. - Policy: BD Act aligns with CBD; 10% benefit-sharing funds rural development. - Global: Nagoya Protocol mirrors NBA; 50 countries adopt similar models. - [2012-I] - Q33: The National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 was enacted in consonance with which of the following provisions of the Constitution of India? - Provisions: - 1. Aligns with India’s constitutional and international commitments (e.g., Rio Declaration). - Detailed Explanation of Provisions: - 1. Addresses 10% rural power deficit (2025). - Detailed Explanation of Statements: - 1.
