Why is this phenomenon a cause of concern? - Reasons: - 1. The growth and survival of calcareous phytoplankton will be adversely affected - 2. The growth and survival of coral reefs will be adversely affected - 3. The survival of some animals that have phytoplanktonic larvae will be adversely affected - 4. The cloud seeding and formation of clouds will be adversely affected - Which of the statements given above is/are correct? - Options: - (a) 1, 2 and 3 only - (b) 2 only - (c) 1 and 3 only - (d) 1, 2, 3 and 4 - Answer: - (a) 1, 2 and 3 only - Analysis: - Ocean Acidification Context: - CO₂ absorption forms carbonic acid (\( \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \to \text{H}_2\text{CO}_3 \to \text{H}^+ + \text{HCO}_3^- \)); pH dropped 0.1 units (30% acidity increase) since 1800s. Oceans absorb 10 GtCO₂/year. - Detailed Explanation of Reasons: - 1. Calcareous phytoplankton: - Correct: Coccolithophores’ CaCO₃ shells dissolve at pH <8.0; 20% growth decline. Example: Arabian Sea coccolithophores support 10% fish biomass. - 2. Coral reefs: - Correct: Acidification reduces CaCO₃ deposition (\( \text{Ca}^{2+} + \text{CO}_3^{2-} \to \text{CaCO}_3 \)); 30% coral loss in Andamans. Global reefs: $1T ecosystem value. - 3. Phytoplanktonic larvae: - Correct: Mollusks, crabs face 40% larval mortality at pH <7.8. Example: India’s shrimp industry (₹30,000 crore) at risk. - 4. Cloud seeding: - Incorrect: Acidification impacts marine ecosystems, not atmospheric cloud formation. - Why Not Other Options?: - (b) 2 only: - Incorrect: Phytoplankton, larvae also affected. - (c) 1 and 3: - Incorrect: Corals (2) also impacted. - (d) 1, 2, 3, 4: - Incorrect: Cloud seeding (4) irrelevant. - Additional Insights: - India: 15% coastal fisheries at risk; ₹5,000 crore loss projected. - Policy: NAPCC’s Marine Mission monitors acidification; 10% coral restoration. - Global: 50% reefs threatened by 2050; acidification key for SDG 14. - Q37: The increasing amount of carbon dioxide in the air is slowly raising the temperature of the atmosphere, because it absorbs: - Options: - (a) The water vapour of the air and retains its heat - (b) The ultraviolet part of the solar radiation - (c) All the solar radiations - (d) The infrared part of the solar radiation - Answer: - (d) The infrared part of the solar radiation - Analysis: - Greenhouse Effect Context: - CO₂ (410 ppm, 2025) absorbs infrared (IR, 4–15 μm), contributing 30% to 0.8°C warming since 1850. India’s emissions ~3.5 GtCO₂e/year. - Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer: - Infrared radiation: - CO₂ traps Earth’s outgoing IR (\( \text{CO}_2 \to \text{vibrational excitation} \)), raising temperatures. Example: 0.5 W/m² forcing from India’s CO₂. - Impact: 0.1°C/decade global warming; India’s heatwaves up 20%. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Water vapour heat: - Incorrect: CO₂ absorbs IR directly; water vapour amplifies (60% forcing). - (b) Ultraviolet radiation: - Incorrect: UV absorbed by ozone (O₃); CO₂ transparent to UV. - (c) All solar radiation: - Incorrect: CO₂ selectively absorbs IR, not visible/UV. - Additional Insights: - India: 7% global CO₂; NAPCC targets 20% emission intensity cut. - Challenges: 50% coal reliance; 0.1°C/decade regional warming. - Global: CO₂ drives 70% greenhouse effect; critical for 1.5°C target. - Q38: Consider the following protected areas: - Areas: - 1. Example: Keoladeo bans grazing; protects 400 bird species. - Impact: Preserves 80% park biodiversity; reduces 90% habitat disturbance. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Biosphere Reserves: - Incorrect: Buffer zones allow sustainable use (e.g., Nilgiri NTFP collection). - (c) Ramsar Wetlands: - Incorrect: Wise use permits fishing, agriculture (e.g., Chilika supports 0.2 million fisherfolk). - (d) Wildlife Sanctuaries: - Incorrect: Limited biomass collection allowed (e.g., Ranthambore permits grazing). - Additional Insights: - India: 106 National Parks vs. 573 sanctuaries; 5% land protected. - Policy: WPA enforces strict rules; 20% parks face encroachment. - Global: Strict PAs (IUCN Category II) cover 3% global land; India’s model rigorous. - Q40: Which of the following can be threats to the biodiversity of a geographical area? - Threats: - 1. Which one of the following is supporting service? - Options: (a) Production of food and water (b) Control of climate and disease (c) Nutrient cycling and crop pollination (d) Maintenance of diversity - Answer: (c) Nutrient cycling and crop pollination - Analysis: - Ecosystem Services Overview: - The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment (2005) classifies ecosystem services into four types: - Provisioning: Tangible products like food, water, timber. - Supporting: Foundational processes enabling other services, e.g., nutrient cycling, pollination, soil formation. - Regulating: Benefits like climate regulation, disease control, water purification. - Cultural: Non-material benefits like recreation, spiritual enrichment. - Supporting services sustain ecosystems over long periods without direct human consumption. - Key Terms: - Nutrient cycling: The process of recycling essential elements like nitrogen (\(N_2 \to NH_3\) via fixation) and carbon (\(C_6H_{12}O_6 \to 6CO_2 + 6H_2O\) via decomposition) through ecosystems. - Crop pollination: The transfer of pollen by insects (e.g., bees) to enable plant reproduction, critical for ~75% of global crops. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Production of food and water is a provisioning service, as it involves direct ecosystem products consumed by humans. - (b) Control of climate and disease is a regulating service, moderating environmental conditions. - (d) Maintenance of diversity is an outcome of ecosystem health, not a primary supporting process like nutrient cycling or pollination. - Relevant Information: - Nutrient cycling supports soil fertility, e.g., nitrogen fixation by Rhizobium bacteria in legumes. - Pollination enhances yields of crops like mustard in India. - Supporting services are critical for long-term ecosystem stability. - Q42: What is the difference between the antelopes Oryx and Chiru? - Options: (a) Oryx is adapted to live in hot and arid areas whereas Chiru is adapted to live in steppes and semi-desert areas of cold high mountains (b) Oryx is poached for its antlers whereas Chiru is poached for its musk (c) Oryx exists in western India only whereas Chiru exists in north-east India only (d) None of the statements (a), (b) and (c) given above is correct - Answer: (a) Oryx is adapted to live in hot and arid areas whereas Chiru is adapted to live in steppes and semi-desert areas of cold high mountains - Analysis: - Species Description: - Oryx: A genus of antelopes (e.g., Arabian oryx) adapted to hot, arid deserts with physiological traits like efficient water conservation (e.g., concentrated urine) and heat tolerance. - Chiru (Tibetan antelope, Pantholops hodgsonii): Found in high-altitude steppes and semi-deserts of the Tibetan Plateau (~3,000-5,000 m), adapted to cold climates with thick fur for insulation. - Key Terms: - Adaptation: Traits developed through natural selection to survive specific environmental conditions (e.g., Oryx’s ability to withstand dehydration; Chiru’s fur for cold). - Steppes: Grassland ecosystems with extreme temperatures, typical of high-altitude regions like Ladakh. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect, as Oryx is not poached for antlers (antelopes have horns, not antlers); Chiru is poached for shahtoosh (underwool), not musk (musk is from musk deer). - (c) Incorrect, as Oryx is not native to India (introduced in some regions), and Chiru is found in Ladakh (northwest), not northeast India. - (d) Incorrect, as option (a) accurately describes their habitat adaptations. - Relevant Information: - Chiru is protected under Schedule I of India’s Wildlife Protection Act, 1972, due to poaching for shahtoosh. - Oryx species, like the Arabian oryx, are conserved in arid regions globally but are not native to India. - Q43: Which of the following can be threats to the biodiversity of a geographical area? - Threats: 1. Global warming 2. Fragmentation of habitat 3. Invasion of alien species 4. Promotion of vegetarianism - Options: (a) 1, 2 and 3 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1 and 4 only (d) 1, 2, 3 and 4 - Answer: (a) 1, 2 and 3 only - Analysis: - Biodiversity Threats Overview: - Biodiversity loss occurs due to factors disrupting ecosystems, reducing species populations, or altering habitats. - Key Terms: - Global warming: Rising global temperatures due to greenhouse gas emissions (e.g., CO₂, CH₄), altering habitats (e.g., coral bleaching from ocean warming). - Habitat fragmentation: Division of ecosystems into smaller patches, reducing species’ living space and genetic diversity. - Invasion of alien species: Non-native species outcompeting native ones, disrupting ecosystems (e.g., water hyacinth in Indian wetlands). - Vegetarianism: A dietary choice reducing meat consumption, not directly linked to biodiversity loss. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Excludes global warming, which shifts habitats (e.g., Himalayan species moving to higher altitudes). - (c) Excludes fragmentation and invasion, both major biodiversity threats. - (d) Includes vegetarianism, which may reduce pressure on livestock-related deforestation but is not a direct biodiversity threat. - Relevant Information: - Global warming impacts India’s biodiversity, e.g., melting Himalayan glaciers affecting river ecosystems. - Fragmentation in the Western Ghats threatens endemic species like the lion-tailed macaque. - Alien species like Lantana camara disrupt Indian forests. - Q44: Consider the following agricultural practices: - Practices: 1. Contour bunding 2. Relay cropping 3. Zero tillage - In the context of global climate change, which of the above helps/help in carbon sequestration/storage in the soil? - Options: (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 3 only (c) 1, 2 and 3 (d) None of them - Answer: (b) 3 only - Analysis: - Carbon Sequestration Overview: - Carbon sequestration involves storing carbon in soils or biomass to mitigate climate change by reducing atmospheric CO₂. - Key Terms: - Contour bunding: Terracing slopes to reduce soil erosion and water runoff, indirectly aiding soil health but not significantly increasing carbon storage. - Relay cropping: Planting a second crop before harvesting the first, maintaining soil cover but not directly enhancing long-term carbon sequestration. - Zero tillage: Avoiding soil plowing to minimize disturbance, promoting organic matter accumulation and carbon storage (\(C_{org}\) in soil). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Contour bunding and relay cropping improve soil health but do not significantly sequester carbon compared to zero tillage. - (c) Incorrect, as only zero tillage directly enhances soil carbon storage. - (d) Incorrect, as zero tillage contributes to carbon sequestration. - Relevant Information: - Zero tillage increases soil organic carbon by 0.3-0.6 tC/ha/year, per studies. - Practices like contour bunding are used in India’s hilly regions (e.g., Northeast) to prevent erosion. - Relay cropping is common in rice-wheat systems in North India. - Q45: What would happen if phytoplankton of an ocean is completely destroyed for some reason? - Effects: 1. The ocean as a carbon sink would be adversely affected 2. The food chains in the ocean would be adversely affected 3. The density of ocean water would drastically decrease - Options: (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 2 only (c) 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (a) 1 and 2 only - Analysis: - Phytoplankton Role: - Phytoplankton are microscopic marine algae performing photosynthesis (\(6CO_2 + 6H_2O \to C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2\)), forming the base of marine food chains and acting as a major carbon sink. - Key Terms: - Carbon sink: A system absorbing more CO₂ than it releases, e.g., oceans via phytoplankton photosynthesis. - Food chain: A sequence of organisms where each is eaten by the next, starting with primary producers like phytoplankton. - Ocean density: Determined by salinity and temperature, not directly by phytoplankton. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Excludes the carbon sink impact, as phytoplankton absorb ~50% of global CO₂. - (c) Incorrect, as phytoplankton loss does not significantly affect ocean density (salinity/temperature-driven). - (d) Includes density decrease, which is not a direct consequence of phytoplankton loss. - Relevant Information: - Phytoplankton like diatoms support marine ecosystems, e.g., fish populations in the Arabian Sea. - Loss of phytoplankton would disrupt carbon sequestration, increasing atmospheric CO₂. - Q46: Vultures which used to be very common in Indian countryside some years ago are rarely seen nowadays. This is attributed to: - Options: (a) The destruction of their nesting sites by new invasive species (b) A drug used by cattle owners for treating their diseased cattle (c) Scarcity of food available to them (d) A widespread, persistent and fatal disease among them - Answer: (b) A drug used by cattle owners for treating their diseased cattle - Analysis: - Vulture Decline Overview: - India’s vulture populations (e.g., Gyps bengalensis) declined by ~99% since the 1990s due to diclofenac, a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug used in cattle. - Key Terms: - Diclofenac: A veterinary drug toxic to vultures, causing kidney failure when they feed on treated carcasses. - Biomagnification: Accumulation of toxins (like diclofenac) in higher trophic levels, affecting scavengers like vultures. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Invasive species have not significantly destroyed vulture nesting sites. - (c) Food scarcity is not the primary issue, as cattle carcasses remain abundant. - (d) No widespread disease directly affects vultures; diclofenac poisoning is the main cause. - Relevant Information: - India banned diclofenac for veterinary use in 2006, promoting meloxicam as a safer alternative. - Vulture conservation includes breeding centers in Haryana and Assam. - Q47: Due to improper/indiscriminate disposal of old and used computers or their parts, which of the following are released into the environment as e-waste? - Substances: 1. Beryllium 2. Cadmium 3. Chromium 4. Heptachlor 5. Mercury 6. Lead 7. Plutonium - Options: (a) 1, 3, 4, 6 and 7 only (b) 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6 only (c) 2, 4, 5 and 7 only (d) 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 - Answer: (b) 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6 only - Analysis: - E-Waste Overview: - E-waste from computers contains heavy metals and toxic substances, polluting soil and water when improperly disposed. - Key Terms: - Beryllium: Found in computer motherboards, toxic to lungs. - Cadmium: In batteries and circuit boards, causes kidney damage. - Chromium: Used in coatings, toxic in hexavalent form. - Heptachlor: A pesticide, not typically in e-waste. - Mercury: In LCD screens, affects nervous systems. - Lead: In solder and CRT monitors, neurotoxic. - Plutonium: A radioactive element, not used in electronics. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Includes heptachlor and plutonium, which are not e-waste components. - (c) Excludes beryllium and lead, includes heptachlor and plutonium, which are incorrect. - (d) Incorrectly includes heptachlor and plutonium. - Relevant Information: - India generates ~2 million tonnes of e-waste annually, with poor recycling infrastructure. - The E-Waste Management Rules, 2016, regulate disposal in India. - Q48: With reference to food chains in ecosystems, consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. A food chain illustrates the order in which a chain of organisms feed upon each other 2. Food chains are found within the populations of a species 3. A food chain illustrates the numbers of each organism which are eaten by others - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 1 and 2 only (c) 1, 2 and 3 (d) None - Answer: (a) 1 only - Analysis: - Food Chain Overview: - A food chain represents the linear transfer of energy and nutrients from one organism to another in an ecosystem, starting with producers and moving to consumers. - Key Terms: - Food chain: A sequence like grass → deer → tiger, showing trophic levels. - Trophic level: The position an organism occupies in a food chain (e.g., producer, primary consumer). - Why Not Others?: - (b) Statement 2 is incorrect, as food chains involve multiple species across trophic levels, not within a single species’ population. - (c) Statement 3 is incorrect, as food chains show feeding order, not population sizes or numbers eaten (food webs may illustrate interactions). - (d) Incorrect, as statement 1 is correct. - Relevant Information: - Food chains are simplified models; food webs show complex interactions. - Example: In Indian wetlands, phytoplankton → zooplankton → fish → birds. - Q49: In which of the following States is lion-tailed macaque found in its natural habitat? - States: 1. Tamil Nadu 2. Kerala 3. Karnataka 4. Andhra Pradesh - Options: (a) 1, 2 and 3 only (b) 2 only (c) 1, 3 and 4 only (d) 1, 2, 3 and 4 - Answer: (a) 1, 2 and 3 only - Analysis: - Lion-Tailed Macaque Overview: - The lion-tailed macaque (Macaca silenus) is an endangered primate endemic to the Western Ghats, living in evergreen forests. - Key Terms: - Endemic: A species native to a specific region, like the Western Ghats for the lion-tailed macaque. - Western Ghats: A biodiversity hotspot spanning Tamil Nadu, Kerala, and Karnataka, with moist deciduous and evergreen forests. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Excludes Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, where the macaque is also found. - (c) Includes Andhra Pradesh, where the Western Ghats’ range is limited, and the macaque is not naturally found. - (d) Incorrectly includes Andhra Pradesh. - Relevant Information: - Found in Silent Valley (Kerala), Anamalai Hills (Tamil Nadu), and Agumbe (Karnataka). - Protected under Schedule I of the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972. - Q50: Which one of the following terms describes not only the physical space occupied by an organism, but also its functional role in the community of organisms? - Options: (a) Ecotone (b) Ecological niche (c) Habitat (d) Home range - Answer: (b) Ecological niche - Analysis: - Ecological Concepts: - An ecological niche encompasses an organism’s habitat, resource use, interactions, and role in its ecosystem. - Key Terms: - Ecotone: A transition zone between two ecosystems (e.g., forest-grassland boundary). - Ecological niche: The role and position a species has in its environment, including diet, behavior, and interactions (e.g., a tiger’s role as a top predator). - Habitat: The physical area where an organism lives (e.g., a forest). - Home range: The area an animal uses for daily activities, not including its ecological role. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Ecotone refers to a boundary, not an organism’s role. - (c) Habitat is only the physical space, not the functional role. - (d) Home range describes movement area, not ecological interactions. - Relevant Information: - Example: The niche of bees includes pollination and nectar collection. - Niche overlap can lead to competition, affecting biodiversity. - Q51: Consider the following: - Fauna: 1. Star tortoise 2. Monitor lizard 3. Pygmy hog 4. Spider monkey - Which of the above are naturally found in India? - Options: (a) 1, 2 and 3 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1 and 4 only (d) 1, 2, 3 and 4 - Answer: (a) 1, 2 and 3 only - Analysis: - Indian Fauna: - India’s biodiversity includes unique reptiles, mammals, and other species, many endemic to specific regions. - Key Terms: - Star tortoise (Geochelone elegans): A tortoise native to India, found in dry forests and scrublands. - Monitor lizard (Varanus spp.): Reptiles like the Bengal monitor, widespread in India. - Pygmy hog (Porcula salvania): A critically endangered small mammal endemic to Assam’s grasslands. - Spider monkey: A primate native to Central and South America, not India. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Excludes star tortoise, which is native to India. - (c) Includes spider monkey, which is not found in India. - (d) Incorrectly includes spider monkey. - Relevant Information: - Pygmy hog is conserved in Manas National Park, Assam. - Star tortoise is protected under Schedule IV of the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972. - Q52: Which of the following can be found as pollutants in the drinking water in some parts of India? - Pollutants: 1. Arsenic 2. Sorbitol 3. Fluoride 4. Formaldehyde 5. Uranium - Options: (a) 1 and 3 only (b) 2, 4 and 5 only (c) 1, 3 and 5 only (d) 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 - Answer: (c) 1, 3 and 5 only - Analysis: - Water Pollution in India: - Groundwater contamination is a significant issue in India due to natural and anthropogenic sources. - Key Terms: - Arsenic: A toxic metalloid found in groundwater, causing health issues like cancer (e.g., in West Bengal). - Sorbitol: A sugar alcohol used as a sweetener, not a common water pollutant. - Fluoride: A mineral causing fluorosis at high levels, prevalent in Rajasthan and Gujarat. - Formaldehyde: A chemical used industrially, rarely a significant groundwater pollutant. - Uranium: A radioactive element found in groundwater, e.g., in Punjab, causing health risks. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Excludes uranium, a known pollutant in India. - (b) Includes sorbitol and formaldehyde, which are not typical water pollutants. - (d) Incorrectly includes sorbitol and formaldehyde. - Relevant Information: - Arsenic contamination affects ~20 million people in India, per WHO. - Fluoride mitigation includes defluoridation plants in affected states. - Q53: Consider the following pairs: - Pairs: 1. Nokrek Biosphere Reserve: Garo Hills 2. Logtak (Loktak) Lake: Barail Range 3. Namdapha National Park: Dafla Hills - Which of the above pairs is/are correctly matched? - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1, 2 and 3 (d) None - Answer: (a) 1 only - Analysis: - Protected Areas in India: - India’s biosphere reserves and national parks protect unique ecosystems and biodiversity. - Key Terms: - Nokrek Biosphere Reserve: Located in Garo Hills, Meghalaya, known for red panda and citrus diversity. - Loktak Lake: A Ramsar site in Manipur, part of the Indo-Burma hotspot, not near the Barail Range (a hill range in Assam). - Namdapha National Park: In Arunachal Pradesh, part of the Mishmi Hills, not Dafla Hills. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect, as both pairs 2 and 3 are mismatched. - (c) Incorrect, as only pair 1 is correct. - (d) Incorrect, as pair 1 is correct. - Relevant Information: - Nokrek is a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve. - Loktak Lake supports the unique floating phumdis (vegetation mats). - Q54: In the grasslands, trees do not replace the grasses as a part of an ecological succession because of: - Options: (a) Insects and fungi (b) Limited sunlight and paucity of nutrients (c) Water limits and fire (d) None of the above - Answer: (c) Water limits and fire - Analysis: - Ecological Succession: - Succession is the process of ecosystem change over time, where species composition shifts (e.g., from grass to forest). - In grasslands, succession to forests is prevented by environmental factors. - Key Terms: - Water limits: Insufficient rainfall in grasslands restricts tree growth, favoring drought-tolerant grasses. - Fire: Periodic fires, natural or human-induced, destroy tree seedlings but allow grasses to regrow from roots. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Insects and fungi may affect plants but are not primary barriers to tree succession. - (b) Grasslands have sufficient sunlight; nutrient paucity is secondary to water and fire. - (d) Incorrect, as water limits and fire are significant factors. - Relevant Information: - Indian grasslands, like the Terai, face frequent fires, maintaining grass dominance. - Water scarcity in semi-arid grasslands (e.g., Deccan) limits tree establishment. - Q55: Which one of the following is the correct sequence of ecosystems in the order of decreasing productivity? - Options: (a) Oceans, lakes, grasslands, mangroves (b) Mangroves, oceans, grasslands, lakes (c) Mangroves, grasslands, lakes, oceans (d) Oceans, mangroves, lakes, grasslands - Answer: (c) Mangroves, grasslands, lakes, oceans - Analysis: - Ecosystem Productivity: - Productivity is the rate of biomass production per unit area, measured as gC/m²/year. - Mangroves: High productivity (~2,500 gC/m²/year) due to nutrient-rich, warm coastal environments. - Grasslands: Moderate productivity (~600-1,500 gC/m²/year) due to seasonal growth. - Lakes: Lower productivity (~200-1,000 gC/m²/year) due to limited light penetration. - Oceans: Lowest productivity (~50-150 gC/m²/year) due to vast areas with low nutrient availability. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect, as oceans are less productive than lakes and mangroves. - (b) Incorrect, as mangroves are more productive than oceans. - (d) Incorrect, as oceans are the least productive. - Relevant Information: - Mangroves like Sundarbans have high biomass due to tidal nutrient inputs. - Oceanic productivity is higher in upwelling zones but low overall. - Q56: Consider the following fauna of India: - Fauna: 1. Gharial 2. Leatherback turtle 3. Swamp deer - Which of the above is/are endangered? - Options: (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 3 only (c) 1, 2 and 3 (d) None - Answer: (c) 1, 2 and 3 - Analysis: - Endangered Species: - Endangered species face a high extinction risk, per IUCN or India’s Wildlife Protection Act. - Gharial (Gavialis gangeticus): Critically Endangered, due to river pollution and habitat loss. - Leatherback turtle (Dermochelys coriacea): Vulnerable globally, endangered in India due to fishing and nesting threats. - Swamp deer (Cervus duvaucelii): Vulnerable, endangered in India due to wetland loss. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Excludes swamp deer, which is endangered in India. - (b) Excludes gharial and leatherback turtle, both endangered. - (d) Incorrect, as all three are endangered. - Relevant Information: - Gharials are protected in Chambal Sanctuary. - Leatherback turtles nest in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. - Swamp deer is conserved in Dudhwa National Park. - Q57: With reference to the food chains in ecosystems, which of the following kinds of organism is/are known as decomposer organism/organisms? - Organisms: 1. Virus 2. Fungi 3. Bacteria - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1 and 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (b) 2 and 3 only - Analysis: - Decomposers Overview: - Decomposers break down dead organic matter, recycling nutrients into ecosystems. - Key Terms: - Virus: Non-living outside hosts, not decomposers; they parasitize living cells. - Fungi: Decomposers (e.g., mushrooms) that break down organic matter via enzymes. - Bacteria: Decomposers (e.g., Bacillus) that decompose organic material, releasing nutrients like nitrogen. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Viruses do not decompose organic matter. - (c) Excludes fungi, which are key decomposers. - (d) Incorrectly includes viruses. - Relevant Information: - Fungi and bacteria drive nutrient cycling, e.g., \(C_6H_{12}O_6 \to CO_2 + H_2O\). - Example: Soil bacteria in Indian forests recycle leaf litter. - [2013-I] - Q58: Consider the following international agreements: - Agreements: 1. The International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture 2. The United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification 3. The World Heritage Convention - Which of the above has/have a bearing on the biodiversity? - Options: (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 3 only (c) 1 and 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Analysis: - Biodiversity Agreements: - International agreements protect biodiversity by addressing genetic resources, habitats, and degradation. - Key Terms: - International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources (2004): Ensures conservation and sustainable use of plant genetic resources for food security. - UN Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD, 1994): Addresses land degradation, impacting biodiversity in arid regions. - World Heritage Convention (1972): Protects sites of natural significance, including biodiversity hotspots. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Excludes World Heritage Convention, which protects biodiverse sites like Sundarbans. - (b) Excludes treaties critical for plant and habitat conservation. - (c) Excludes UNCCD, which impacts biodiversity through land management. - Relevant Information: - India is a signatory to all three agreements. - Example: Western Ghats is a World Heritage Site with rich biodiversity. - Q59: Consider the following statements regarding 'Earth Hour': - Statements: 1. It is an initiative of UNEP and UNESCO 2. It is a movement in which the participants switch off the lights for one hour on a certain day every year 3. It is a movement to raise the awareness about the climate change and the need to save the planet - Options: (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 2 only (c) 2 and 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (c) 2 and 3 only - Analysis: - Earth Hour Overview: - Earth Hour is a global movement to raise awareness about climate change by encouraging energy conservation. - Key Terms: - Earth Hour: Organized by WWF, participants switch off non-essential lights for one hour annually (last Saturday of March). - Climate change: Global environmental changes driven by greenhouse gas emissions (e.g., CO₂, CH₄). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect, as Earth Hour is a WWF initiative, not UNEP/UNESCO. - (b) Excludes statement 3, which is correct about raising awareness. - (d) Includes statement 1, which is incorrect. - Relevant Information: - Initiated in 2007 in Sydney, Earth Hour is observed in over 180 countries. - In India, landmarks like India Gate participate. - Q60: Which one of the following is the correct sequence of a food chain? - Options: (a) Diatoms-Crustaceans-Herrings (b) Crustaceans-Diatoms-Herrings (c) Diatoms-Herrings-Crustaceans (d) Crustaceans-Herrings-Diatoms - Answer: (a) Diatoms-Crustaceans-Herrings - Analysis: - Food Chain Overview: - A food chain shows energy transfer from producers to consumers in an ecosystem. - Key Terms: - Diatoms: Photosynthetic phytoplankton, primary producers in marine ecosystems (\(6CO_2 + 6H_2O \to C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2\)). - Crustaceans: Zooplankton (e.g., copepods), primary consumers feeding on phytoplankton. - Herrings: Small fish, secondary consumers eating crustaceans. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect, as crustaceans (consumers) cannot precede diatoms (producers). - (c) Incorrect, as herrings do not directly eat diatoms; crustaceans are intermediate. - (d) Incorrect, as diatoms are producers, not at the end of the chain. - Relevant Information: - Marine food chains support fisheries, e.g., in the Arabian Sea. - Diatoms contribute ~50% of oceanic primary production. - Q61: If a wetland of international importance is brought under the 'Montreux Record', what does it imply? - Options: (a) Changes in ecological character have occurred, are occurring or are likely to occur in the wetland as a result of human interference (b) The country in which the wetland is located should enact a law to prohibit any human activity within five kilometres from the edge of the wetland (c) The survival of the wetland depends on the cultural practices and traditions of certain communities living in its vicinity and therefore the cultural diversity therein should not be destroyed (d) It is given the status of 'World Heritage Site' - Answer: (a) Changes in ecological character have occurred, are occurring or are likely to occur in the wetland as a result of human interference - Analysis: - Montreux Record Overview: - The Montreux Record, under the Ramsar Convention, lists wetlands where ecological changes threaten their integrity. - Key Terms: - Ecological character: The combination of ecosystem components (e.g., flora, fauna) and processes (e.g., hydrology) defining a wetland. - Ramsar Convention: An international treaty (1971) for wetland conservation and wise use. - Why Not Others?: - (b) No specific 5-km law is mandated by the Montreux Record. - (c) Cultural practices are not the focus of the Montreux Record. - (d) Montreux Record is distinct from World Heritage status. - Relevant Information: - India’s Chilika Lake was on the Montreux Record (1993-2002) due to siltation but was removed after restoration. - The record prioritizes conservation actions for listed wetlands. - Q62: With reference to Bombay Natural History Society (BNHS), consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. It is an autonomous organization under the Ministry of Environment and Forests 2. It strives to conserve nature through action-based research, education and public awareness 3. It organizes and conducts nature trails and camps for the general public - Options: (a) 1 and 3 only (b) 2 only (c) 2 and 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (c) 2 and 3 only - Analysis: - BNHS Overview: - The Bombay Natural History Society (BNHS), founded in 1883, is a leading NGO for biodiversity conservation in India. - Key Terms: - Autonomous organization: Independent of direct government control, unlike a statutory body. - Action-based research: Scientific studies informing conservation (e.g., vulture decline studies). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Statement 1 is incorrect, as BNHS is an NGO, not under MoEF. - (b) Excludes statement 3, which is correct about BNHS’s public outreach. - (d) Includes incorrect statement 1. - Relevant Information: - BNHS publishes the Journal of the Bombay Natural History Society. - It conducts programs like the Salim Ali Nature Camps. - Q63: With reference to 'Global Environment Facility', which of the following statements is/are correct? - Options: (a) It serves as financial mechanism for 'Convention on Biological Diversity' and 'United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change' (b) It undertakes scientific research on environmental issues at global level (c) It is an agency under OECD to facilitate the transfer of technology and funds to underdeveloped countries with specific aim to protect their environment (d) Both (a) and (b) - Answer: (a) It serves as financial mechanism for 'Convention on Biological Diversity' and 'United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change' - Analysis: - GEF Overview: - The Global Environment Facility (GEF), established in 1991, funds environmental projects globally. - Key Terms: - Financial mechanism: A system providing funds for treaty implementation (e.g., CBD, UNFCCC). - CBD: Convention on Biological Diversity (1992) for biodiversity conservation. - UNFCCC: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (1992) for climate action. - Why Not Others?: - (b) GEF funds research but does not directly conduct it. - (c) GEF is a partnership, not an OECD agency. - (d) Incorrect, as statement (b) is not accurate. - Relevant Information: - GEF supports projects in India, e.g., biodiversity conservation in the Western Ghats. - It also funds the Montreal Protocol and UNCCD. - Q64: Consider the following pairs: - Pairs: 1. Dampa Tiger Reserve: Mizoram 2. Gumti Wildlife Sanctuary: Sikkim 3. Saramati Peak: Nagaland - Which of the above pairs is/are correctly matched? - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1 and 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (c) 1 and 3 only - Analysis: - Protected Areas and Geography: - India’s conservation areas and geographical features are critical for biodiversity. - Key Terms: - Dampa Tiger Reserve: Located in Mizoram, known for tigers and clouded leopards. - Gumti Wildlife Sanctuary: In Tripura, not Sikkim, hosting elephants and sambar deer. - Saramati Peak: Nagaland’s highest peak, in the Naga Hills. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Excludes pair 3, which is correct. - (b) Incorrect, as pair 2 is mismatched (Gumti is in Tripura). - (d) Includes incorrect pair 2. - Relevant Information: - Dampa is part of Project Tiger. - Saramati Peak is near the Indo-Myanmar border, a biodiversity hotspot. - Q65: With reference to a conservation organization called 'Wetlands International', which of the following statements is/are correct? - Statements: 1. It is an intergovernmental organization formed by the countries which are signatories to Ramsar Convention 2. It works at the field level to develop and mobilize knowledge, and use the practical experience to advocate for better policies - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: (b) 2 only - Analysis: - Wetlands International Overview: - Wetlands International is a global NGO focused on wetland conservation and sustainable use. - Key Terms: - Intergovernmental organization: Formed by governments via treaties, unlike NGOs. - Ramsar Convention: Promotes wetland conservation through international cooperation. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Statement 1 is incorrect, as Wetlands International is an NGO, not intergovernmental. - (c) Incorrect, as statement 1 is wrong. - (d) Excludes statement 2, which is correct about field-level work and advocacy. - Relevant Information: - Wetlands International supports India’s Ramsar sites like Chilika Lake. - It promotes wetland restoration and sustainable management. - Q66: Other than poaching, what are the possible reasons for the decline in the population of Ganges River Dolphins? - Reasons: 1. Construction of dams and barrages on rivers 2. Increase in the population of crocodiles in rivers 3. Getting trapped in fishing nets accidentally 4. Use of synthetic fertilizers and other agricultural chemicals in crop-fields in the vicinity of rivers - Options: (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1, 3 and 4 only (d) 1, 2, 3 and 4 - Answer: (c) 1, 3 and 4 only - Analysis: - Ganges River Dolphin Decline: - The Ganges River Dolphin (Platanista gangetica) is endangered due to habitat degradation. - Key Terms: - Dams and barrages: Structures fragmenting rivers, reducing dolphin habitats. - Fishing nets: Entangle dolphins, causing mortality. - Synthetic fertilizers: Runoff pollutes rivers with nitrates, affecting water quality. - Crocodile population: Not a significant threat to dolphins. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Includes crocodile increase, which is not a major factor. - (b) Excludes dams and pollution, includes incorrect crocodile factor. - (d) Incorrectly includes crocodile population. - Relevant Information: - Dolphins are protected under Schedule I of the Wildlife Protection Act. - The Ganga Action Plan addresses river pollution affecting dolphins. - Q67: Which of the following adds/add carbon dioxide to the carbon cycle on the planet Earth? - Processes: 1. Volcanic action 2. Respiration 3. Photosynthesis 4. Decay of organic matter - Options: (a) 1 and 3 only (b) 2 only (c) 1, 2 and 4 only (d) 1, 2, 3 and 4 - Answer: - (c) 1, 2 and 4 only - Analysis: - Carbon Cycle Overview: - The carbon cycle regulates Earth’s climate by moving CO₂ between atmosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere, and lithosphere. - Natural fluxes: ~210 GtC/year exchanged; Human activities add ~10 GtC/year, upsetting the balance. - Role of Each Process: - 1. Volcanic action: - Correct: Releases CO₂ stored in the mantle (~0.15–0.26 Gt/year). - Contributes to long-term carbon flux (geological time scale). - 2. Respiration: - Correct: Organisms break down glucose, releasing CO₂. - Equation: \(C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 \to 6CO_2 + 6H_2O + Energy\). - Global contribution: ~60 GtC/year recycled by plants, animals, microbes. - 3. Photosynthesis: - Incorrect: This process removes CO₂ from the atmosphere, fixing it into biomass. - Equation: \(6CO_2 + 6H_2O \to C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2\). - Net sink: ~120 GtC/year absorbed, counterbalancing respiration and decay. - 4. Decay of organic matter: - Correct: Microbial decomposition releases CO₂ (and CH₄ under anaerobic conditions). - Major recycling pathway, particularly in soils and wetlands. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1 and 3 only: - Incorrect; photosynthesis removes CO₂, not adds. - (b) 2 only: - Incorrect; ignores volcanic action and decay. - (d) 1, 2, 3 and 4: - Incorrect; wrongly includes photosynthesis. - Additional Insights: - Anthropogenic CO₂ (~10 GtC/year from fossil fuels and deforestation) dwarfs volcanic output (~0.2 GtC/year). - Decomposition and respiration maintain short-term carbon cycle balance, but deforestation reduces photosynthetic uptake. - Climate change accelerates soil respiration, potentially releasing an extra ~0.1–0.3 GtC/year by 2100. - Quantitative Insight: - Natural additions (volcanoes + respiration + decay): ~60–65 GtC/year. - Natural removals (photosynthesis): ~120 GtC/year. - Net imbalance today is due to humans, not natural cycle. - Q68: If you walk through countryside, you are likely to see some birds stalking alongside the cattle to seize the insects disturbed by their movement through grasses. Which of the following is/are such bird/birds? - Birds: 1. Painted Stork 2. Common Myna 3. Black-necked Crane - Options: (a) 1 and 2 (b) 2 only (c) 2 and 3 (d) 3 only - Answer: (b) 2 only - Analysis: - Bird Behavior: - Some birds follow grazing animals to feed on disturbed insects, a behavior called commensalism. - Key Terms: - Painted Stork: A wading bird feeding on fish in wetlands, not associated with cattle. - Common Myna: An omnivorous bird often seen near cattle, feeding on insects disturbed by grazing. - Black-necked Crane: A migratory bird in high-altitude wetlands, not associated with cattle grazing. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Painted Stork does not typically follow cattle. - (c) Black-necked Crane is not a cattle-associated species. - (d) Excludes Common Myna, which is correct. - Relevant Information: - Common Mynas are widespread in rural India, benefiting from cattle grazing. - Example: Mynas follow cattle in Punjab’s farmlands. - Q69: With reference to 'Eco-Sensitive Zones', which of the following statements is/are correct? - Statements: 1. Eco-Sensitive Zones are the areas that are declared under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 2. The purpose of the declaration of Eco-Sensitive Zones is to prohibit all kinds of human activities in those zones except agriculture - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Analysis: - Eco-Sensitive Zones Overview: - ESZs are buffer areas around protected areas to minimize human impact on ecosystems. - Key Terms: - Eco-Sensitive Zones: Declared under the Environment Protection Act, 1986, not the Wildlife Protection Act. - Purpose: Regulate activities like mining or industry, allowing sustainable practices like agriculture and eco-tourism. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect, as ESZs are under the Environment Protection Act. - (b) Incorrect, as ESZs allow regulated activities beyond agriculture. - (c) Both statements are incorrect. - Relevant Information: - ESZs extend 0-10 km around national parks, e.g., around Ranthambore. - India’s MoEFCC notifies ESZs to balance conservation and development. - Q70: Consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. Animal Welfare Board of India is established under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 2. National Tiger Conservation Authority is a statutory body 3. National Ganga River Basin Authority is chaired by the Prime Minister - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 2 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (b) 2 and 3 only - Analysis: - Conservation Bodies: - India has established bodies to protect wildlife, animals, and rivers. - Key Terms: - Animal Welfare Board of India (AWBI): Established under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960, not the Environment Protection Act. - National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA): A statutory body under the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972, overseeing Project Tiger. - National Ganga River Basin Authority (NGRBA): Chaired by the Prime Minister, created under the Environment Protection Act for Ganga conservation. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect, as AWBI is under a different act. - (c) Excludes NGRBA, which is correct. - (d) Includes incorrect statement 1. - Relevant Information: - NTCA manages 53 tiger reserves in India. - NGRBA supports the Namami Gange Programme. - Q71: Which of the following have coral reefs? - Areas: 1. Andaman and Nicobar Islands 2. Gulf of Kachchh 3. Gulf of Mannar 4. Sunderbans - Options: (a) 1, 2 and 3 only (b) 2 and 4 only (c) 1 and 3 only (d) 1, 2, 3 and 4 - Answer: (a) 1, 2 and 3 only - Analysis: - Coral Reefs Overview: - Coral reefs are calcium carbonate structures built by marine animals, thriving in warm, shallow waters. - Key Terms: - Coral reefs: Ecosystems requiring clear, warm waters (20-32°C) and low sedimentation. - Andaman and Nicobar: Hosts fringing reefs, rich in coral diversity. - Gulf of Kachchh: Supports patch reefs despite turbidity. - Gulf of Mannar: A biosphere reserve with coral reefs. - Sunderbans: Mangrove ecosystem, not suitable for corals due to high sedimentation. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Includes Sunderbans, which lacks coral reefs. - (c) Excludes Gulf of Kachchh, which has reefs. - (d) Incorrectly includes Sunderbans. - Relevant Information: - Gulf of Mannar is a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve. - Coral bleaching threatens Indian reefs due to warming oceans. - Q72: In India, the problem of soil erosion is associated with which of the following? - Factors: 1. Terrace cultivation 2. Deforestation 3. Tropical climate - Options: (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1 and 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (b) 2 and 3 only - Analysis: - Soil Erosion Overview: - Soil erosion is the loss of topsoil due to water, wind, or human activities, reducing fertility. - Key Terms: - Terrace cultivation: A method to reduce erosion by creating steps on slopes, retaining water. - Deforestation: Removal of trees, exposing soil to erosion by rain and wind. - Tropical climate: High rainfall in India’s monsoon drives water erosion. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Includes terrace cultivation, which mitigates erosion. - (c) Excludes deforestation, a major erosion cause. - (d) Incorrectly includes terrace cultivation. - Relevant Information: - Deforestation in the Western Ghats increases erosion. - India’s Soil Conservation Programmes promote contour bunding. - Q73: The most important strategy for the conservation of biodiversity together with traditional human life is the establishment of: - Options: (a) Biosphere reserves (b) Botanical gardens (c) National parks (d) Wildlife sanctuaries - Answer: (a) Biosphere reserves - Analysis: - Biodiversity Conservation: - Conservation balances biodiversity protection with human needs. - Key Terms: - Biosphere reserves: UNESCO-designated areas with core, buffer, and transition zones, promoting conservation and sustainable human activities. - Botanical gardens: Ex-situ conservation for plants, not supporting traditional human life. - National parks: Strict conservation areas prohibiting most human activities. - Wildlife sanctuaries: Protect wildlife with limited human use. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Botanical gardens are ex-situ, not supporting traditional communities. - (c) National parks restrict human activities, unlike biosphere reserves. - (d) Wildlife sanctuaries allow limited use but lack the integrated approach of biosphere reserves. - Relevant Information: - India has 18 biosphere reserves, e.g., Nilgiri, supporting tribal livelihoods. - Biosphere reserves promote sustainable practices like agroforestry. - Q74: The scientific view is that the increase in global temperature should not exceed 2 °C above pre-industrial level. If the global temperature increases beyond 3 °C above the pre-industrial level, what can be its possible impact/impacts on the world? - Impacts: 1. Terrestrial biosphere tends toward a net carbon source 2. Widespread coral mortality will occur 3. All the global wetlands will permanently disappear 4. Cultivation of cereals will not be possible anywhere in the world - Options: (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 2 only (c) 1 and 3 only (d) 1, 2, 3 and 4 - Answer: (b) 2 only - Analysis: - Climate Change Context: - A rise of >3 °C above pre-industrial levels is considered catastrophic in climate science, yet different impacts manifest at different thresholds. Here, coral ecosystems are identified as the most immediate and certain victims. - Detailed Explanation: - Impact 2: Correct - Coral mortality: - At ~1.5–2 °C, corals experience bleaching; beyond 3 °C, large-scale mortality occurs due to thermal stress and ocean acidification. - Mechanism: Warming disrupts symbiotic algae (zooxanthellae), reducing photosynthesis and starving corals. Acidification (\(CO_2 + H_2O \to H_2CO_3\)) reduces carbonate ion availability, weakening skeleton formation. - Data: IPCC AR6 projects >90% coral loss beyond 3 °C; reefs in Andaman, Nicobar, and Lakshadweep are especially vulnerable. - Impact 1: Not included here - While forests like the Amazon may flip into carbon sources, the declared answer excludes this as a certain outcome within the scope of this question. - Impact 3: Incorrect - Wetlands may shrink or degrade under higher warming, but “all permanently disappearing” is exaggerated and not supported by scientific projections. - Impact 4: Incorrect - Global cereal production faces regional declines (e.g., wheat in tropics), but not universal impossibility. Adaptation, crop relocation, and technology buffer impacts. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Includes impact 1, which is not accepted in this framing. - (c) Incorrect, as wetlands will not fully disappear. - (d) Overstates effects by including 3 and 4. - Additional Insights: - India: Coral reefs (~5,000 km²) protect ~500 coastal communities; >3 °C could erase most by 2100, disrupting fisheries (~₹10,000 crore annually). - Global: Coral reefs support ~25% of marine biodiversity and ~$375 billion in ecosystem services yearly; their collapse threatens SDG 14 (Life Below Water). - Challenges: Ocean warming is accelerating faster than terrestrial systems, making corals “early warning indicators” of climate overshoot. - Q75: Lichens, which are capable of initiating ecological succession even on a bare rock, are actually a symbiotic association of: - Options: (a) Algae and bacteria (b) Algae and fungi (c) Bacteria and fungi (d) Fungi and mosses - Answer: (b) Algae and fungi - Analysis: - Lichens Overview: - Lichens are pioneer species in ecological succession, colonizing bare surfaces. - Key Terms: - Symbiosis: A mutualistic relationship where both organisms benefit. - Lichens: Composed of fungi (providing structure) and algae/cyanobacteria (performing photosynthesis, \(6CO_2 + 6H_2O \to C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2\)). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Bacteria are not primary lichen components. - (c) Bacteria and fungi do not form lichens. - (d) Mosses are plants, not part of lichen symbiosis. - Relevant Information: - Lichens in the Himalayas initiate succession on rocks. - They are bioindicators of air quality due to pollution sensitivity. - Q76: Which of the following are some important pollutants released by steel industry in India? - Pollutants: 1. Oxides of sulphur 2. Oxides of nitrogen 3. Carbon monoxide 4. Carbon dioxide - Options: (a) 1, 3 and 4 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1 and 4 only (d) 1, 2, 3 and 4 - Answer: (d) 1, 2, 3 and 4 - Analysis: - Steel Industry Pollution: - Steel production emits gases from smelting and combustion processes. - Key Terms: - Oxides of sulphur (SOₓ): From sulfur in coal/coke, causing acid rain. - Oxides of nitrogen (NOₓ): From high-temperature combustion, contributing to smog. - Carbon monoxide (CO): From incomplete combustion in blast furnaces. - Carbon dioxide (CO₂): From carbon-based fuel use, a greenhouse gas. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Excludes NOₓ, a significant steel industry pollutant. - (b) Excludes SOₓ and CO₂, both emitted in steel production. - (c) Excludes NOₓ and CO, key pollutants. - Relevant Information: - India’s steel industry (e.g., Jamshedpur plants) is a major CO₂ emitter. - Pollution control includes scrubbers and cleaner technologies. - Q77: Every year, a monthlong ecologically important campaign/festival is held during which certain communities/tribes plant saplings of fruit-bearing trees. Which of the following are such communities/tribes? - Options: (a) Bhutia and Lepcha (b) Gond and Korku (c) Irula and Toda (d) Sahariya and Agariya - Answer: (b) Gond and Korku - Analysis: - Tribal Conservation Practices: - Some Indian tribes integrate ecological conservation with cultural practices, planting trees during festivals. - Key Terms: - Gond: A major tribe in Central India, known for planting fruit trees during festivals like Hareli. - Korku: A tribe in Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra, participating in similar tree-planting traditions. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Bhutia and Lepcha (Sikkim) focus on Buddhist cultural practices, not known for monthlong tree-planting festivals. - (c) Irula and Toda (Tamil Nadu) have other cultural practices, not specifically tree-planting campaigns. - (d) Sahariya and Agariya are not associated with such festivals. - Relevant Information: - Gond and Korku tribes plant trees like mango and mahua, supporting biodiversity. - Such practices align with India’s afforestation goals. - Q78: In India, cluster bean (Guar) is traditionally used as a vegetable or animal feed, but recently the cultivation of this has assumed significance. Which one of the following statements is correct in this context? - Options: (a) The oil extracted from seeds is used in the manufacture of biodegradable plastics (b) The gum made from its seeds is used in the extraction of shale gas (c) The leaf extract of this plant has the properties of antihistamines (d) It is a source of high quality biodiesel - Answer: (b) The gum made from its seeds is used in the extraction of shale gas - Analysis: - Guar Overview: - Cluster bean (Cyamopsis tetragonoloba) is a drought-tolerant crop grown in India, primarily in Rajasthan. - Key Terms: - Guar gum: A polysaccharide extracted from guar seeds, used as a thickening agent in hydraulic fracturing (fracking) for shale gas extraction. - Shale gas: Natural gas trapped in shale rock, extracted via fracking. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Guar seeds yield gum, not oil for plastics. - (c) No evidence supports antihistamine properties in guar leaf extract. - (d) Guar is not a significant biodiesel source; crops like jatropha are used instead. - Relevant Information: - India exports ~80% of global guar gum, boosting its economic significance. - Guar cultivation supports arid region farmers. - Q79: Which one of the following National Parks has a climate that varies from tropical to subtropical, temperate and arctic? - Options: (a) Khangchendzonga National Park (b) Nandadevi National Park (c) Neora Valley National Park (d) Namdapha National Park - Answer: (d) Namdapha National Park - Analysis: - National Park Climates: - India’s Himalayan national parks span diverse climates due to altitudinal gradients. - Key Terms: - Namdapha National Park: In Arunachal Pradesh, spans 200-4,500 m, covering tropical (lowlands), subtropical, temperate, and arctic (alpine) climates. - Khangchendzonga: In Sikkim, primarily temperate to arctic, less tropical. - Nandadevi: In Uttarakhand, temperate to arctic, limited tropical range. - Neora Valley: In West Bengal, subtropical to temperate, not arctic. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Lacks extensive tropical climate. - (b) Primarily temperate and arctic. - (c) Does not reach arctic climate. - Relevant Information: - Namdapha hosts diverse fauna like snow leopards and clouded leopards. - It is part of the Eastern Himalayas biodiversity hotspot. - [2014-I] - Q80: 'BioCarbon Fund Initiative for Sustainable Forest Landscapes' is managed by the: - Options: (a) Asian Development Bank (b) International Monetary Fund (c) United Nations Environment Programme (d) World Bank - Answer: (d) World Bank - Analysis: - Initiative Overview: - The BioCarbon Fund Initiative for Sustainable Forest Landscapes (ISFL) is a multilateral fund that promotes reducing greenhouse gas emissions from the land sector, including REDD+ (Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and Forest Degradation+), sustainable agriculture, and smarter land-use planning. - It supports large-scale programs in countries like Colombia, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Mexico, and Zambia, focusing on climate-smart land use across agriculture, forestry, and other land-use sectors. - Key Terms: - REDD+: A mechanism under the UNFCCC to incentivize developing countries to reduce emissions from deforestation and forest degradation while promoting conservation and sustainable management. - Sustainable Forest Landscapes: Integrated approaches to land management that balance carbon sequestration, biodiversity, and livelihoods. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Asian Development Bank: Incorrect, as ADB supports similar initiatives but does not manage ISFL. - (b) International Monetary Fund: Incorrect, as IMF focuses on economic stability, not environmental funds like ISFL. - (c) United Nations Environment Programme: Incorrect, as UNEP hosts related biodiversity initiatives but ISFL is World Bank-managed. - Relevant Information: - ISFL builds on the original BioCarbon Fund (launched 2004), which generated carbon credits; ISFL emphasizes jurisdictional-scale programs. - It addresses deforestation, land degradation, and climate change through private sector engagement and policy reforms. - Q81: With reference to 'Forest Carbon Partnership Facility', which of the following statements is/are correct? - Statements: 1. It is a global partnership of governments, businesses, civil society and indigenous peoples 2. It provides financial aid to universities, individual scientists and institutions involved in scientific forestry research to develop eco-friendly and climate adaptation technologies for sustainable forest management 3. It assists the countries in their 'REDD+ (Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and Forest Degradation+)' efforts by providing them with financial and technical assistance - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1 and 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (c) 1 and 3 only - Analysis: - Facility Overview: - The Forest Carbon Partnership Facility (FCPF), established in 2007 by the World Bank, supports REDD+ readiness and implementation in developing countries through its Readiness Fund and Carbon Fund. - Key Terms: - REDD+: Framework for reducing emissions from deforestation and degradation, conserving carbon stocks, sustainable forest management, and enhancing carbon stocks. - Carbon Fund: Pilots performance-based payments for verified emission reductions. - Statement Analysis: - 1. Global partnership: Correct. FCPF involves 47 participating countries, donors, civil society, and indigenous peoples. - 2. Financial aid for research: Incorrect. FCPF focuses on country-level REDD+ support, not direct aid to universities or scientists. - 3. Assistance for REDD+: Correct. Provides financial and technical help for readiness, strategy development, and emission reductions. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Excludes statement 3, which is correct. - (b) Includes incorrect statement 2, excludes correct statement 1. - (d) Includes incorrect statement 2. - Relevant Information: - FCPF has supported 47 countries, with the Carbon Fund operational since 2011 for emission reduction payments. - It collaborates with UN-REDD Programme for safeguards and capacity building. - Q82: With reference to an organization known as 'Birdlife International', which of the following statements is/are correct? - Statements: 1. It is a Global Partnership of Conservation Organizations 2. The concept of 'biodiversity hotspots' originated from this organization 3. It identifies the sites known/referred to as 'Important Bird and Biodiversity Areas' - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1 and 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (c) 1 and 3 only - Analysis: - Organization Overview: - BirdLife International is a global partnership of over 120 conservation organizations, focusing on bird conservation as indicators of biodiversity health. - Key Terms: - Biodiversity Hotspots: Areas with exceptional plant endemism and habitat loss, originally defined by Norman Myers in 1988 and 2000, with BirdLife contributing to bird data but not originating the concept. - Important Bird and Biodiversity Areas (IBAs): Globally significant sites for bird conservation, identified using standardized criteria. - Statement Analysis: - 1. Global Partnership: Correct. Comprises national partners in 120+ countries. - 2. Biodiversity Hotspots Origin: Incorrect. Concept originated with Norman Myers; BirdLife uses it but did not create it. - 3. IBAs Identification: Correct. BirdLife leads the global IBA Programme, identifying 13,000+ sites. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Excludes statement 3, which is correct. - (b) Includes incorrect statement 2, excludes correct statement 1. - (d) Includes incorrect statement 2. - Relevant Information: - IBAs cover 8% of land and 2% of sea, protecting half of bird species and much broader biodiversity. - BirdLife co-hosts the Key Biodiversity Areas (KBAs) Partnership with IUCN. - Q83: In India, in which one of the following types of forests is teak a dominant tree species? - Options: (a) Tropical moist deciduous forest (b) Tropical rain forest (c) Tropical thorn scrub forest (d) Temperate forest with grasslands - Answer: (a) Tropical moist deciduous forest - Analysis: - Forest Types Overview: - India's forests are classified by Champion and Seth based on climate, rainfall, and vegetation. - Key Terms: - Tropical Moist Deciduous Forest: Receives 100-200 cm annual rainfall; sheds leaves in dry season; dominant species include teak (Tectona grandis), sal, and bamboo. - Teak: A valuable timber tree, native to India, thriving in moist deciduous areas with well-drained soils. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Tropical Rain Forest: Evergreen, high rainfall (>200 cm); dominated by rosewood, ebony, not teak. - (c) Tropical Thorn Scrub Forest: Arid, low rainfall (<70 cm); acacia, prosopis dominant, not teak. - (d) Temperate Forest with Grasslands: Cooler climates; conifers like pine, oak dominant, not teak. - Relevant Information: - Major teak forests in Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Karnataka; India produces ~50% of global teak. - Teak is used for furniture, shipbuilding; protected under Forest Conservation Act. - Q84: Which one of the following is the best description of the term 'ecosystem'? - Options: (a) A community of organisms interacting with one another (b) That part of the Earth which is inhabited by living organisms (c) A community of organisms together with the environment in which they live (d) The flora and fauna of a geographical area - Answer: (c) A community of organisms together with the environment in which they live - Analysis: - Ecosystem Concept: - An ecosystem is a dynamic complex of biotic (living) and abiotic (non-living) components interacting through energy flows and nutrient cycles. - Key Terms: - Biotic Components: Producers (plants), consumers (animals), decomposers (bacteria, fungi). - Abiotic Components: Soil, water, climate, minerals. - Interactions: Food chains, nutrient cycling (e.g., nitrogen cycle: \(N_2 \to NH_3 \to NO_3^-\)). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Focuses only on biotic interactions, ignoring abiotic factors. - (b) Describes biosphere, not a specific ecosystem. - (d) Refers to biota in a region, excluding environmental interactions. - Relevant Information: - Ecosystems range from small (pond) to large (forest); India's Sundarbans is a mangrove ecosystem. - Human impacts like pollution disrupt ecosystem balance. - Q85: Which of the following National Parks is unique in being a swamp with floating vegetation that supports a rich biodiversity? - Options: (a) Bhitarkanika National Park (b) Keibul Lamjao National Park (c) Keoladeo Ghana National Park (d) Sultanpur National Park - Answer: (b) Keibul Lamjao National Park - Analysis: - Park Overview: - Keibul Lamjao National Park, in Manipur, is a freshwater swamp on Loktak Lake, the largest freshwater lake in Northeast India. - Key Terms: - Phumdis: Floating masses of vegetation (islands) formed by organic debris and reeds, unique to Loktak Lake, supporting endemic species. - Biodiversity Hotspot: Hosts the endangered Sangai deer (Rucervus eldii eldii), adapted to phumdis. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Bhitarkanika: Mangrove ecosystem, not swamp with floating vegetation. - (c) Keoladeo: Wetland for birds, but not characterized by floating vegetation swamps. - (d) Sultanpur: Migratory bird sanctuary, grassland-wetland, not swamp. - Relevant Information: - UNESCO Ramsar site; phumdis cover 40 sq km, threatened by hydropower projects. - Supports otters, fishing cats, and over 200 bird species. - Q86: With reference to the International Union for Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources (IUCN) and the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), which of the following statements is/are correct? - Statements: 1. IUCN is an organ of the United Nations and CITES is an international agreement between governments 2. IUCN runs thousands of field projects around the world to better manage natural environments 3. CITES is legally binding on the States that have joined it, but this Convention does not take the place of national laws - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1 and 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (b) 2 and 3 only - Analysis: - Organizations Overview: - IUCN: A global union of governments and NGOs for nature conservation, founded 1948. - CITES: International treaty (1973) regulating trade in endangered species. - Key Terms: - IUCN Red List: Assesses species extinction risk. - CITES Appendices: I (banned trade), II (regulated), III (monitored). - Statement Analysis: - 1. IUCN as UN organ: Incorrect. IUCN is independent, collaborates with UN but not an organ. - 2. Field Projects: Correct. IUCN implements 1,000+ projects for conservation. - 3. CITES Binding: Correct. Legally binding on parties, complements national laws. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Includes incorrect statement 1. - (c) Includes incorrect statement 1. - (d) Includes incorrect statement 1. - Relevant Information: - 181 CITES parties; IUCN has 1,400+ members. - India: CITES member since 1976; IUCN assesses Indian species like tiger (Endangered). - Q87: With reference to 'dugong', a mammal found in India, which of the following statements is/are correct? - Statements: 1. It is a herbivorous marine animal 2. It is found along the entire coast of India 3. It is given legal protection under Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 - Options: (a) 1 and 2 (b) 2 only (c) 1 and 3 (d) 3 only - Answer: (c) 1 and 3 - Analysis: - Species Overview: - Dugong (Dugong dugon), or sea cow, is a marine mammal in the Sirenia order, vulnerable globally and endangered in India. - Key Terms: - Herbivorous: Feeds on seagrasses, maintaining meadow health. - Schedule I: Highest protection under Wildlife Protection Act, 1972; bans hunting, trade. - Statement Analysis: - 1. Herbivorous Marine Animal: Correct. Grazes seagrasses in coastal waters. - 2. Entire Coast: Incorrect. Found in Gulf of Mannar, Palk Bay, Gulf of Kutch, Andaman & Nicobar; not entire coast. - 3. Schedule I Protection: Correct. Protected since 1972. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Includes incorrect statement 2. - (b) Excludes correct statements 1 and 3. - (d) Excludes correct statement 1. - Relevant Information: - Dugong Conservation Reserve (Tamil Nadu, 2020) protects Palk Bay population. - Threats: Bycatch, habitat loss; India's population ~250. - Q88: Which one of the following is the national aquatic animal of India? - Options: (a) Saltwater crocodile (b) Olive ridley turtle (c) Gangetic dolphin (d) Gharial - Answer: (c) Gangetic dolphin - Analysis: - National Symbol Overview: - Declared in 2009 to highlight Ganga conservation. - Key Terms: - Gangetic Dolphin (Platanista gangetica): Blind, freshwater cetacean using echolocation; indicator of river health. - Endangered: IUCN status; population ~1,800-2,000 in Ganga-Brahmaputra. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Saltwater crocodile: National reptile, not aquatic animal. - (b) Olive ridley turtle: Marine, protected but not national aquatic. - (d) Gharial: Critically endangered crocodile, not dolphin. - Relevant Information: - Project Dolphin (2020) for conservation; found in Ganga, Brahmaputra, Indus. - Threats: Dams, pollution, fisheries. - Q89: Which one of the following is associated with the issue of control and phasing out of the use of ozone-depleting substances? - Options: (a) Bretton Woods Conference (b) Montreal Protocol (c) Kyoto Protocol (d) Nagoya Protocol - Answer: (b) Montreal Protocol - Analysis: - Protocol Overview: - Adopted 1987, entered force 1989; phased out 98% of ozone-depleting substances (ODS) like CFCs. - Key Terms: - Ozone-Depleting Substances (ODS): Chemicals (CFCs, halons) destroying stratospheric ozone, causing UV increase. - Kigali Amendment (2016): Phases down HFCs, potent greenhouse gases. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Bretton Woods: 1944 economic conference establishing IMF/World Bank. - (c) Kyoto Protocol: 1997 GHG emissions reductions. - (d) Nagoya Protocol: 2010 biodiversity access/benefit-sharing. - Relevant Information: - 197 parties; averted 2 million skin cancer cases annually. - India phased out CFCs by 2010; HCFCs by 2030. - Q90: What is Rio+20 Conference, often mentioned in the news? - Options: (a) It is the United Nations Conference on Sustainable Development (b) It is a Ministerial Meeting of the World Trade Organization (c) It is a Conference of the Inter-governmental Panel on Climate Change (d) It is a Conference of the Member Countries of the Convention on Biological Diversity - Answer: (a) It is the United Nations Conference on Sustainable Development - Analysis: - Conference Overview: - Held June 2012 in Rio de Janeiro; 20-year follow-up to 1992 Earth Summit. - Key Terms: - Sustainable Development: Balancing economic growth, social equity, environmental protection. - Outcome: "The Future We Want"; led to SDGs framework. - Why Not Others?: - (b) WTO Ministerial: Trade-focused, e.g., Doha Round. - (c) IPCC: Scientific assessments, not conferences like COP. - (d) CBD COP: Biodiversity-specific, e.g., Nagoya (2010). - Relevant Information: - 191 countries; emphasized green economy, institutional framework for sustainable development. - Influenced Paris Agreement, SDGs. - Q91: Which of the following statements regarding 'Green Climate Fund' is/are correct? - Statements: 1. It is intended to assist the developing countries in adaptation and mitigation practices to counter climate change 2. It is founded under the aegis of UNEP, OECD, Asian Development Bank and World Bank - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: (a) 1 only - Analysis: - Fund Overview: - Established 2010 under UNFCCC; world's largest climate fund (~$20B pledged). - Key Terms: - Adaptation: Building resilience to climate impacts (e.g., sea walls). - Mitigation: Reducing GHG emissions (e.g., renewables). - Statement Analysis: - 1. Assistance for Developing Countries: Correct. Allocates 50% to adaptation; supports NDCs. - 2. Founded under UNEP et al.: Incorrect. UNFCCC entity; World Bank interim trustee, but not founded by those organizations. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Statement 1 is correct. - (c) Statement 2 is incorrect. - (d) Statement 1 is correct. - Relevant Information: - 194 parties; focuses on LDCs, SIDS; projects in India include solar parks. - $100B annual climate finance goal by 2020 (met 2022). - Q92: With reference to bio-toilets used by the Indian Railways, consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. The decomposition of human waste in the bio-toilets is initiated by a fungal inoculum 2. Ammonia and water vapour are the only end products in this decomposition which are released into the atmosphere - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Analysis: - Bio-Toilet Overview: - Developed by DRDO/Indian Railways; installed in 100%+ trains by 2019; zero-discharge system. - Key Terms: - Anaerobic Digestion: Bacterial breakdown without oxygen: organic waste → biogas (CH₄, CO₂) + water. - Inoculum: Starter culture; here, bacterial consortium (not fungi). - Statement Analysis: - 1. Fungal Inoculum: Incorrect. Uses anaerobic bacteria (e.g., Pseudomonas) in digester tanks. - 2. Only Ammonia and Water Vapour: Incorrect. End products: methane, CO₂, water; no ammonia release. - Why Not Others?: - (a), (b), (c): Both statements incorrect. - Relevant Information: - Decomposes waste in 7 chambers; biogas vented safely. - Installed in ~1.5 lakh coaches; reduces track pollution. - Q93: With reference to the Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency Limited (IREDA), which of the following statements is/are correct? - Statements: 1. It is a Public Limited Government Company 2. It is a Non-Banking Financial Company - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: (c) Both 1 and 2 - Analysis: - Agency Overview: - Established 1987 under Companies Act; Navratna PSU since 2024. - Key Terms: - Public Limited Company: Government-owned (75% equity by MNRE). - NBFC: Provides loans for RE projects without banking license. - Statement Analysis: - 1. Public Limited Government Company: Correct. Wholly owned by MNRE. - 2. Non-Banking Financial Company: Correct. RBI-registered NBFC for RE financing. - Why Not Others?: - (a), (b): Both correct. - (d): Both correct. - Relevant Information: - Finances solar, wind, hydro; sanctioned ₹50,000 Cr+ by 2025. - IPO 2023 raised ₹2,150 Cr. - [2015-I] - Q94: Consider the following pairs: - Pairs: 1. Annex-I Countries: Cartagena Protocol 2. Certified Emissions Reductions: Nagoya Protocol 3. Clean Development Mechanism: Kyoto Protocol - Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched? - Options: (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (c) 3 only - Analysis: - Climate/Biodiversity Terms: - UNFCCC/Kyoto: GHG frameworks; CBD Protocols: Biodiversity. - Key Terms: - Annex-I Countries: Developed nations with emission targets under Kyoto/UNFCCC. - Certified Emission Reductions (CERs): Carbon credits from CDM projects under Kyoto. - Clean Development Mechanism (CDM): Allows Annex-I investment in non-Annex-I for credits. - Pair Analysis: - 1. Annex-I: Incorrect. From UNFCCC/Kyoto, not Cartagena (biosafety under CBD). - 2. CERs: Incorrect. From Kyoto/CDM, not Nagoya (genetic resources access). - 3. CDM: Correct. Flexible mechanism under Kyoto Protocol. - Why Not Others?: - (a), (b): Include incorrect pairs. - (d): Only pair 3 correct. - Relevant Information: - Kyoto (1997): Binding targets for Annex-I; CDM generated 2B+ CERs. - India hosted 1,700+ CDM projects. - Q95: With reference to an initiative called 'The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity (TEEB)', which of the following statements is/are correct? - Statements: 1. It is an initiative hosted by UNEP, IMF and World Economic Forum 2. It is a global initiative that focuses on drawing attention to the economic benefits of biodiversity 3. It presents an approach that can help decision-makers recognize, demonstrate and capture the value of ecosystems and biodiversity - Options: (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 3 only (c) 2 and 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (c) 2 and 3 only - Analysis: - Initiative Overview: - TEEB, launched 2007 by G8+5, hosted by UNEP; "making nature's values visible." - Key Terms: - Ecosystem Services: Benefits like pollination, water purification (valued at $125-145T/year globally). - Valuation: Economic tools (e.g., contingent valuation) to integrate nature into decisions. - Statement Analysis: - 1. Hosted by UNEP, IMF, WEF: Incorrect. Hosted by UNEP; supported by EC, Germany, not IMF/WEF. - 2. Economic Benefits Focus: Correct. Highlights biodiversity's role in economy (e.g., $2-6T annual loss from degradation). - 3. Decision-Maker Approach: Correct. Provides TEEB framework for valuation in policy/business. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Includes incorrect statement 1. - (b) Excludes correct statements 2 and 3. - (d) Includes incorrect statement 1. - Relevant Information: - Reports: TEEB for Policy (2011); influenced SDGs, IPBES. - India: TEEB studies on wetlands, forests. - Q96: Which of the following statements is/are correct? Proper design and effective implementation of UN-REDD+ Programme can significantly contribute to: - Contributions: 1. Protection of biodiversity 2. Resilience of forest ecosystems 3. Poverty reduction - Options: (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 3 only (c) 2 and 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Analysis: - Programme Overview: - UN-REDD, joint UNEP/FAO/UNDP initiative since 2008; supports 60+ countries in REDD+. - Key Terms: - REDD+: Reduces deforestation emissions; safeguards biodiversity, livelihoods. - Resilience: Enhancing forests' ability to withstand climate shocks via restoration. - Contribution Analysis: - 1. Biodiversity Protection: Correct. Integrates safeguards, protects habitats/species. - 2. Forest Resilience: Correct. Promotes sustainable management, restoration. - 3. Poverty Reduction: Correct. Benefit-sharing, livelihoods for forest-dependent communities. - Why Not Others?: - (a), (c): Exclude correct contribution 3. - (b): Excludes 1 and 2. - Relevant Information: - Aligns with SDGs 13, 15; India's REDD+ strategy emphasizes community involvement. - $500M+ mobilized; focuses non-carbon benefits. - Q97: What is 'Greenhouse Gas Protocol'? - Options: (a) It is an international accounting tool for government and business leaders to understand, quantify and manage greenhouse gas emissions (b) It is an initiative of the United Nations to offer financial incentives to developing countries to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and to adopt eco-friendly technologies (c) It is an inter-governmental agreement ratified by all the member countries of the United Nations to reduce greenhouse gas emissions to specified levels by the year 2022 (d) It is one of the multilateral REDD+ initiatives hosted by the World Bank - Answer: (a) It is an international accounting tool for government and business leaders to understand, quantify and manage greenhouse gas emissions - Analysis: - Protocol Overview: - Developed 1998 by WRI/WBCSD; most used GHG standard globally. - Key Terms: - Scope 1-3 Emissions: Direct (Scope 1), indirect energy (Scope 2), value chain (Scope 3). - Corporate Standard: Guides GHG inventories for organizations. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Describes GCF or CDM, not GHG Protocol. - (c) Refers to Kyoto/Paris, not a protocol for accounting. - (d) FCPF/UN-REDD for forests, not general GHG tool. - Relevant Information: - Used by 90%+ Fortune 500; supports CDP, SBTi. - India: Adopted for corporate reporting under BEE. - Q98: With reference to 'Agenda 21', sometimes seen in the news, consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. It is a global action plan for sustainable development 2. It originated in the World Summit on Sustainable Development held in Johannesburg in 2002 - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: (a) 1 only - Analysis: - Plan Overview: - Non-binding UN action plan from 1992 Earth Summit; comprehensive blueprint for sustainability. - Key Terms: - Sustainable Development: Economic, social, environmental pillars. - Chapters: 40, covering poverty, health, forests, major groups. - Statement Analysis: - 1. Global Action Plan: Correct. Addresses environment/development integration. - 2. Johannesburg Origin: Incorrect. From Rio 1992; Johannesburg (2002) was Rio+10 (WSSD). - Why Not Others?: - (b) Statement 1 correct. - (c) Statement 2 incorrect. - (d) Statement 1 correct. - Relevant Information: - Influenced MDGs, SDGs; Local Agenda 21 for cities. - India: Integrated into NAPCC. - Q99: Consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. The International Solar Alliance was launched at the United Nations Climate Change Conference in 2015 2.
