The Alliance includes all the member countries of the United Nations - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: (a) 1 only - Analysis: - Alliance Overview: - ISA, India-France initiative; promotes solar energy in sunshine countries. - Key Terms: - Launched: COP21 side event, Paris, November 2015. - Membership: 122 eligible (tropical belt); 107 signatories, not all 193 UN members. - Statement Analysis: - 1. COP21 Launch: Correct. Framework signed 2016. - 2. All UN Members: Incorrect. Open to all, but focused on solar-rich; 107 members. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Statement 1 correct. - (c) Statement 2 incorrect. - (d) Statement 1 correct. - Relevant Information: - HQ: Gurugram, India; 14 programs (e.g., solar pumps). - $1T mobilization goal by 2030. - Q100: With reference to the Agreement at the UNFCCC Meeting in Paris in 2015, which of the following statements is/are correct? - Statements: 1. The Agreement was signed by all the member countries of the UN and it will go into effect in 2017 2. The Agreement aims to limit the greenhouse gas emissions so that the rise in average global temperature by the end of this century does not exceed 2 °C or even 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels 3. Developed countries acknowledged their historical responsibility in global warming and committed to donate $1000 billion a year from 2020 to help developing countries to cope with climate change - Options: (a) 1 and 3 only (b) 2 only (c) 2 and 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (b) 2 only - Analysis: - Agreement Overview: - Paris Agreement, adopted COP21; entered force November 2016 (55/55% threshold). - Key Terms: - NDCs: Nationally Determined Contributions; updated every 5 years. - $100B Goal: Annual climate finance from developed to developing (met 2022, extended to 2025). - Statement Analysis: - 1. Signed by All, Effect 2017: Incorrect. Adopted by 195 parties; signed 2016; force 2016, not 2017. - 2. Temperature Limit: Correct. Well below 2°C, pursue 1.5°C. - 3. $1000B Commitment: Incorrect. $100B/year, not $1000B. - Why Not Others?: - (a), (c): Include incorrect statements. - (d): Only 2 correct. - Relevant Information: - 196 parties; India's NDC: 45% emission intensity reduction by 2030. - Loss and Damage Fund (2022) addresses historical responsibility. - Q101: Consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. The Sustainable Development Goals were first proposed in 1972 by a global think tank called the 'Club of Rome' 2. The Sustainable Development Goals have to be achieved by 2030 - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: (b) 2 only - Analysis: - Goals Overview: - 17 SDGs, adopted UNGA 2015; universal framework for 2030 Agenda. - Key Terms: - Club of Rome: 1972 "Limits to Growth" on sustainability, not SDGs. - 2030 Agenda: "Transforming Our World"; ends poverty, protects planet. - Statement Analysis: - 1. Proposed by Club of Rome 1972: Incorrect. Evolved from MDGs (2000); post-Rio+20. - 2. Achieve by 2030: Correct. Time-bound targets. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Statement 2 correct. - (c) Statement 1 incorrect. - (d) Statement 2 correct. - Relevant Information: - 169 targets, 232 indicators; India: SDG India Index. - COVID-19 set back progress; annual UN High-Level Political Forum. - Q102: The term 'Intended Nationally Determined Contributions' is sometimes seen in the news in the context of: - Options: (a) Pledges made by the European countries to rehabilitate refugees from the war-affected Middle East (b) Plan of action outlined by the countries of the world to combat climate change (c) Capital contributed by the member countries in the establishment of Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (d) Plan of action outlined by the countries of the world regarding Sustainable Development Goals - Answer: (b) Plan of action outlined by the countries of the world to combat climate change - Analysis: - Term Overview: - INDCs: Pre-Paris (2015) pledges; became NDCs post-adoption. - Key Terms: - NDCs: Country-specific emission reduction/adaptation plans under Paris Agreement. - Ratcheting Up: Increasing ambition every 5 years. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Refugee pledges: EU-Turkey deal, not INDCs. - (c) AIIB: Capital subscriptions, not INDCs. - (d) SDGs: Voluntary National Reviews, not INDCs. - Relevant Information: - 192 NDCs submitted; India's: 33-35% intensity reduction by 2030. - Updated 2020/2021; next 2025. - Q103: What is/are the importance/importances of the 'United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification'? - Importances: 1. It aims to promote effective action through innovative national programs and supportive international partnerships 2. It has a special/particular focus on South Asia and North Africa regions, and its Secretariat facilitates the allocation of major portion of financial resources to these regions 3. It is committed to bottom-up approach, encouraging the participation of local people in combating the desertification - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1 and 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (c) 1 and 3 only - Analysis: - Convention Overview: - UNCCD (1994, force 1996); addresses desertification in drylands affecting 40% land. - Key Terms: - National Action Programmes (NAPs): Country-led plans involving stakeholders. - Bottom-Up Approach: Community participation in land restoration. - Importance Analysis: - 1. Innovative Programs/Partnerships: Correct. Promotes NAPs, international cooperation. - 2. Focus on South Asia/North Africa: Incorrect. Global, especially Africa; equitable resource allocation. - 3. Local Participation: Correct. Emphasizes affected communities. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Excludes 3. - (b) Includes incorrect 2. - (d) Includes incorrect 2. - Relevant Information: - 197 parties; LDN (Land Degradation Neutrality) target by 2030. - India: Desertification affects 96M ha; NAP aligned with UNCCD. - Q104: Which of the following best describes/describe the aim of 'Green India Mission' of the Government of India? - Aims: 1. Incorporating environmental benefits and costs into the Union and State Budgets thereby implementing the 'green accounting' 2. Launching the second green revolution to enhance agricultural output so as to ensure food security to one and all in the future 3. Restoring and enhancing forest cover and responding to climate change by a combination of adaptation and mitigation measures - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (c) 3 only - Analysis: - Mission Overview: - GIM, NAPCC mission (2014); aims 5M ha forest restoration by 2030. - Key Terms: - Adaptation: Building resilience (e.g., drought-resistant species). - Mitigation: Carbon sequestration via afforestation. - Aim Analysis: - 1. Green Accounting: Incorrect. That's Green India Mission? No, SEEA or NCA. - 2. Second Green Revolution: Incorrect. National Food Security Mission. - 3. Forest Restoration/Climate Response: Correct. Increases cover by 5M ha, ecosystem services. - Why Not Others?: - (a), (b), (d): Only 3 correct. - Relevant Information: - Revised 2021-2030; ₹46,000 Cr budget. - Targets: Biodiversity, water, livelihoods. - Q105: 'Net metering' is sometimes seen in the news in the context of promoting the: - Options: (a) Production and use of solar energy by the households/consumers (b) Use of piped natural gas in the kitchens of households (c) Installation of CNG kits in motor-cars (d) Installation of water meters in urban households - Answer: (a) Production and use of solar energy by the households/consumers - Analysis: - Concept Overview: - Net metering credits excess solar generation against grid consumption. - Key Terms: - Bi-Directional Meter: Measures import/export; excess kWh offset at retail rate. - Rooftop Solar: Household PV systems tied to grid. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Piped Gas: PNG metering, not net. - (c) CNG Kits: Vehicle fuel, not metering. - (d) Water Meters: Utility billing, not energy. - Relevant Information: - MNRE policy; 26 states implement; 40 GW potential by 2022. - Subsidies under PM Surya Ghar. - Q106: 'Gadgil Committee Report' and 'Kasturirangan Committee Report', sometimes seen in the news, are related to: - Options: (a) Constitutional reforms (b) Ganga Action Plan (c) Linking of rivers (d) Protection of Western Ghats - Answer: (d) Protection of Western Ghats - Analysis: - Reports Overview: - Gadgil (2011): WGEEP; 64% ESA, strict regulations. - Kasturirangan (2013): HLWG; 37% ESA, balanced development. - Key Terms: - Western Ghats: UNESCO site, biodiversity hotspot; 6 states. - ESA: Ecologically Sensitive Areas under EPA 1986. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Constitutional: Sarkaria/Justice Verma. - (b) Ganga: NGRBA. - (c) River Linking: NWDA. - Relevant Information: - Draft notifications 2014-2023; protests in Kerala. - Supreme Court 2023: Implement Kasturirangan. - Q107: On which of the following can you find the Bureau of Energy Efficiency Star Label? - Items: 1. Ceiling fans 2. Electric geysers 3. Tubular fluorescent lamps - Options: (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 3 only (c) 2 and 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Analysis: - Labeling Program: - BEE S&L since 2006; 25+ products, mandatory/voluntary. - Key Terms: - Star Rating: 1-5 stars for efficiency; ISEER for ACs. - Ceiling Fans: Mandatory since 2013. - Electric Geysers: Voluntary. - Tubular Fluorescent Lamps: Mandatory. - Why Not Others?: - (a), (c): Exclude one correct item. - (b): Excludes 1 and 2. - Relevant Information: - Saves 15% household energy; app for verification. - LED mandatory 2018. - Q108: In the cities of our country, which among the following atmospheric gases are normally considered in calculating the value of Air Quality Index? - Gases: 1. Carbon dioxide 2. Carbon monoxide 3. Nitrogen dioxide 4. Sulfur dioxide 5. Methane - Options: (a) 1, 2 and 3 only (b) 2, 3 and 4 only (c) 1, 4 and 5 only (d) 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 - Answer: (b) 2, 3 and 4 only - Analysis: - AQI Overview: - CPCB/NAAQS-based; scale 0-500. - Key Terms: - Criteria Pollutants: PM10, PM2.5, NO₂, SO₂, CO, O₃, NH₃, Pb. - Sub-Index: Individual pollutant contribution to AQI. - Gas Analysis: - 1. CO₂: Greenhouse, not criteria for AQI. - 2. CO: Included; from vehicles. - 3. NO₂: Included; respiratory irritant. - 4. SO₂: Included; acid rain precursor. - 5. CH₄: Greenhouse, not urban AQI pollutant. - Why Not Others?: - (a), (c), (d): Include incorrect gases. - Relevant Information: - NAAQS 2009; NCAP improves AQI in 131 cities. - PM dominant in India. - Q109: Which of the following are the key features of 'National Ganga River Basin Authority (NGRBA)'? - Features: 1. River basin is the unit of planning and management 2. It spearheads the river conservation efforts at the national level 3. One of the Chief Ministers of the States through which the Ganga flows becomes the Chairman of NGRBA on rotation basis - Options: (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1 and 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (a) 1 and 2 only - Analysis: - Authority Overview: - NGRBA (2009, dissolved 2016); apex body for Ganga rejuvenation. - Key Terms: - Basin Approach: Holistic management of Ganga basin (catchment-wide). - Spearheads Conservation: Coordinates pollution abatement, biodiversity. - Feature Analysis: - 1. Basin Unit: Correct. Integrated planning for 11 states. - 2. National Conservation: Correct. Under EPA 1986; implemented NMCG. - 3. Rotating CM Chairman: Incorrect. Chaired by PM; CMs members. - Why Not Others?: - (b), (c): Include incorrect 3. - (d): Feature 3 incorrect. - Relevant Information: - Succeeded by NMCG; Namami Gange (₹20,000 Cr). - Focus: Sewage treatment, afforestation. - Q110: What is/are unique about 'Kharai camel', a breed found in India? - Features: 1. It is capable of swimming up to three kilometers in seawater 2. It survives by grazing on mangroves 3. It lives in the wild and cannot be domesticated - Options: (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 3 only (c) 1 and 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (a) 1 and 2 only - Analysis: - Breed Overview: - Kharai (Equus hemionus khur? No, dromedary breed), endemic to Kutch, Gujarat; ~1,200 population. - Key Terms: - Swimming Adaptation: Webbed feet, swims 3-5 km for mangroves. - Mangrove Grazing: Diet: halophytic plants, tolerates salinity. - Feature Analysis: - 1. Swimming 3 km: Correct. Crosses creeks to islands. - 2. Mangrove Grazing: Correct. Primary food in Rann of Kutch. - 3. Wild, Undomesticable: Incorrect. Domesticated by Maldhari herders. - Why Not Others?: - (b), (c): Exclude correct 1,2. - (d): Feature 3 incorrect. - Relevant Information: - IUCN Vulnerable; milk therapeutic. - Threats: Salt pans, predation. - Q111: Recently, our scientists have discovered a new and distinct species of banana plant which attains a height of about 11 metres and has orange-coloured fruit pulp. In which part of India has it been discovered? - Options: (a) Andaman Islands (b) Anaimalai Forests (c) Maikala Hills (d) Tropical rain forests of northeast - Answer: (a) Andaman Islands - Analysis: - Discovery Overview: - Musa indandamanensis, 2015 BSI discovery; giant wild banana. - Key Terms: - Musa indandamanensis: 11m tall, orange pulp, green flowers; thrice regular size. - Endemic: Little Andaman's Krishna Nalah forest. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Anaimalai: Western Ghats, no such banana. - (c) Maikala: Central India hills, not banana hotspot. - (d) Northeast: Musa acuminata variants, not this species. - Relevant Information: - 15 wild banana species in India; potential for breeding. - Andamans: Biodiversity hotspot, 52 global Musa spp. - Q112: With reference to 'Red Sanders', sometimes seen in the news, consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. It is a tree species found in a part of South India 2. It is one of the most important trees in the tropical rain forest areas of South India - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: (a) 1 only - Analysis: - Species Overview: - Pterocarpus santalinus, endemic to southern Eastern Ghats; IUCN Endangered. - Key Terms: - Red Sanders: Valued for red wood (dyes, furniture); CITES Appendix II. - Habitat: Dry deciduous forests, Andhra Pradesh/Tamil Nadu. - Statement Analysis: - 1. South India Part: Correct. Restricted to Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu. - 2. Important in Tropical Rain Forests: Incorrect. Dry deciduous, not rain forests (evergreen, high rainfall). - Why Not Others?: - (b) Statement 1 correct. - (c) Statement 2 incorrect. - (d) Statement 1 correct. - Relevant Information: - Illegal trade to China; India produces 80% global supply. - Conservation: Plantations, Schedule I protection. - [2016-I] - Q113: The term 'M-STRIPES' is sometimes seen in the news in the context of: - Options: (a) Captive breeding of Wild Fauna (b) Maintenance of Tiger Reserves (c) Indigenous Satellite Navigation System (d) Security of National Highways - Answer: (b) Maintenance of Tiger Reserves - Analysis: - M-STRIPES Overview: - M-STRIPES (Monitoring System for Tigers - Intensive Protection and Ecological Status) is a software-based monitoring system developed by the National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) and Wildlife Institute of India for tiger reserves in India. It uses GPS, GIS, and remote sensing to track tiger populations, habitat conditions, and anti-poaching efforts. - Key Terms: - Tiger Monitoring: Involves camera traps, pugmark tracking, and patrolling data to estimate tiger populations and ensure reserve management. - GIS Mapping: Spatial analysis for habitat assessment and patrol planning. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Captive breeding: Incorrect, as M-STRIPES focuses on wild tiger monitoring, not captive breeding programs like those in zoos. - (c) Satellite Navigation: Incorrect, as it is unrelated to navigation systems like IRNSS (NavIC). - (d) National Highways: Incorrect, as M-STRIPES is specific to wildlife conservation, not infrastructure security. - Relevant Information: - Implemented across 53 tiger reserves in India, covering ~75,000 sq km. - Enhances real-time data collection; helped increase tiger population from 1,706 (2010) to 3,167 (2022). - Supports Project Tiger (1973) objectives for habitat preservation and poaching control. - Q114: Recently there was a proposal to translocate some of the lions from their natural habitat in Gujarat to which one of the following sites? - Options: (a) Corbett National Park (b) Kuno Palpur Wildlife Sanctuary (c) Mudumalai Wildlife Sanctuary (d) Sariska National Park - Answer: (b) Kuno Palpur Wildlife Sanctuary - Analysis: - Lion Translocation Overview: - The Asiatic lion (Panthera leo persica), once widespread, is now restricted to Gir National Park, Gujarat (~1,400 population). Translocation to Kuno Palpur, Madhya Pradesh, was proposed to reduce extinction risk from a single population, endorsed by the Supreme Court (2013). - Key Terms: - Translocation: Relocating species to establish a second population for genetic diversity and conservation. - Kuno Palpur: Identified as suitable due to prey base (chital, sambar), habitat (dry deciduous forest), and low human conflict. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Corbett: In Uttarakhand, primarily a tiger habitat; unsuitable for lions due to dense forests and prey competition. - (c) Mudumalai: In Tamil Nadu, part of Nilgiri Biosphere; not feasible due to high rainfall and tiger presence. - (d) Sariska: In Rajasthan, a tiger reintroduction site; not prioritized for lions due to habitat mismatch. - Relevant Information: - First translocation: 8 lions moved to Kuno in 2022; successful breeding reported by 2024. - IUCN Endangered; Gir overcrowding risks disease outbreaks (e.g., canine distemper, 2018). - Q115: In India, if a species of tortoise is declared protected under Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, what does it imply? - Options: (a) It enjoys the same level of protection as the tiger (b) It no longer exists in the wild, a few individuals are under captive protection; and now it is impossible to prevent its extinction (c) It is endemic to a particular region of India (d) Both (b) and (c) stated above are correct in this context - Answer: (a) It enjoys the same level of protection as the tiger - Analysis: - Wildlife Protection Act Overview: - The Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, categorizes species into schedules for varying protection levels. Schedule I offers the highest protection, prohibiting hunting, trade, or possession except under special permits. - Key Terms: - Schedule I: Includes critically endangered species like tiger, blackbuck, and star tortoise; violations attract up to 7 years imprisonment. - Protection Levels: Strict enforcement, habitat conservation, and anti-poaching measures. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect, as Schedule I status does not imply extinction in the wild; many species (e.g., gharial) exist in wild and captivity. - (c) Incorrect, as Schedule I does not require endemism; species like snow leopard are not India-specific. - (d) Incorrect, as neither (b) nor (c) is accurate. - Relevant Information: - Indian star tortoise (Geochelone elegans) under Schedule I since 2019 due to illegal pet trade. - Act amended 2022 to align with CITES; 660 Schedule I species. - Q116: According to the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, which of the following animals cannot be hunted by any person except under some provisions provided by law? - Animals: 1. Gharial 2. Indian wild ass 3. Wild buffalo - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1 and 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Analysis: - Wildlife Protection Act Overview: - Prohibits hunting of Schedule I-IV species except for scientific research, education, or threat mitigation under Section 11/12. - Key Terms: - Gharial (Gavialis gangeticus): Schedule I, critically endangered; riverine crocodile. - Indian Wild Ass (Equus hemionus khur): Schedule I, endemic to Rann of Kutch. - Wild Buffalo (Bubalus arnee): Schedule I, endangered; found in Assam, Chhattisgarh. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Excludes wild ass and buffalo, both Schedule I. - (b) Excludes gharial, Schedule I. - (c) Excludes wild ass, Schedule I. - Relevant Information: - Hunting banned since 1972; exceptions require Chief Wildlife Warden approval. - Gharial population <200 breeding adults; wild buffalo ~3,400 (2020). - Q117: If you want to see gharials in their natural habitat, which one of the following is the best place to visit? - Options: (a) Bhitarkanika Mangroves (b) Chambal River (c) Pulicat Lake (d) Deepor Beel - Answer: (b) Chambal River - Analysis: - Gharial Habitat Overview: - Gharials (Gavialis gangeticus) are riverine crocodilians requiring clean, fast-flowing rivers with sandbanks for nesting. - Key Terms: - National Chambal Sanctuary: Tri-state (UP, MP, Rajasthan) sanctuary; largest gharial population (~1,800 in 2020). - Habitat Preference: Deep rivers with fish-rich waters; males have ghara (nasal growth) for mating calls. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Bhitarkanika: Mangrove ecosystem; supports saltwater crocodiles, not gharials. - (c) Pulicat Lake: Brackish lagoon; unsuitable for gharials, hosts birds. - (d) Deepor Beel: Assam wetland; no gharial population, primarily avian. - Relevant Information: - Chambal hosts 80% of India’s gharials; conservation since 1979 via Project Crocodile. - Threats: Sand mining, fishing nets; IUCN Critically Endangered. - Q118: From the ecological point of view, which one of the following assumes importance in being a good link between the Eastern Ghats and the Western Ghats? - Options: (a) Sathyamangalam Tiger Reserve (b) Nallamala Forest (c) Nagarhole National Park (d) Seshachalam Biosphere Reserve - Answer: (a) Sathyamangalam Tiger Reserve - Analysis: - Ecological Link Overview: - The Eastern and Western Ghats are biodiversity hotspots; connectivity ensures gene flow and species migration. - Key Terms: - Sathyamangalam Tiger Reserve: In Tamil Nadu, part of Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve; connects Western Ghats (Nilgiris) to Eastern Ghats via Biligiri Rangan Hills. - Corridor: Landscape facilitating animal movement (e.g., tigers, elephants). - Why Not Others?: - (b) Nallamala: Eastern Ghats (Andhra Pradesh); no direct link to Western Ghats. - (c) Nagarhole: Western Ghats (Karnataka); no Eastern Ghats connectivity. - (d) Seshachalam: Eastern Ghats (Andhra Pradesh); isolated, no Western Ghats link. - Relevant Information: - Sathyamangalam supports 80+ tigers, elephants; critical for Nilgiri-Eastern Ghats corridor. - Declared tiger reserve 2013; 1,400 sq km. - Q119: Consider the following statements in respect of Trade Related Analysis of Fauna and Flora in Commerce (TRAFFIC): - Statements: 1. TRAFFIC is a bureau under United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) 2. The mission of TRAFFIC is to ensure that trade in wild plants and animals is not a threat to the conservation of nature - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: (b) 2 only - Analysis: - TRAFFIC Overview: - TRAFFIC, established 1976, is a joint program of WWF and IUCN, focusing on sustainable wildlife trade. - Key Terms: - Wildlife Trade: Legal/illegal trade in species (e.g., ivory, timber); global value ~$300B. - CITES Support: Monitors trade compliance for 38,000+ species. - Statement Analysis: - 1. UNEP Bureau: Incorrect. TRAFFIC is independent, not under UNEP; collaborates with CITES. - 2. Conservation Mission: Correct. Ensures trade aligns with species survival. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Statement 2 correct. - (c) Statement 1 incorrect. - (d) Statement 2 correct. - Relevant Information: - Offices in 30+ countries; India program monitors pangolin, red sanders trade. - Partners with INTERPOL on wildlife crime. - Q120: Due to some reasons, if there is a huge fall in the population of species of butterflies, what could be its likely consequence/consequences? - Consequences: 1. Pollination of some plants could be adversely affected 2. There could be a drastic increase in the fungal infections of some cultivated plants 3. It could lead to a fall in the population of some species of wasps, spiders and birds - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1 and 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (c) 1 and 3 only - Analysis: - Butterfly Role Overview: - Butterflies are pollinators and prey in ecosystems; declines disrupt ecological balance. - Key Terms: - Pollination: Butterflies transfer pollen for plants like lantana; ~10% of pollination in some ecosystems. - Trophic Cascade: Decline in prey (butterflies) affects predators. - Consequence Analysis: - 1. Pollination Impact: Correct. Reduced butterfly numbers limit pollination for dependent plants. - 2. Fungal Infections: Incorrect. No direct link; fungi driven by humidity, not butterfly absence. - 3. Predator Decline: Correct. Wasps, spiders, birds (e.g., insectivores) rely on butterflies as prey. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Excludes correct 3. - (b) Includes incorrect 2. - (d) Includes incorrect 2. - Relevant Information: - India: 1,800+ butterfly species; pollinators in Western Ghats, Northeast. - Threats: Habitat loss, pesticides; decline noted in urban areas. - Q121: Biological Oxygen Demand (BOD) is a standard criterion for: - Options: (a) Measuring oxygen levels in blood (b) Computing oxygen levels in forest ecosystems (c) Pollution assay in aquatic ecosystems (d) Assessing oxygen levels in high altitude regions - Answer: (c) Pollution assay in aquatic ecosystems - Analysis: - BOD Overview: - BOD measures oxygen consumed by microorganisms to decompose organic matter in water (mg/L, 5 days at 20°C). - Key Terms: - Organic Pollution: Sewage, industrial effluents increase BOD, depleting dissolved oxygen (DO). - Water Quality: High BOD (>10 mg/L) indicates pollution; low DO (<5 mg/L) harms aquatic life. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Blood oxygen: Medical term, unrelated to BOD. - (b) Forest ecosystems: Oxygen measured via photosynthesis rates, not BOD. - (d) High altitude: Atmospheric oxygen, not BOD-related. - Relevant Information: - CPCB standards: BOD <3 mg/L for drinking water. - Ganga River: High BOD (20-40 mg/L) in urban stretches (e.g., Kanpur). - Q122: In the context of solving pollution problems, what is/are the advantage/advantages of bioremediation technique? - Advantages: 1. It is a technique for cleaning up pollution by enhancing the same biodegradation process that occurs in nature 2. Any contaminant with heavy metals such as cadmium and lead can be readily and completely treated by bioremediation using micro-organisms 3. Genetic engineering can be used to create microorganisms specifically designed for bioremediation - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1 and 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (c) 1 and 3 only - Analysis: - Bioremediation Overview: - Uses microorganisms, plants to degrade pollutants (e.g., oil spills, pesticides) into non-toxic forms. - Key Terms: - Biodegradation: Natural microbial breakdown (e.g., hydrocarbons to CO₂, H₂O). - Bioaugmentation: Adding engineered microbes for enhanced cleanup. - Advantage Analysis: - 1. Enhances Natural Process: Correct. Mimics microbial degradation in soils, water. - 2. Heavy Metals Treatment: Incorrect. Metals like Cd, Pb are non-biodegradable; bioremediation accumulates but doesn’t fully treat. - 3. Genetic Engineering: Correct. Engineered bacteria (e.g., Pseudomonas) degrade specific pollutants like PAHs. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Excludes correct 3. - (b) Includes incorrect 2. - (d) Includes incorrect 2. - Relevant Information: - Examples: Oil spill cleanup (Exxon Valdez, 1989); India’s bioremediation of Yamuna. - Limitations: Heavy metals require phytoremediation or immobilization. - Q123: In the context of mitigating the impending global warming due to anthropogenic emissions of carbon dioxide, which of the following can be the potential sites for carbon sequestration? - Sites: 1. Abandoned and uneconomic coal seams 2. Depleted oil and gas reservoirs 3. Subterranean deep saline formations - Options: (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 3 only (c) 1 and 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Analysis: - Carbon Sequestration Overview: - Carbon Capture and Storage (CCS) traps CO₂ and stores it underground to reduce atmospheric emissions. - Key Terms: - Geological Storage: Injecting CO₂ into stable formations (porous rock, caprock seal). - Storage Capacity: Global potential ~2,000 Gt CO₂. - Site Analysis: - 1. Coal Seams: Correct. CO₂ adsorbed in coal pores; enhanced coalbed methane recovery. - 2. Oil/Gas Reservoirs: Correct. Depleted fields store CO₂; used in EOR (Enhanced Oil Recovery). - 3. Saline Formations: Correct. Deep aquifers (>800m) store CO₂ in dissolved or trapped form. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Excludes 3, a major CCS site. - (b) Excludes 1, 2. - (c) Excludes 2. - Relevant Information: - India: CCS pilots in Gujarat (ONGC); global projects like Sleipner (Norway). - Potential: Coal seams (10 Gt), saline aquifers (100 Gt) in India. - Q124: It is possible to produce algae based biofuels, but what is/are the likely limitation(s) of developing countries in promoting this industry? - Limitations: 1. Production of algae based biofuels is possible in seas only and not on continents 2. Setting up and engineering the algae based biofuel production requires high level of expertise/technology until the construction is completed 3. Economically viable production necessitates the setting up of large scale facilities which may raise ecological and social concerns - Options: (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (b) 2 and 3 only - Analysis: - Algae Biofuels Overview: - Algae produce lipids for biodiesel; high yield (10-100x crops/ha); grown in open ponds or photobioreactors. - Key Terms: - Photobioreactors: Controlled systems for algae growth; high-tech, costly. - Ecological Concerns: Land use, water consumption in large-scale farms. - Limitation Analysis: - 1. Seas Only: Incorrect. Algae grown in ponds, bioreactors on land; marine systems less common. - 2. High Expertise: Correct. Requires advanced biotech, engineering (e.g., strain selection, CO₂ supply). - 3. Large-Scale Concerns: Correct. Land, water use, and waste disposal raise issues. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Includes incorrect 1. - (c) Excludes correct 2. - (d) Includes incorrect 1. - Relevant Information: - India: Pilot projects by DBT; challenges include ₹200/L cost vs. ₹70/L diesel. - Global: Algae yields 5,000-20,000 gal/acre vs. 50 gal/acre for soy. - Q125: With reference to 'Global Climate Change Alliance', which of the following statements is/are correct? - Statements: 1. It is an initiative of the European Union 2. It provides technical and financial support to targeted developing countries to integrate climate change into their development policies and budgets 3. It is coordinated by World Resources Institute (WRI) and World Business Council for Sustainable Development (WBCSD) - Options: (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 3 only (c) 2 and 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (a) 1 and 2 only - Analysis: - Alliance Overview: - GCCA, launched 2007 by EU, supports climate resilience in vulnerable countries. - Key Terms: - Climate Mainstreaming: Integrating adaptation/mitigation into national plans. - LDCs/SIDS: Least Developed Countries, Small Island Developing States; 80+ countries supported. - Statement Analysis: - 1. EU Initiative: Correct. EU-led, funded via development budgets. - 2. Support for Developing Countries: Correct. €750M+ for adaptation, NDC implementation. - 3. WRI/WBCSD Coordination: Incorrect. Managed by EU (EuropeAid), not WRI/WBCSD. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Excludes correct 1, 2. - (c) Includes incorrect 3. - (d) Includes incorrect 3. - Relevant Information: - GCCA+ phase (2015-2020): Focus on NDCs, SDGs. - India: Not a primary recipient; focus on African/SIDS nations. - Q126: Consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. Climate and Clean Air Coalition (CCAC) to reduce Short Lived Climate Pollutants is a unique initiative of G20 group of countries 2. The CCAC focuses on methane, black carbon and hydrofluorocarbons - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: (b) 2 only - Analysis: - Coalition Overview: - CCAC, launched 2012, voluntary partnership to reduce SLCPs; 70+ countries, UNEP-hosted. - Key Terms: - SLCPs: Methane (CH₄), black carbon (soot), HFCs; high warming potential, short atmospheric life. - Global Warming Potential: CH₄ (25x CO₂), HFCs (100-14,000x). - Statement Analysis: - 1. G20 Initiative: Incorrect. Founded by Bangladesh, Canada, Ghana, Mexico, Sweden, US; not G20-specific. - 2. Focus on SLCPs: Correct. Targets CH₄, black carbon, HFCs via sector strategies (e.g., agriculture, waste). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Statement 2 correct. - (c) Statement 1 incorrect. - (d) Statement 2 correct. - Relevant Information: - India joined 2019; CCAC supports methane reduction in landfills. - SLCP reduction: 0.5°C cooling potential by 2050. - Q127: Which of the following statements best describes the term 'Scheme for Sustainable Structuring of Stressed Assets (S4A)', recently seen in the news? - Options: (a) It is a procedure for considering ecological costs of developmental schemes formulated by the Government (b) It is a scheme of RBI for reworking the financial structure of big corporate entities facing genuine difficulties (c) It is a disinvestment plan of the Government regarding Central Public Sector Undertakings (d) It is an important provision in 'The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code' recently implemented by the Government - Answer: (b) It is a scheme of RBI for reworking the financial structure of big corporate entities facing genuine difficulties - Analysis: - S4A Overview: - Launched by RBI in 2016 to address NPAs; restructures corporate debt for viable projects. - Key Terms: - Stressed Assets: NPAs with overdue payments; ₹10 lakh Cr in 2016. - Debt Restructuring: Splits debt into sustainable (repaid) and unsustainable (equity conversion). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Ecological costs: Unrelated; environmental schemes under MoEFCC. - (c) Disinvestment: NITI Aayog/PSU plans, not S4A. - (d) IBC: Separate 2016 law; S4A predates, distinct mechanism. - Relevant Information: - Targeted firms with ₹500 Cr+ debt; 20% resolution rate by 2018. - Replaced by IBC-led resolutions post-2018. - [2017-I] - Q128: Why is a plant called Prosopis juliflora often mentioned in news? - Options: (a) Its extract is widely used in cosmetics (b) It tends to reduce the biodiversity in the area in which it grows (c) Its extract is used in the synthesis of pesticides (d) None of the above - Answer: (b) It tends to reduce the biodiversity in the area in which it grows - Analysis: - Plant Overview: - Prosopis juliflora (mesquite, vilayati kikar), invasive shrub introduced from South America; widespread in India. - Key Terms: - Invasive Species: Outcompetes natives, reducing species richness; allelopathic chemicals inhibit other plants. - Biodiversity Loss: Disrupts ecosystems, e.g., native grasses in arid zones. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Cosmetics: No significant use; Prosopis used for fuel/charcoal. - (c) Pesticides: No evidence of extract use in synthesis. - (d) Option (b) correct. - Relevant Information: - Spread in Rajasthan, Gujarat; impacts Banni grasslands. - Control: Manual removal, biocontrol trials; economic use in biomass. - Q129: Which of the following statements best describes "carbon fertilization"? - Options: (a) Increased plant growth due to increased concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere (b) Increased temperature of Earth due to increased concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere (c) Increased acidity of oceans as a result of increased concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere (d) Adaptation of all living beings on Earth to the climate change brought about by the increased concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere - Answer: (a) Increased plant growth due to increased concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere - Analysis: - Concept Overview: - Carbon fertilization enhances photosynthesis due to elevated atmospheric CO₂, boosting plant growth (C₃ plants: \(6CO_2 + 6H_2O \to C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2\)). - Key Terms: - C₃ vs. C₄ Plants: C₃ (e.g., wheat) benefit more; C₄ (e.g., maize) less responsive. - Growth Yield: ~1% yield increase per 10 ppm CO₂ rise (current ~420 ppm). - Why Not Others?: - (b) Temperature increase: Greenhouse effect, not fertilization. - (c) Ocean acidity: Ocean acidification (CO₂ + H₂O \to H₂CO₃). - (d) Adaptation: Evolutionary, not fertilization effect. - Relevant Information: - Limits: Nutrient availability (N, P) constrains benefits. - India: Rice, wheat yields up 10-20% in CO₂-enriched experiments. - Q130: The term "sixth mass extinction/sixth extinction" is often mentioned in the news in the context of the discussion of: - Options: (a) Widespread monoculture practices in agriculture and large-scale commercial farming with indiscriminate use of chemicals in many parts of the world that may result in the loss of good native ecosystems (b) Fears of a possible collision of a meteorite with the Earth in the near future in the manner it happened 65 million years ago that caused the mass extinction of many species including those of dinosaurs (c) Large scale cultivation of genetically modified crops in many parts of the world and promoting their cultivation in other parts of the world which may cause the disappearance of good native crop plants and the loss of food biodiversity (d) Mankind's over-exploitation/misuse of natural resources, fragmentation/loss of natural habitats, destruction of ecosystems, pollution and global climate change - Answer: (d) Mankind's over-exploitation/misuse of natural resources, fragmentation/loss of natural habitats, destruction of ecosystems, pollution and global climate change - Analysis: - Extinction Overview: - Sixth mass extinction: Ongoing, human-driven loss of species; 1M species at risk (IPBES, 2019). - Key Terms: - Mass Extinction: >75% species loss in short geological time; previous five (e.g., Cretaceous, 65 Mya). - Anthropogenic Drivers: Habitat loss (70%), overexploitation (50%), climate change (20%). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Monoculture: Contributes, but narrower than (d). - (b) Meteorite: Hypothetical, not current driver. - (c) GM crops: Minor role compared to broader impacts in (d). - Relevant Information: - India: 10% of 50,000+ species threatened (IUCN). - Global: 1-10% species loss per decade; amphibians, corals worst hit. - Q131: How is the National Green Tribunal (NGT) different from the Central Pollution Control Board? - Statements: 1. The NGT has been established by an Act whereas the CPCB has been created by an executive order of the Government 2. The NGT provides environmental justice and helps reduce the burden of litigation in the higher courts whereas the CPCB promotes cleanliness of streams and wells, and aims to improve the quality of air in the country - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: (b) 2 only - Analysis: - Organizational Background: - NGT: Established by the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, with judicial powers to adjudicate environmental disputes. - CPCB: Constituted under the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974; later assigned powers under the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981. - Statement-wise Check: - Statement 1: Incorrect. - CPCB was not created by an executive order; it is a statutory body under an Act of Parliament. - Hence, the claim that it was created by executive order is wrong. - Statement 2: Correct. - NGT = quasi-judicial body ensuring environmental justice and reducing case load in higher courts. - CPCB = primarily a regulatory and monitoring agency, working on air and water quality, standards, and pollution control programmes. - Why not other options?: - (a) Incorrect → ignores the valid role differentiation in statement 2. - (c) Incorrect → includes the false statement 1. - (d) Incorrect → because statement 2 is valid. - Relevant Information: - NGT: Handles cases like Yamuna pollution, sand mining, industrial pollution. Has multiple benches and ensures time-bound resolution (within 6 months). - CPCB: Key role in National Clean Air Programme (NCAP), monitors 131 cities, maintains Air Quality Index (AQI) and Biological Oxygen Demand (BOD) standards for rivers. - Q132: Consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. The definition of "Critical Wildlife Habitat" is incorporated in the Forest Rights Act, 2006 2. For the first time in India, Baigas have been given Habitat Rights 3. Union Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change officially decides and declares Habitat Rights for Primitive and Vulnerable Tribal Groups in any part of India - Options: (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (a) 1 and 2 only - Analysis: - FRA Overview: - Forest Rights Act, 2006, recognizes rights of forest-dwelling communities, including tribals. - Key Terms: - Critical Wildlife Habitat (CWH): Forest areas inviolable for wildlife; defined under FRA Section 2(b). - Habitat Rights: Community rights to traditional habitats for Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs). - Statement Analysis: - 1. CWH in FRA: Correct. Defined for wildlife protection; relocation only with consent. - 2. Baiga Habitat Rights: Correct. First granted in MP (2016) for traditional forest use. - 3. MoEFCC Declares Habitat Rights: Incorrect. State governments, with MoEFCC guidelines, grant rights. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Includes incorrect 3. - (c) Excludes correct 1, 2. - (d) Includes incorrect 3. - Relevant Information: - Baiga: PVTG in MP; ~1,000 families got rights in Dindori. - FRA: 4M+ titles issued by 2025; CWH in 20+ PAs. - Q133: In which one of the following States is Pakhui Wildlife Sanctuary located? - Options: (a) Arunachal Pradesh (b) Manipur (c) Meghalaya (d) Nagaland - Answer: (a) Arunachal Pradesh - Analysis: - Sanctuary Overview: - Pakhui (Pakke) Wildlife Sanctuary, 862 sq km, in East Kameng, Arunachal Pradesh; part of Eastern Himalayas. - Key Terms: - Biodiversity Hotspot: Hosts tigers, hornbills, clouded leopards; Kameng River supports aquatic species. - Tiger Reserve: Declared 2002; ~60 tigers (2022). - Why Not Others?: - (b) Manipur: Keibul Lamjao, not Pakhui. - (c) Meghalaya: Balphakram, not Pakhui. - (d) Nagaland: Intanki, not Pakhui. - Relevant Information: - Adjacent to Nameri (Assam); key elephant corridor. - Community conservation by Nyishi tribe; eco-tourism focus. - Q134: The Partnership for Action on Green Economy (PAGE), a UN mechanism to assist countries transition towards greener and more inclusive economies, emerged at: - Options: (a) The Earth Summit on Sustainable Development 2002, Johannesburg (b) The United Nations Conference on Sustainable Development 2012, Rio de Janeiro (c) The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change 2015, Paris (d) The World Sustainable Development Summit 2016, New Delhi - Answer: (b) The United Nations Conference on Sustainable Development 2012, Rio de Janeiro - Analysis: - PAGE Overview: - Launched 2013, post-Rio+20; UNEP, UNDP, ILO, UNIDO, UNITAR partnership for green economy transitions. - Key Terms: - Green Economy: Low-carbon, inclusive growth; aligns with SDGs. - Rio+20: "The Future We Want" outcome catalyzed PAGE. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Johannesburg 2002: WSSD, focused JPOI, not PAGE. - (c) Paris 2015: Climate-focused, not green economy. - (d) WSDS 2016: TERI event, not UN-linked. - Relevant Information: - Supports 20+ countries; India joined 2018 for green policies. - Focus: Green jobs, renewable energy; $50M+ funding. - Q135: "Momentum for Change: Climate Neutral Now" is an initiative launched by: - Options: (a) The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (b) The UNEP Secretariat (c) The UNFCCC Secretariat (d) The World Meteorological Organisation - Answer: (c) The UNFCCC Secretariat - Analysis: - Initiative Overview: - Launched 2015 by UNFCCC; encourages carbon neutrality via measure-reduce-offset approach. - Key Terms: - Carbon Neutrality: Net-zero emissions through reductions, offsets (e.g., CERs). - Momentum for Change: UNFCCC program for climate solutions (e.g., lighthouses). - Why Not Others?: - (a) IPCC: Assesses science, not initiatives. - (b) UNEP: Hosts CCAC, not this. - (d) WMO: Weather data, not neutrality programs. - Relevant Information: - Aligns with Paris Agreement; 500+ organizations pledged. - India: Companies like Infosys use it for net-zero goals. - [2018-I] - Q136: Consider the following statements: - Statements: - 1. The Environment Protection Act, 1986 empowers the Government of India to state the requirement of public participation in the process of environmental protection, and the procedure and manner in which it is sought - 2. The Environment Protection Act, 1986 lays down the standards for emission or discharge of environmental pollutants from various sources - Which of the statements given above is/are correct? - Options: - (a) 1 only - (b) 2 only - (c) Both 1 and 2 - (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: - (b) 2 only - Analysis: - Overview of the Environment Protection Act, 1986: - Enacted post-Bhopal Gas Tragedy (1984), the EPA is India's cornerstone environmental legislation, aiming to protect and improve environmental quality, control pollution, and implement international commitments (e.g., Stockholm 1972). - Legal Framework: Empowers the Central Government under Section 3 to take all measures necessary for environmental protection, including rule-making, standard-setting, and coordination with State Governments. - Institutional Mechanism: Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) and State Pollution Control Boards (SPCBs) enforce standards; penalties under Sections 15–17 include fines (up to ₹1 lakh) and imprisonment (up to 7 years for repeated offenses). - Detailed Explanation of Statements: - Statement 1 (Public Participation): - Claim: EPA empowers the Government to mandate public participation and specify its procedure. - Analysis: Incorrect. The EPA's core text (Act No. 29 of 1986) focuses on governmental authority (e.g., Section 3(2) for measures like inspections, restrictions on industries). It does not explicitly mandate public participation or outline specific procedures for it. - Context: Public participation is incorporated indirectly through subordinate legislation, such as the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) Notification, 2006 (issued under EPA Rules), which mandates public hearings for projects like mining or dams. However, the Act itself is silent on requiring or detailing public involvement, making the statement factually inaccurate. - Evidence: Section 3(2)(v) allows restrictions on areas for environmental protection but does not mention public consultation. The EIA process, while critical, is a rule, not the Act's provision. - Statement 2 (Emission/Discharge Standards): - Claim: EPA lays down standards for pollutant emissions/discharges. - Analysis: Correct. Section 3(2)(b) empowers the Central Government to establish standards for environmental quality and pollutant emissions/discharges. The Environment (Protection) Rules, 1986, specify these standards (e.g., Schedule I for industrial effluents, Schedule VI for vehicular emissions). - Process: Standards cover parameters like BOD (Biochemical Oxygen Demand, e.g., <30 mg/L for inland discharge), PM2.5 (e.g., 40 μg/m³ annual mean), and SO₂ emissions (e.g., 50 kg/day for small boilers). CPCB monitors compliance, with industries required to submit Environmental Statements (Rule 14). - Example: National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS, 2009) set under EPA limit pollutants like NO₂ (\( \leq 40 \mu g/m^3 \)) annually. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1 only: - Incorrect: Statement 1 is false, as the EPA does not explicitly empower public participation mandates in its text. The focus is on regulatory control, not public involvement. - (c) Both 1 and 2: - Incorrect: While Statement 2 is true, Statement 1 is false, ruling out this option. Public participation, while encouraged in practice (e.g., via EIA), is not a core EPA provision. - (d) Neither 1 nor 2: - Incorrect: Statement 2 is accurate, as the EPA directly addresses emission/discharge standards, a key regulatory tool. - Additional Insights: - Policy Impact: EPA enabled India’s compliance with global agreements (e.g., Montreal Protocol for CFCs). It regulates ~2.7 million industries (CPCB, 2020). - Challenges: Enforcement gaps; only 60% of industries comply with standards (CAG 2019). Public participation, while valuable, faces issues like inadequate awareness (e.g., 30% EIA hearings lack quorum). - Global Comparison: Unlike the US Clean Air Act, which mandates public input, India’s EPA delegates this to rules, reflecting centralized governance. - Q137: In India, 'extended producer responsibility' was introduced as an important feature in which of the following? - Options: - (a) The Bio-medical Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 1998 - (b) The Recycled Plastic (Manufacturing and Usage) Rules, 1999 - (c) The e-Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 2011 - (d) The Food Safety and Standard Regulations, 2011 - Answer: - (c) The e-Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 2011 - Analysis: - Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) Concept: - Definition: EPR mandates producers (manufacturers/importers) to manage the end-of-life disposal, recycling, or treatment of their products to reduce environmental impact, aligning with the polluter-pays principle. - Mechanism: Producers must register with CPCB, establish collection systems (e.g., take-back centers), and meet recycling targets (e.g., 30% e-waste by weight in year 1, scaling to 70% by year 7). - Global Context: Rooted in OECD frameworks and Basel Convention (hazardous waste); India’s EPR aligns with EU’s WEEE Directive. - Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer: - e-Waste Rules, 2011: - Introduction: First Indian legislation to formalize EPR for electronic/electrical equipment (EEE) like mobiles, TVs, and computers. - Provisions: Producers must ensure environmentally sound management (ESM) of e-waste, including collection, storage, and recycling. Authorized recyclers process ~0.22 MT annually (2020). - Impact: India generates ~3.2 MT e-waste/year (Global E-waste Monitor, 2020); EPR targets reduce landfill dumping (70% e-waste informally handled). - Evolution: E-Waste Rules, 2016/2022 strengthened EPR with PROs (Producer Responsibility Organizations) and EPR certificate trading, akin to carbon credits. - Process Example: A mobile manufacturer must set up buy-back kiosks, channel e-waste to CPCB-authorized recyclers, and report compliance annually. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Bio-medical Waste Rules, 1998: - Incorrect: Focus on waste segregation, treatment (e.g., autoclaving, incineration at \( 850^\circ C \)), and disposal by generators (hospitals, clinics). Responsibility lies with occupiers, not producers (e.g., syringe manufacturers). - Analysis: ~0.6 MT biomedical waste/day (CPCB, 2020); no EPR framework, as focus is on point-source management. - (b) Recycled Plastic Rules, 1999: - Incorrect: Regulated plastic bag thickness (>20 microns), recycling marks, and banned single-use carry bags. EPR introduced later in Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016 (e.g., plastic producers manage 100% waste by 2024). - Analysis: Plastic waste ~9.4 MT/year; 1999 rules lacked producer accountability. - (d) Food Safety Regulations, 2011: - Incorrect: Under FSS Act, 2006, these regulate food quality, labeling, and contaminants (e.g., pesticide residues <0.01 mg/kg). No waste management or EPR provisions. - Analysis: Focus on consumer safety, not post-consumer waste. - Additional Insights: - EPR Expansion: Extended to plastics (2016), batteries (2020), tyres (2022); supports Swachh Bharat’s circular economy goals. - Challenges: Only 10% e-waste formally recycled; informal sector handles 90%, risking heavy metal leaching (e.g., Pb, Cd in soils). - Global Benchmark: EU achieves 55% e-waste recycling via EPR; India targets 60% by 2023. - Q138: Consider the following statements: - Statements: - 1. Asiatic lion is naturally found in India only - 2. Double-humped camel is naturally found in India only - 3. One-horned rhinoceros is naturally found in India only - Which one of the statement given above is/are correct? - Options: - (a) 1 only - (b) 2 only - (c) 1 and 3 only - (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: - (a) 1 only - Analysis: - Statement 1 (Asiatic Lion): - Correct. Asiatic lion (*Panthera leo persica*) survives only in the wild in India (Gir Forest and nearby areas, Gujarat). - Globally extinct in natural habitats outside India; last in Iran died mid-20th century. - Statement 2 (Double-humped Camel): - Incorrect. The double-humped (Bactrian) camel is native to Mongolia/China (wild populations in the Gobi Desert). - In India, found in Ladakh (Nubra Valley), but introduced and domesticated, not a unique natural range. - Statement 3 (One-horned Rhinoceros): - Incorrect in strict sense of “only in India.” - Greater one-horned rhino (*Rhinoceros unicornis*) exists in India (Kaziranga, Pobitora, Dudhwa) and Nepal (Chitwan, Bardiya). - Hence, not confined to India alone. - Why option (a) is correct: - Only Statement 1 is true. - Statement 2 is false, and Statement 3 is partially true but invalidated since Nepal also has a natural population. - Extra Insights: - India holds ~100% of Asiatic lions and ~80–85% of one-horned rhinos. - UPSC frames “naturally found only” strictly, hence option (a). - Q139: In the context of which of the following do some scientists suggest the use of cirrus cloud thinning technique and the injection of sulphate aerosol into stratosphere? - Options: - (a) Creating the artificial rains in some regions - (b) Reducing the frequency and intensity of tropical cyclones - (c) Reducing the adverse effects of the solar wind on the earth - (d) Reducing the global warming - Answer: - (d) Reducing the global warming - Analysis: - Geoengineering Overview: - Geoengineering involves large-scale interventions to mitigate climate change, divided into Carbon Dioxide Removal (CDR, e.g., afforestation) and Solar Radiation Management (SRM, e.g., albedo modification). - Scientific Context: IPCC AR6 (2021) evaluates SRM with low confidence due to risks but notes potential for 1–2°C cooling. - Detailed Explanation of Techniques: - Cirrus Cloud Thinning (CCT): - Process: Injects ice-nucleating particles (e.g., bismuth triiodide, \( BiI_3 \)) into the upper troposphere (10–15 km) to enhance ice crystal formation in cirrus clouds (high-altitude, 20–30% cloud cover). - Mechanism: Larger crystals reduce cloud optical depth, increasing outgoing longwave radiation (\( \lambda > 10 \mu m \), e.g., \( F = \sigma T^4 \), where \( \sigma = 5.67 \times 10^{-8} \, W/m^2K^4 \)). Net cooling effect ~0.5–1°C (Storelvmo et al., 2013). - Challenges: Limited to polar regions; microphysics uncertain (e.g., ice nucleation efficiency varies with \( T < -38^\circ C \)). - Sulphate Aerosol Injection (SAI): - Process: Injects sulphur dioxide (\( SO_2 \)) into the stratosphere (15–25 km) via aircraft or balloons, forming sulphate aerosols (\( H_2SO_4 \)). - Mechanism: Aerosols increase planetary albedo (reflectivity) by 1–2%, scattering shortwave radiation (\( \lambda = 0.3–0.7 \mu m \)). Mimics volcanic eruptions (e.g., Pinatubo 1991: 10 Tg \( SO_2 \), -0.5°C global cooling for 2 years). Radiative forcing reduction ~1–3 W/m². - Challenges: Risks ozone depletion (\( Cl + O_3 \to ClO + O_2 \)), acid rain, and monsoon disruption (e.g., 10% rainfall reduction in Sahel models). - Purpose: Both are SRM techniques to reduce global warming by counteracting greenhouse gas forcing (\( \Delta F \approx 3.7 \, W/m^2 \) for doubled CO₂). - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Creating artificial rains: - Incorrect: Rainmaking uses cloud seeding (e.g., silver iodide, \( AgI \), for cumulus clouds at 0–5 km). CCT/SAI target high-altitude cirrus/stratosphere, unrelated to precipitation. - Analysis: Seeding enhances droplet formation (\( H_2O_{(l)} \to H_2O_{(s)} \)); SRM focuses on radiation balance. - (b) Reducing tropical cyclones: - Incorrect: SRM may alter atmospheric dynamics (e.g., temperature gradients), but no direct evidence targets cyclone frequency/intensity. Models suggest mixed impacts (e.g., reduced Atlantic hurricanes, increased Indian Ocean). - Analysis: Cyclones driven by SSTs (\( T > 26.5^\circ C \)); SAI cools globally, not locally. - (c) Solar wind: - Incorrect: Solar wind (charged particles) affects magnetosphere; CCT/SAI operate in troposphere/stratosphere, irrelevant to space weather. - Analysis: Earth’s magnetic field deflects solar wind; no link to climate interventions. - Additional Insights: - Research: Harvard’s Solar Geoengineering Research Program (SCoPEx) tests SAI (1 kg \( CaCO_3 \)); CCT trials limited to models. - Ethical Issues: Governance gaps; unilateral deployment risks (e.g., termination shock if stopped abruptly, warming rebound ~1°C/decade). - India’s Stance: Opposes SRM (UNEA 2019); prioritizes mitigation (e.g., 500 GW renewables by 2030). - [2019-I] - Q140: Which one of the following is the Agasthyamala Biosphere Reserve? - Options: - (a) Neyyar, Peppara and Shendurney Wildlife Sanctuaries and Kalakad Mundanthurai Tiger Reserve - (b) Mudumalai, Sathyamangalam and Wayanad Wildlife Sanctuaries and Silent Valley National Park - (c) Kaundinya, Gundla Bhrameshwaram and Papikonda Wildlife Sanctuaries and Mukurthi National Park - (d) Kawal and Shree Venkateshwara Wildlife Sanctuaries; and Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam Tiger Reserve - Answer: - (a) Neyyar, Peppara and Shendurney Wildlife Sanctuaries and Kalakad Mundanthurai Tiger Reserve - Analysis: - Biosphere Reserve Context: - UNESCO’s Man and Biosphere (MAB) program designates biosphere reserves to balance biodiversity conservation, sustainable development, and research. India has 18 reserves (2023), with Agasthyamala added in 2016. - Structure: Core (inviolate), buffer (research/community use), and transition zones (human settlements). - Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer: - Agasthyamala Biosphere Reserve (ABR): - Location: Southern Western Ghats, spanning Kerala and Tamil Nadu (~3,500 km²). - Components: Includes Neyyar, Peppara, and Shendurney Wildlife Sanctuaries (Kerala) and Kalakad Mundanthurai Tiger Reserve (KMTR, Tamil Nadu). - Biodiversity: ~2,254 plant species (405 endemics), 87 mammals (e.g., lion-tailed macaque, Nilgiri tahr), 89 reptiles. Agasthyakoodam peak (1,868 m) is a biodiversity hotspot. - Ecological Role: Protects evergreen forests, regulates monsoon water flows (e.g., Neyyar River), and supports tribal communities like Kanikkar (~30,000 individuals). - Conservation: KMTR hosts ~80 tigers (2022 census); UNESCO status enhances global funding. - Why Not Other Options?: - (b) Mudumalai, Sathyamangalam, Wayanad, Silent Valley: - Incorrect: These form part of the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve (1986, ~5,520 km²), covering Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, and Kerala. Silent Valley is a national park, not in ABR. - Analysis: Nilgiri focuses on Nilgiri tahr, elephants; geographically distinct (northern Ghats vs. ABR’s southern tip). - (c) Kaundinya, Gundla Bhrameshwaram, Papikonda, Mukurthi: - Incorrect: Kaundinya, Gundla Bhrameshwaram, Papikonda are in Eastern Ghats (Andhra Pradesh); Mukurthi is in Nilgiri Biosphere (Tamil Nadu). Not part of ABR. - Analysis: Eastern Ghats have dry deciduous forests, unlike ABR’s wet evergreen; Mukurthi is Nilgiri-specific. - (d) Kawal, Shree Venkateshwara, Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam: - Incorrect: Located in Telangana/Andhra Pradesh (Deccan Plateau), part of Eastern Ghats or separate reserves. Unrelated to Western Ghats’ ABR. - Analysis: Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam is a tiger reserve (3,728 km²), not a biosphere reserve. - Additional Insights: - Threats: Deforestation (20% forest loss since 1980s), monoculture plantations (tea/rubber), and mining. - Community Role: Kanikkar tribes use ~200 medicinal plants; ABR promotes eco-tourism (e.g., Thenmala). - Global Significance: ABR’s 7.7% endemic flora vs. 3% global average; supports Paris Agreement biodiversity goals. - Q141: Consider the following pairs: - Wildlife: Naturally found in - 1. Blue-finned Mahseer: Cauvery River - 2. Irrawaddy Dolphin: Chambal River - 3. Rusty-spotted Cat: Eastern Ghats - Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched? - Options: - (a) 1 and 2 only - (b) 2 and 3 only - (c) 1 and 3 only - (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: - (c) 1 and 3 only - Analysis: - Wildlife Habitat Context: - Natural range refers to wild, non-introduced populations. India’s biodiversity (~8% global species) includes unique aquatic and terrestrial fauna. - Conservation Status: All species protected under Wildlife Protection Act (WPA), 1972; varying IUCN statuses. - Detailed Explanation of Pairs: - Pair 1 (Blue-finned Mahseer: Cauvery River): - Correct: Blue-finned Mahseer (Tor khudree, hump-backed phenotype) is endemic to fast-flowing rivers of the Western Ghats, notably Cauvery (Karnataka, Tamil Nadu). - Ecology: Migratory fish (spawns in headwaters, travels 100–200 km); supports ~75% of artisanal fishery yields in Cauvery (e.g., 10–15 tonnes/year in Hogenakkal). - Status: IUCN Endangered due to overfishing, dams (e.g., Mettur reduces spawning by 40%). - Pair 2 (Irrawaddy Dolphin: Chambal River): - Incorrect: Irrawaddy dolphin (Orcaella brevirostris) inhabits coastal waters, estuaries, and rivers like Chilika Lake (Odisha, ~150 individuals), Ganges-Brahmaputra delta. Chambal River (Rajasthan/MP) hosts Ganges river dolphin (Platanista gangetica, ~50 in Chambal). - Analysis: Irrawaddy is euryhaline (tolerates salinity gradients); Chambal’s freshwater ecology suits Ganges dolphin (India’s National Aquatic Animal). - Pair 3 (Rusty-spotted Cat: Eastern Ghats): - Correct: Rusty-spotted cat (Prionailurus rubiginosus), world’s smallest felid (~1–1.5 kg), inhabits dry deciduous forests and scrublands of Eastern Ghats (e.g., Andhra Pradesh, Odisha). - Ecology: Nocturnal, preys on rodents/birds; density ~0.5–1/km² in protected areas like Sri Venkateswara. - Status: IUCN Near Threatened; WPA Schedule I. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1 and 2 only: - Incorrect: Pair 2 is false (Irrawaddy not in Chambal); only Pair 1 is correct. - (b) 2 and 3 only: - Incorrect: Pair 2 is false; Pair 3 is correct but insufficient alone. - (d) 1, 2 and 3: - Incorrect: Pair 2’s inaccuracy rules out this option. - Additional Insights: - Conservation Efforts: Mahseer protected via river sanctuaries (e.g., Coorg); Ganges dolphin under Project Dolphin (2020); rusty-spotted cat benefits from Eastern Ghats corridors. - Threats: Dams (Cauvery: 30% flow reduction), pollution (Chambal: heavy metals), habitat loss (Eastern Ghats: 15% forest cover loss). - Global Context: India hosts ~90% of global Mahseer populations; Irrawaddy dolphins ~6,000 globally. - Q142: Why is there a great concern about the microbeads that are released into the environment? - Options: - (a) They are considered harmful to marine ecosystems - (b) They are considered to cause skin cancer in children - (c) They are small enough to be absorbed by crop plants in irrigated fields - (d) They are often found to be used as food adulterants - Answer: - (a) They are considered harmful to marine ecosystems - Analysis: - Microbeads Overview: - Definition: Tiny plastic particles (<5 mm, typically 10–500 μm) used as exfoliants in cosmetics (e.g., face washes, toothpaste) or industrial abrasives; made of polyethylene (PE) or polystyrene (PS). - Environmental Pathway: Enter waterways via wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs, remove <99% due to small size); ~8 trillion beads/day globally (NOAA, 2015). - Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer: - Marine Ecosystem Impact: - Ingestion: Mistaken for plankton by marine organisms (e.g., zooplankton, fish); bioaccumulates in food chains (e.g., tuna, sharks). - Toxicity: Adsorb persistent organic pollutants (POPs, e.g., PCBs at \( 10^5–10^6 \) times water concentration); cause liver toxicity, reproductive issues (e.g., 20% reduced fecundity in copepods). - Scale: ~1,500–1.1 million beads/m² in Great Lakes; Indian Ocean estimates ~0.1–1 mg/L in surface waters. - Physical Harm: Entangle corals, clog gills (e.g., 30% mortality in juvenile fish). - Example: Arabian Sea studies show microplastics in 80% of fish samples, impacting India’s fisheries (~3.5 MT/year). - Why Not Other Options?: - (b) Skin cancer in children: - Incorrect: Microbeads are rinsed off during use; no evidence links topical exposure to cancer. Carcinogens like benzene in cosmetics are unrelated. - Analysis: Health concerns focus on inhalation of volatile compounds, not microbeads. - (c) Absorption by crop plants: - Incorrect: Microplastics accumulate in soils (e.g., 0.1–1% by weight in agricultural fields), but absorption is minimal (nanoplastics <100 nm may translocate). Primary concern is marine, not terrestrial. - Analysis: Irrigation spreads microplastics, but plant uptake is negligible vs. marine ingestion. - (d) Food adulterants: - Incorrect: Microbeads are not used in food; contamination occurs via environmental pathways (e.g., fish consumption). - Analysis: Food safety laws (FSSAI) address chemical adulterants, not plastics. - Additional Insights: - Policy Response: India banned microbeads in cosmetics (Plastic Waste Rules, 2022); US Microbead-Free Waters Act (2015); EU REACH restriction (2023). - Alternatives: Natural exfoliants (e.g., sugar, apricot shells); biodegradable polymers (e.g., PLA). - Global Scale: ~94,500 tonnes/year microbeads; 8 MT plastics enter oceans annually. - Q143: Consider the following: - Substances: - 1. Carbon monoxide - 2. Methane - 3. Ozone - 4. Sulphur dioxide - Which of the above are released into the atmosphere due to the burning of crop/biomass residue? - Options: - (a) 1 and 2 only - (b) 2, 3 and 4 only - (c) 1 and 4 only - (d) 1, 2, 3 and 4 - Answer: - (d) 1, 2, 3 and 4 - Analysis: - Biomass Burning Context: - Crop residue burning (e.g., rice/wheat stubble) is prevalent in India (~92 MT/year, Punjab/Haryana); contributes ~25% to Delhi’s PM2.5 during winter (IITM, 2020). - Chemistry: Incomplete combustion releases gases and aerosols; governed by \( C_xH_yO_z + O_2 \to CO, CO_2, CH_4, SO_2, VOCs + \text{particulates} \). - Detailed Explanation of Substances: - 1. Carbon Monoxide (CO): - Process: Incomplete combustion (\( C + \frac{1}{2}O_2 \to CO \)) due to low oxygen; ~10–20% of emissions (824 Gg/year, TERI 2019). - Impact: Toxic, reduces O₂-carrying capacity in blood (binds hemoglobin 200x stronger); contributes to urban smog. - 2. Methane (CH₄): - Process: Released from anaerobic pockets in biomass fires; ~1–2% of emissions (0.5 Tg/year). Formed via pyrolysis (\( C_6H_{12}O_6 \to CH_4 + \text{volatiles} \)). - Impact: GHG with GWP 28x CO₂ over 100 years; amplifies warming (~0.5 W/m² forcing). - 3. Ozone (O₃): - Process: Not directly emitted; formed via photochemical reactions of precursors (VOCs, NOx) from burning (\( VOC + NO + h\nu \to O_3 \)). Biomass burning contributes ~5–10% to tropospheric O₃ in India. - Impact: Ground-level O₃ damages crops (e.g., 10–15% wheat yield loss) and respiratory health. - 4. Sulphur Dioxide (SO₂): - Process: Oxidation of sulfur in biomass (\( S + O_2 \to SO_2 \)); ~0.1–0.5% emissions due to low sulfur content (~0.2% in crop residue). - Impact: Forms sulfate aerosols (\( SO_2 + OH \to H_2SO_4 \)), contributing to acid rain and PM2.5. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1 and 2 only: - Incorrect: Misses O₃ (secondary) and SO₂ (direct); both significant in biomass burning. - (b) 2, 3 and 4 only: - Incorrect: Excludes CO, a primary pollutant (~15% emission share). - (c) 1 and 4 only: - Incorrect: Misses CH₄ (direct) and O₃ (secondary); both critical in stubble burning. - Additional Insights: - Scale: India emits ~211 Tg CO₂e from crop burning annually; Punjab alone burns 20 MT residue. - Mitigation: Happy Seeder machines (reduces burning by 80%), bioenergy conversion (e.g., 1 MT residue = 0.4 MW electricity). - Global Context: Biomass burning contributes ~20% global CO, 10% CH₄ emissions (IPCC AR6). - Q144: Consider the following statements: - Statements: - 1. Agricultural soils release nitrogen oxides into the environment - 2. Cattle release ammonia into the environment - 3. Poultry industry releases reactive nitrogen compounds into the environment - Which of the statements given above is/are correct? - Options: - (a) 1 and 3 only - (b) 2 and 3 only - (c) 2 only - (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: - (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Analysis: - Reactive Nitrogen (Nr) Context: - Nr includes compounds like NOₓ (NO, NO₂), N₂O, NH₃; agriculture contributes ~70% global Nr emissions (120 Tg N/year, IPCC AR6). - Impact: Eutrophication, air pollution (PM2.5), GHG emissions (N₂O GWP 265x CO₂). - Detailed Explanation of Statements: - Statement 1 (Agricultural soils release nitrogen oxides): - Correct: Soils emit NO and N₂O via microbial processes: - Nitrification: \( NH_4^+ + 2O_2 \to NO_3^- + 2H^+ + H_2O \), releases NO as byproduct. - Denitrification: \( NO_3^- \to NO_2^- \to NO \to N_2O \to N_2 \), releases NO/N₂O. - Scale: India’s soils emit ~0.8 Tg N₂O-N/year (70% of national N₂O); fertilizer overuse (e.g., 20 MT urea/year) amplifies emissions. - Example: Paddy fields emit ~0.3–0.5 kg N₂O/ha annually. - Statement 2 (Cattle release ammonia): - Correct: Cattle manure/urine hydrolyzes urea (\( (NH_2)_2CO + H_2O \to 2NH_3 + CO_2 \)); ~80% of India’s NH₃ emissions (4 Tg/year) from livestock. - Scale: India’s 192 million cattle (2019 census) emit ~15–20% of excreted N as NH₃ via volatilization. - Impact: NH₃ forms ammonium aerosols, contributing to PM2.5 (e.g., 30% winter smog in Delhi). - Statement 3 (Poultry industry releases reactive nitrogen): - Correct: Poultry excreta (uric acid, \( C_5H_4N_4O_3 \)) decomposes to NH₃ and other Nr compounds (e.g., nitrates via \( C_5H_4N_4O_3 \to NH_4^+ \)). - Scale: India’s poultry (850 million birds, 6% annual growth) emits ~0.4 Tg Nr/year (CPCB, 2020). - Impact: NH₃ from poultry farms contributes to localized eutrophication (e.g., 10–15% lake nutrient loading). - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1 and 3 only: - Incorrect: Excludes cattle (major NH₃ source, ~60% of ag NH₃). - (b) 2 and 3 only: - Incorrect: Misses soil NOₓ/N₂O, a significant GHG source. - (c) 2 only: - Incorrect: Ignores soil and poultry contributions, both substantial. - Additional Insights: - Mitigation: Precision fertigation (reduces N₂O by 20%), manure management (e.g., anaerobic digesters cut NH₃ by 50%). - Policy: National Clean Air Programme (NCAP) targets NH₃ reduction; India’s Nr emissions ~10% global total. - Environmental Impact: Nr causes 30% of India’s water body eutrophication; N₂O contributes 6% to national GHG inventory. - [2020-I] - Q145: Which of the following are the reasons/factors for exposure to benzene pollution? - Factors: - 1. Automobile exhaust - 2. Tobacco smoke - 3. Wood burning - 4. Using varnished wooden furniture - 5. Using products made of polyurethane - Select the correct answer using the code given below: - Options: - (a) 1, 2 and 3 only - (b) 2 and 4 only - (c) 1, 3 and 4 only - (d) 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 - Answer: - (a) 1, 2 and 3 only - Analysis: - Benzene Pollution Context: - Benzene (C₆H₆): Volatile organic compound (VOC), IARC Group 1 carcinogen; exposure mainly through combustion and smoke. - Primary urban sources are transport, tobacco smoke, and biomass burning. - Detailed Explanation of Factors: - 1. Automobile Exhaust: - Correct. Incomplete combustion of petrol releases benzene (~50% of ambient urban benzene). - 2. Tobacco Smoke: - Correct. Cigarettes release significant benzene (~500 μg/cigarette), major indoor contributor. - 3. Wood Burning: - Correct. Biomass stoves and firewood release benzene during pyrolysis, key source in rural households. - 4. Varnished Wooden Furniture: - Not counted in UPSC framing. While varnishes may emit VOCs, benzene is rarely a dominant component in regulated furniture finishes. - 5. Polyurethane Products: - Not included. Off-gassing mainly releases isocyanates and other VOCs, not significant benzene exposure. - Why option (a) is correct: - Only 1, 2, 3 are standardly recognized as benzene sources in UPSC context. - 4 and 5 are minor/indirect, not part of UPSC’s expected answer key. - Extra Insights: - Health: Chronic benzene exposure → bone marrow suppression, leukemia. - India: Ambient benzene in cities often 2–3× WHO limits. - Q146: With reference to India’s Desert National Park, which of the following statements are correct? - Statements: - 1. It is spread over two districts - 2. There is no human habitation inside the Park - 3. It is one of the natural habitats of the Great Indian Bustard - Select the correct answer using the code given below: - Options: - (a) 1 and 2 only - (b) 2 and 3 only - (c) 1 and 3 only - (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: - (c) 1 and 3 only - Analysis: - Desert National Park (DNP) Context: - Located in Thar Desert, Rajasthan; ~3,162 km²; established 1980 to conserve arid biodiversity. - Features: Fossil beds (180 MYA), sand dunes, grasslands; critical for IUCN Critically Endangered species. - Detailed Explanation of Statements: - Statement 1 (Spread over two districts): - Correct: DNP spans Jaisalmer (1,900 km²) and Barmer (1,262 km²), Rajasthan. - Evidence: MoEFCC delineates DNP’s administrative boundaries across these districts. - Statement 2 (No human habitation): - Incorrect: ~500 Maldhari and pastoralist villages exist within DNP’s buffer/transition zones; ~5,000 people engage in grazing, small-scale farming. - Analysis: WPA allows regulated human activity in buffer zones; relocations ongoing but not complete. - Statement 3 (Great Indian Bustard habitat): - Correct: DNP is a primary habitat for Great Indian Bustard (Ardeotis nigriceps, ~150 individuals); supports breeding grounds in grasslands. - Conservation: GIB population declined 90% since 1970s; DNP hosts ~30% of India’s GIB. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1 and 2 only: - Incorrect: Statement 2 is false due to human presence. - (b) 2 and 3 only: - Incorrect: Statement 2 is false. - (d) 1, 2 and 3: - Incorrect: Statement 2’s inaccuracy rules it out. - Additional Insights: - Biodiversity: DNP hosts chinkara, desert fox, 40 reptile species; 180 MYA fossils unique globally. - Threats: Solar farms, wind turbines reduce GIB habitat (~20% loss since 2000). - Policy: GIB recovery plan (2017) includes DNP fencing, power line burial. - Q147: Consider the following statements: - Statements: - 1. 36% of India’s districts are classified as “overexploited” or “critical” by the Central Ground Water Authority (CGWA) - 2. CGWA was formed under the Environment (Protection) Act - 3. India has the largest area under groundwater irrigation in the world - Which of the statements given above is/are correct? - Options: - (a) 1 only - (b) 2 and 3 only - (c) 2 only - (d) 1 and 3 only - Answer: - (b) 2 and 3 only - Analysis: - Groundwater Context: - India extracts ~251 BCM groundwater annually (CGWA, 2020), ~25% of global total; agriculture uses 89%. - CGWA regulates via Ground Water Extraction (GWE) norms under EPA, 1986. - Detailed Explanation of Statements: - Statement 1 (36% districts overexploited/critical): - Incorrect: CGWA’s 2020 assessment (7,327 units) classifies ~17% (1,186 overexploited, 313 critical) of assessment units, not districts. Districts (~739) don’t align with hydrogeological units. - Analysis: Overexploitation defined as extraction > recharge; Punjab/Haryana >100% stage of extraction. - Statement 2 (CGWA under EPA): - Correct: CGWA constituted under Section 3(3) of EPA, 1986, as an apex regulatory body to manage groundwater, notify critical areas, and issue NOCs for extraction. - Role: Regulates ~1.5 million industrial/agricultural bores; fines up to ₹2 crore for violations. - Statement 3 (Largest groundwater irrigation area): - Correct: India irrigates ~39 million ha via groundwater (67% of total irrigated area), surpassing China (~19 million ha) and USA (~17 million ha). - Evidence: 20 million tube wells; ~90% of rural water supply. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1 only: - Incorrect: Statement 1 is false; 17% units, not 36% districts. - (c) 2 only: - Incorrect: Statement 3 is true, reflecting India’s global lead. - (d) 1 and 3 only: - Incorrect: Statement 1 is false. - Additional Insights: - Challenges: 63% national groundwater stage; 30% wells show declining levels (0.3 m/year). - Policy: Atal Bhujal Yojana (2020) targets 78 districts; micro-irrigation saves 20–30% water. - Global: India’s extraction ~2x sustainable recharge in northern states. - Q148: Among the following Tiger Reserves, which one has the largest area under “Critical Tiger Habitat”? - Options: - (a) Corbett - (b) Ranthambore - (c) Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam - (d) Sunderbans - Answer: - (c) Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam - Analysis: - Critical Tiger Habitat (CTH) Context: - Defined under WPA 1972 (2006 amendment); inviolate core zones for tiger breeding, minimum 800–1,000 km²; no human activity permitted post-relocation. - India’s 53 tiger reserves cover ~75,000 km²; NTCA oversees. - Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer: - Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam Tiger Reserve (NSTR): - Location: Andhra Pradesh/Telangana, Nallamala Hills; total area ~3,728 km², CTH ~1,200 km² (largest in India). - Features: Dry deciduous forests, supports ~60 tigers (2022); Chenchu tribes relocated. - Evidence: NTCA’s 2018 delineation confirms CTH extent. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Corbett: - Incorrect: Uttarakhand, ~821 km² CTH; smaller than NSTR. - Analysis: ~70 tigers, Himalayan foothills, but less core area. - (b) Ranthambore: - Incorrect: Rajasthan, ~392 km² CTH; smallest among options. - Analysis: ~50 tigers, high tourism but limited inviolate zone. - (d) Sunderbans: - Incorrect: West Bengal, ~1,699 km² total, ~1,000 km² CTH; mangroves limit core expansion. - Analysis: ~90 tigers, unique saline habitat. - Additional Insights: - Tiger Population: India hosts 3,167 tigers (2022, 70% global); NSTR’s large CTH critical for genetic diversity. - Challenges: Poaching, human-wildlife conflict (e.g., 10% tiger mortality in NSTR). - Policy: Project Tiger (1973) expanded CTHs; India aims for 4,000 tigers by 2030. - Q149: If a particular plant species is placed under Schedule VI of The Wildlife Protection Act, 1972, what is the implication? - Options: - (a) A licence is required to cultivate that plant - (b) Such a plant cannot be cultivated under any circumstances - (c) It is a Genetically Modified crop plant - (d) Such a plant is invasive and harmful to the ecosystem - Answer: - (a) A licence is required to cultivate that plant - Analysis: - Schedule VI Context: - WPA 1972 (amended 2002) lists six protected plant species in Schedule VI to prevent overexploitation; includes Red Vanda, Blue Vanda, Kuth, Pitcher plant, Beddomes’ cycad, Ladies slipper orchid. - Provisions: Prohibits picking, uprooting, or trading wild specimens; cultivation regulated via permits. - Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer: - Implication: Cultivation of Schedule VI plants requires a license from the Chief Wildlife Warden (CWLW) under Section 17C; ensures sustainable use, prevents illegal trade. - Process: Applicants submit cultivation plans; licenses issued for nurseries, research (e.g., ~100 permits/year for orchids). - Example: Red Vanda (Vanda tessellata) cultivation in Kerala nurseries requires CWLW approval to curb wild harvesting. - Why Not Other Options?: - (b) Cannot be cultivated under any circumstances: - Incorrect: Cultivation is permitted with a license;
