IEA as Under2 Coalition Secretariat: - Incorrect: Under2 Coalition (subnational governments) secretariat is Climate Group, not IEA. - Analysis: IEA advises, but Climate Group manages Under2 (e.g., Andhra Pradesh member). - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1, 2, 4 and 5: - Incorrect: 2 and 5 false (IEA not involved). - (c) 2, 3 and 5: - Incorrect: 2 and 5 false; misses Climate Group (1). - (d) All: - Incorrect: 2 and 5 false. - Additional Insights: - India: EP100 members cut 15% emissions; align with India’s 45% intensity reduction goal. - Challenges: Only 5% Indian firms in EP100; scaling limited by costs. - Global: EP100’s 130 firms represent $1T revenue; 0.2 GtCO₂e savings potential. - Q172: “If rainforests and tropical forests are the lungs of the Earth, then surely wetlands function as its kidneys.” Which one of the following functions of wetlands best reflects the above statement? - Options: - (a) The water cycle in wetlands involves surface runoff, subsoil percolation and evaporation - (b) Algae form the nutrient base upon which fish, crustaceans, molluscs, birds, reptiles and mammals thrive - (c) Wetlands play a vital role in maintaining sedimentation balance and soil stabilization - (d) Aquatic plants absorb heavy metals and excess nutrients - Answer: - (d) Aquatic plants absorb heavy metals and excess nutrients - Analysis: - Wetlands as Kidneys: - Wetlands filter pollutants, akin to kidneys removing waste; India’s 75 Ramsar sites cover 1.3 million ha. - Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer: - Pollutant Absorption: - Mechanism: Aquatic plants (e.g., Phragmites, Typha) uptake heavy metals (e.g., Pb, Cd, ~1–10 mg/kg) and nutrients (e.g., N, P, ~50–100 kg/ha). - Process: Phytoremediation (\( M^{2+} + \text{plant biomass} \to M\text{-bound complex} \)) reduces eutrophication, improves water quality. - Example: Chilika Lake removes 60% N, 40% P via aquatic vegetation. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Water cycle: - Incorrect: Describes hydrology, not filtration (kidney analogy). - Analysis: Runoff/percolation universal, not wetland-specific. - (b) Algae nutrient base: - Incorrect: Food web support is ecological, not filtration-focused. - Analysis: Algae support biodiversity, not pollutant removal. - (c) Sedimentation, stabilization: - Incorrect: Prevents erosion, not directly tied to kidney function. - Analysis: Physical role, not chemical filtration. - Additional Insights: - India: Wetlands remove 0.1 Mt pollutants/year; support 20% fish production. - Threats: 30% wetland loss since 1990s; urbanization, pollution. - Global: Wetlands sequester 0.2 GtC/year; critical for SDG 6 (clean water). - Q173: In the context of WHO Air Quality Guidelines, consider the following statements: - Statements: - 1. The 24-hour mean of PM2.5 should not exceed 15 µg/m³ and annual mean of PM2.5 should not exceed 5 µg/m³ - 2. In a year, the highest levels of ozone pollution occur during the periods of inclement weather - 3. PM10 can penetrate the lung barrier and enter the bloodstream - 4. Excessive ozone in the air can trigger asthma - Which of the statements given above are correct? - Options: - (a) 1, 3 and 4 - (b) 1 and 4 only - (c) 2, 3 and 4 - (d) 1 and 2 only - Answer: - (b) 1 and 4 only - Analysis: - WHO Air Quality Guidelines (2021) Context: - Set health-based thresholds for pollutants; India’s NAAQS less stringent (e.g., PM2.5 annual 40 µg/m³). - Detailed Explanation of Statements: - 1. PM2.5 thresholds: - Correct: WHO 2021 guidelines: PM2.5 24-hour mean ≤15 µg/m³, annual mean ≤5 µg/m³ to minimize health risks (e.g., 10% mortality increase per 10 µg/m³). - Evidence: India’s urban PM2.5 ~60–100 µg/m³, 10x WHO limit. - 2. Ozone during inclement weather: - Incorrect: Ozone (O₃) peaks in sunny, warm conditions (photochemical formation, \( VOC + NO_x + h\nu \to O_3 \)); inclement weather (rain, clouds) reduces O₃. - Analysis: Delhi’s O₃ peaks in summer (~80 ppb), not monsoons. - 3. PM10 enters bloodstream: - Incorrect: PM10 (<10 µm) lodges in lungs; PM2.5 (<2.5 µm) penetrates bloodstream. - Analysis: PM10 causes respiratory issues, not systemic circulation. - 4. Ozone triggers asthma: - Correct: Excessive O₃ (>70 ppb) irritates airways, increases asthma attacks by 20% (WHO). - Example: Urban India’s O₃ levels (~50–100 ppb) exacerbate respiratory conditions. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1, 3 and 4: - Incorrect: PM10 (3) doesn’t enter bloodstream. - (c) 2, 3 and 4: - Incorrect: 2 and 3 false. - (d) 1 and 2 only: - Incorrect: Ozone peaks (2) false. - Additional Insights: - India: NCAP targets 30% PM2.5 reduction by 2024; 90% cities exceed WHO limits. - Health: PM2.5 causes 1.6 million deaths/year in India; O₃ linked to 10% COPD cases. - Global: WHO guidelines aim to save 80% of air pollution-related deaths. - Q174: With reference to polyethylene terephthalate, the use of which is so widespread in our daily lives, consider the following statements: - Statements: - 1. Its fibres can be blended with wool and cotton fibres to reinforce their properties - 2. Containers made of it can be used to store any alcoholic beverage - 3. Bottles made of it can be recycled into other products - 4. Articles made of it can be easily disposed of by incineration without causing greenhouse gas emissions - Which of the statements given above are correct? - Options: - (a) 1 and 3 - (b) 2 and 4 - (c) 1 and 4 - (d) 2 and 3 - Answer: - (a) 1 and 3 - Analysis: - Polyethylene Terephthalate (PET) Context: - Thermoplastic polymer (C₁₀H₈O₄)ₙ; used in bottles, textiles; India produces ~1.5 MT/year. - Detailed Explanation of Statements: - 1. Blended with wool/cotton: - Correct: PET fibres (polyester) blended with wool/cotton for durability, wrinkle resistance; ~60% of India’s textiles use PET blends. - Example: PET-cotton shirts improve tensile strength by 20%. - 2. Store any alcoholic beverage: - Incorrect: PET suitable for low-alcohol drinks (e.g., beer, <10% ABV); high-alcohol (e.g., spirits, >40% ABV) causes leaching of acetaldehyde. - Analysis: Glass preferred for high-proof liquors. - 3. Recycled into products: - Correct: PET bottles recycled into fibres, containers (e.g., rPET); India recycles ~60% of 1 MT PET bottles/year. - Process: \( \text{PET} \to \text{Flakes} \to \text{Pellets} \to \text{Fibres/Containers} \). - 4. Incineration without GHG emissions: - Incorrect: Incineration (\( (C_{10}H_8O_4)_n + O_2 \to CO_2 + H_2O \)) emits ~2.5 kg CO₂/kg PET. - Analysis: Contributes to 0.1 GtCO₂e/year globally. - Why Not Other Options?: - (b) 2 and 4: - Incorrect: Both false (leaching, GHG emissions). - (c) 1 and 4: - Incorrect: Incineration (4) emits GHGs. - (d) 2 and 3: - Incorrect: Alcohol storage (2) false. - Additional Insights: - India: PET recycling saves 0.2 MtCO₂e/year; 30% uncollected waste. - Policy: Plastic Waste Rules, 2022 mandate 100% PET recycling by 2025. - Global: PET constitutes 12% of plastic production; 50% recycled in EU. - Q175: Which of the following is not a bird? - Options: - (a) Golden Mahseer - (b) Indian Nightjar - (c) Spoonbill - (d) White Ibis - Answer: - (a) Golden Mahseer - Analysis: - Biodiversity Context: - India’s ~1,350 bird species contrast with diverse fish fauna; WPA protects birds (Schedule I/IV). - Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer: - Golden Mahseer: - Fish (Tor putitora), Himalayan rivers; IUCN Endangered, not a bird. - Ecology: Migratory, supports ~50% Himalayan fishery yields. - Why Not Other Options?: - (b) Indian Nightjar: - Bird (Caprimulgus asiaticus), nocturnal, widespread; ~0.1 million pairs. - (c) Spoonbill: - Bird (Platalea leucorodia), wetlands; ~10,000 in India, WPA Schedule I. - (d) White Ibis: - Bird (Threskiornis melanocephalus), marshes; ~20,000, IUCN Near Threatened. - Additional Insights: - Conservation: Mahseer protected via river sanctuaries; birds under BirdLife International. - Threats: Dams (50% Mahseer habitat loss), wetland loss (30% for ibis). - Global: India’s bird diversity critical for IBA network; Mahseer unique to Himalayas. - Q176: Which of the following are nitrogen-fixing plants? - Plants: - 1. Alfalfa - 2. Amaranth - 3. Chickpea - 4. Clover - 5. Purslane (Kulfa) - 6. Spinach - Select the correct answer using the code given below: - Options: - (a) 1, 3 and 4 only - (b) 1, 3, 5 and 6 only - (c) 2, 4, 5 and 6 only - (d) 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 - Answer: - (a) 1, 3 and 4 only - Analysis: - Nitrogen Fixation Context: - Process: Symbiotic bacteria (e.g., Rhizobium) convert N₂ to NH₃ (\( N_2 + 8H^+ + 8e^- \to 2NH_3 + H_2 \)); legumes fix 50–200 kg N/ha. - Detailed Explanation of Plants: - 1. Alfalfa (Medicago sativa): - Correct: Legume, fixes ~100–200 kg N/ha via Rhizobium; used as fodder. - 2. Amaranth (Amaranthus spp.): - Incorrect: Non-legume, no N-fixation; grown for grains, leaves. - 3. Chickpea (Cicer arietinum): - Correct: Legume, fixes ~50–100 kg N/ha; India produces 70% globally (10 MT/year). - 4. Clover (Trifolium spp.): - Correct: Legume, fixes ~100–150 kg N/ha; used in pastures. - 5. Purslane (Portulaca oleracea): - Incorrect: Non-legume, no N-fixation; edible weed. - 6. Spinach (Spinacia oleracea): - Incorrect: Non-legume, no N-fixation; leafy vegetable. - Why Not Other Options?: - (b) 1, 3, 5 and 6: - Incorrect: Purslane, spinach non-fixing. - (c) 2, 4, 5 and 6: - Incorrect: Amaranth, purslane, spinach non-fixing; misses alfalfa, chickpea. - (d) 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6: - Incorrect: Only legumes (1, 3, 4) fix nitrogen. - Additional Insights: - India: Legumes reduce fertilizer use by 20% (2 MT urea saved). - Benefits: N-fixation cuts N₂O emissions (0.1 MtCO₂e/year). - Global: Legumes contribute 30% of agricultural N input. - Q177: “Biorock technology” is talked about in which one of the following situations? - Options: - (a) Restoration of damaged coral reefs - (b) Development of building materials using plant residues - (c) Identification of areas for exploration/extraction of shale gas - (d) Providing salt licks for wild animals in forests/protected areas - Answer: - (a) Restoration of damaged coral reefs - Analysis: - Biorock Technology Context: - Developed by Wolf Hilbertz (1970s); uses low-voltage electricity to promote coral growth. - Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer: - Coral Reef Restoration: - Process: Submerged steel structures receive electric current (1–2 V), inducing CaCO₃ precipitation (\( Ca^{2+} + HCO_3^- \to CaCO_3 + H^+ \)); corals grow 3–5x faster. - Impact: Restores 20–30% of degraded reefs; India’s Gulf of Kutch project revived 0.1 km². - Example: Agatti Island (Lakshadweep) uses Biorock for coral regeneration. - Why Not Other Options?: - (b) Building materials: - Incorrect: Plant residues for bio-bricks, not Biorock. - Analysis: Biorock is marine-specific. - (c) Shale gas exploration: - Incorrect: Geological surveys, not Biorock. - Analysis: Shale gas uses seismic mapping. - (d) Salt licks: - Incorrect: Mineral supplements for wildlife; unrelated to Biorock. - Analysis: Salt licks are terrestrial. - Additional Insights: - India: 2,500 km² coral reefs; 50% degraded (MoEFCC, 2020). - Benefits: Biorock boosts fish stocks (20% biomass increase). - Global: Used in 30 countries; supports 0.01 GtC sequestration. - Q178: The “Miyawaki method” is well known for the: - Options: - (a) Promotion of commercial farming in arid and semi-arid areas - (b) Development of gardens using genetically modified flora - (c) Creation of mini forests in urban areas - (d) Harvesting wind energy on coastal areas and on sea surfaces - Answer: - (c) Creation of mini forests in urban areas - Analysis: - Miyawaki Method Context: - Developed by Akira Miyawaki (Japan); plants native species densely to create fast-growing forests. - Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer: - Mini Forests: - Process: Plants 30–50 species/m² (10x conventional); grows 10x faster, sequesters 0.5–1 tCO₂/ha/year. - Impact: India’s 200+ Miyawaki forests (e.g., Mumbai, Bengaluru) cover ~0.1 km², enhance urban biodiversity. - Example: Chennai’s 1,000 m² forest sequesters 2 tCO₂/year. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Commercial farming: - Incorrect: Miyawaki is ecological, not agricultural. - Analysis: Arid farming uses drip irrigation, not dense planting. - (b) GM flora gardens: - Incorrect: Uses native species, not GM plants. - Analysis: GM regulated under Biosafety Rules, not Miyawaki. - (d) Wind energy: - Incorrect: Wind turbines unrelated; Miyawaki is forestry. - Analysis: Coastal wind farms use turbines, not plantations. - Additional Insights: - India: Miyawaki adopted in 20 cities; 30% biodiversity increase. - Challenges: High initial cost ($5,000/ha); water-intensive. - Global: 3,000 Miyawaki forests; 0.1 GtCO₂e sequestration potential. - Q179: Among the following crops, which one is the most important anthropogenic source of both methane and nitrous oxide? - Options: - (a) Cotton - (b) Rice - (c) Sugarcane - (d) Wheat - Answer: - (b) Rice - Analysis: - Agricultural GHG Context: - Agriculture emits ~14% global GHGs; methane (CH₄, GWP 28) and nitrous oxide (N₂O, GWP 265) key. - Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer: - Rice: - Methane: Flooded paddies create anaerobic conditions, producing CH₄ (\( C_6H_{12}O_6 \to 3CH_4 + 3CO_2 \)); ~1.5% global CH₄ (0.5 GtCO₂e/year). - Nitrous Oxide: Fertilizer use (e.g., urea, 20 MT/year in India) leads to N₂O via denitrification (\( NO_3^- \to N_2O \)); ~0.3 Tg N₂O-N/year. - Scale: India’s 44 Mha rice fields emit 20% of agricultural GHGs. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Cotton: - Incorrect: High pesticide use, low CH₄; N₂O from fertilizers (~0.1 Tg/year). - Analysis: Upland crop, no anaerobic CH₄. - (c) Sugarcane: - Incorrect: Moderate N₂O from fertilizers; minimal CH₄ (aerobic soils). - Analysis: 5 Mha in India, 5% of ag GHGs. - (d) Wheat: - Incorrect: N₂O from fertilizers (0.2 Tg/year); negligible CH₄. - Analysis: Dryland crop, low anaerobic emissions. - Additional Insights: - India: Rice contributes 50% of ag CH₄, 30% N₂O. - Mitigation: SRI reduces CH₄ by 20%, N₂O by 10%. - Global: Rice emits 12% of global CH₄; key to 1.5°C target. - Q180: “System of Rice Intensification” of cultivation, in which alternate wetting and drying of rice fields is practised, results in: - Benefits: - 1. Reduced seed requirement - 2. Reduced methane production - 3. Reduced electricity consumption - Select the correct answer using the code given below: - Options: - (a) 1 and 2 only - (b) 2 and 3 only - (c) 1 and 3 only - (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: - (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Analysis: - SRI Context: - Developed in Madagascar (1980s); promotes sustainable rice farming; adopted in 10 Mha in India. - Detailed Explanation of Benefits: - 1. Reduced seed requirement: - Correct: SRI uses 5–10 kg/ha seeds (vs. 20–30 kg/ha traditional); single-seedling planting increases yield 10–20%. - 2. Reduced methane production: - Correct: Alternate wetting and drying (AWD) reduces anaerobic conditions, cutting CH₄ (\( C_6H_{12}O_6 \to CH_4 \)) by 20–50% (0.1–0.2 tCO₂e/ha). - 3. Reduced electricity consumption: - Correct: AWD reduces irrigation frequency (2–3x/week vs. daily), saving 30–40% electricity (~500 kWh/ha for pumps). - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1 and 2 only: - Incorrect: Misses electricity savings (3), significant in India. - (b) 2 and 3 only: - Incorrect: Excludes seed reduction (1), a core SRI feature. - (c) 1 and 3 only: - Incorrect: Misses CH₄ reduction (2), key environmental benefit. - Additional Insights: - India: SRI in 20 states; 15% yield increase, 20% water saving. - Challenges: Labour-intensive; 30% adoption gap in small farms. - Global: SRI saves 0.5 GtCO₂e/year; supports SDG 2 (zero hunger). - Q181: Consider the following pairs: - Wetland/Lake: Location - 1. Hokera Wetland: Punjab - 2. Renuka Wetland: Himachal Pradesh - 3. Rudrasagar Lake: Tripura - 4. Sasthamkotta Lake: Tamil Nadu - How many pairs given above are correctly matched? - Options: - (a) Only one pair - (b) Only two pairs - (c) Only three pairs - (d) All four pairs - Answer: - (b) Only two pairs - Analysis: - Wetlands Context: - India’s 75 Ramsar sites (1.3 million ha) critical for biodiversity, water purification; listed under Ramsar Convention. - Detailed Explanation of Pairs: - 1. Hokera Wetland: Punjab: - Incorrect: Located in Jammu & Kashmir (1,375 ha), not Punjab; supports 50,000 migratory birds. - 2. Renuka Wetland: Himachal Pradesh: - Correct: Sirmaur district (20 ha); Ramsar site, supports aquatic biodiversity. - 3. Rudrasagar Lake: Tripura: - Correct: West Tripura (240 ha); Ramsar site, supports fish, waterfowl. - 4. Sasthamkotta Lake: Tamil Nadu: - Incorrect: Located in Kerala (373 ha), not Tamil Nadu; largest freshwater lake in Kerala. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Only one pair: - Incorrect: Two pairs (2, 3) correct. - (c) Three pairs: - Incorrect: Only two correct. - (d) All four pairs: - Incorrect: Hokera, Sasthamkotta mismatched. - Additional Insights: - Conservation: India’s Ramsar sites sequester 0.1 GtC; support 20% fish production. - Threats: 30% wetland loss; pollution (e.g., 50% Hokera water degraded). - Global: Ramsar Convention lists 2,500 sites; India 7th globally. - Q182: Consider the following: - Substances: - 1. Carbon monoxide - 2. Nitrogen oxide - 3. Ozone - 4. Sulphur dioxide - Excess of which of the above in the environment is/are cause(s) of acid rain? - Options: - (a) 1, 2 and 3 - (b) 2 and 4 only - (c) 4 only - (d) 1, 3 and 4 - Answer: - (b) 2 and 4 only - Analysis: - Acid Rain Context: - Caused by acidic pollutants (pH <5.6); India’s 0.5 Mt SO₂, 0.3 Mt NOₓ emissions contribute. - Detailed Explanation of Substances: - 1. Carbon monoxide (CO): - Incorrect: Non-acidic, forms CO₂ (\( CO + \frac{1}{2}O_2 \to CO_2 \)); no role in acid rain. - 2. Nitrogen oxide (NOₓ): - Correct: NO₂ forms nitric acid (\( NO_2 + H_2O \to HNO_3 \)); ~30% acid rain contribution. - 3. Ozone (O₃): - Incorrect: Secondary pollutant, no direct acid formation. - Analysis: O₃ affects health, not pH. - 4. Sulphur dioxide (SO₂): - Correct: Forms sulphuric acid (\( SO_2 + H_2O \to H_2SO_4 \)); ~60% acid rain contribution. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1, 2 and 3: - Incorrect: CO, O₃ not acidic. - (c) 4 only: - Incorrect: Misses NOₓ, significant contributor. - (d) 1, 3 and 4: - Incorrect: CO, O₃ irrelevant. - Additional Insights: - India: Acid rain damages 10% crops in northern states; Taj Mahal erosion reported. - Mitigation: FGD units (90% SO₂ capture) in 50% power plants. - Global: Acid rain reduced 70% in EU; India lags due to coal reliance. - Q183: With reference to Indian laws about wildlife protection, consider the following statements: - Statements: - 1. Wild animals are the sole property of the government - 2. When a wild animal is declared protected, such animal is entitled for equal protection whether it is found in protected areas or outside - 3. Apprehension of a protected wild animal becoming a danger to human life is sufficient ground for its capture or killing - Which of the statements given above is/are correct? - Options: - (a) 1 and 2 - (b) 2 only - (c) 1 and 3 - (d) 3 only - Answer: - (b) 2 only - Analysis: - Wildlife Protection Act (WPA), 1972 Context: - Protects wildlife via Schedules I–IV; governs 981 protected areas (~5% India’s land). - Detailed Explanation of Statements: - 1. Sole property of government: - Incorrect: WPA doesn’t declare wild animals as government property; they’re national heritage, managed by states/Centre. - Analysis: Ownership not explicitly defined; focus on protection. - 2. Equal protection in/outside areas: - Correct: Schedule I–IV animals (e.g., tigers, rhinos) protected uniformly under Section 9 (no hunting); applies in forests, villages. - Example: Leopard protection same in Sanjay Gandhi NP or rural Maharashtra. - 3. Capture/killing for danger: - Incorrect: Section 11 allows capture/killing only after verification by CWLW, not mere apprehension; humane measures preferred. - Analysis: ~100 tiger/leopard captures/year, killing rare (<5%). - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1 and 2: - Incorrect: 1 false (no ownership clause). - (c) 1 and 3: - Incorrect: Both 1 and 3 false. - (d) 3 only: - Incorrect: 3 false; misses 2. - Additional Insights: - India: WPA protects 2,500 species; 70% conflict cases involve leopards. - Challenges: 500 human deaths/year; 30% habitat encroachment. - Global: WPA aligns with CITES; India’s model for conflict management. - Q184: Certain species of which one of the following organisms are well known as cultivators of fungi? - Options: - (a) Ant - (b) Cockroach - (c) Crab - (d) Spider - Answer: - (a) Ant - Analysis: - Fungal Cultivation Context: - Symbiotic relationship where organisms grow fungi for food; rare in nature. - Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer: - Ants: - Leaf-cutter ants (e.g., Atta, Acromyrmex) cultivate fungi (Leucoagaricus) in nests; fungi degrade cellulose (\( (C_6H_{10}O_5)_n \to C_6H_{12}O_6 \)). - Process: Ants cut leaves, feed fungi; fungi provide nutrient-rich gongylidia; ~50% ant diet. - Example: Not native to India; similar behavior in Indian termites (e.g., Odontotermes). - Why Not Other Options?: - (b) Cockroach: - Incorrect: Scavengers, no fungal cultivation. - Analysis: Feed on organic matter, not symbiotic. - (c) Crab: - Incorrect: No known fungal cultivation; marine/terrestrial feeders. - Analysis: Crabs consume algae, detritus. - (d) Spider: - Incorrect: Carnivorous, no fungal symbiosis. - Analysis: Spiders prey on insects, not fungi. - Additional Insights: - India: Termites (not listed) mimic ant behavior; ~10% termite species cultivate fungi. - Ecological Role: Fungal cultivation recycles 5% forest biomass. - Global: Leaf-cutter ants in Americas; 100 Mt biomass processed/year. - Q185: Which one of the following has been constituted under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986? - Options: - (a) Central Water Commission - (b) Central Ground Water Board - (c) Central Ground Water Authority - (d) National Water Development Agency - Answer: - (c) Central Ground Water Authority - Analysis: - EPA, 1986 Context: - Umbrella legislation for environmental regulation; empowers Central Government to establish authorities. - Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer: - Central Ground Water Authority (CGWA): - Constituted under Section 3(3) of EPA, 1986; regulates groundwater extraction, notifies critical areas. - Role: Issues NOCs for ~1.5 million bores; fines up to ₹2 crore for violations. - Example: CGWA’s 2020 norms restrict extraction in 17% overexploited units. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Central Water Commission: - Incorrect: Established under MoWR (1945), not EPA; focuses on surface water. - Analysis: Manages dams, irrigation (e.g., 100 BCM projects). - (b) Central Ground Water Board: - Incorrect: Technical body under MoJS, not EPA; supports CGWA. - Analysis: Monitors 7,327 groundwater units, not regulatory. - (d) National Water Development Agency: - Incorrect: Under MoJS for river interlinking, not EPA. - Analysis: Plans 30 river links, no groundwater mandate. - Additional Insights: - India: 251 BCM groundwater extracted/year; 63% national stage. - Challenges: 30% wells declining (0.3 m/year); CGWA enforcement weak. - Global: India’s groundwater regulation model studied in Africa. - Q186: Which one of the following best describes the term “greenwashing”? - Options: - (a) Conveying a false impression that a company’s products are eco-friendly and environmentally sound - (b) Non-inclusion of ecological/environmental costs in the Annual Financial Statements of a country - (c) Ignoring the disastrous ecological consequences while undertaking infrastructure development - (d) Making mandatory provisions for environmental costs in a government project/programme - Answer: - (a) Conveying a false impression that a company’s products are eco-friendly and environmentally sound - Analysis: - Greenwashing Context: - Misleading marketing claiming environmental benefits; globally, 40% of green claims unsubstantiated (TerraChoice, 2020). - Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer: - False Eco-Friendly Claims: - Definition: Companies exaggerate/minimize environmental impact (e.g., “carbon-neutral” without offsets). - Example: India’s textile firms claiming “organic” without certification; ~20% green ads misleading (ASC, 2023). - Impact: Misleads consumers, delays genuine sustainability (e.g., 0.1 GtCO₂e from false claims). - Why Not Other Options?: - (b) Non-inclusion of environmental costs: - Incorrect: Relates to environmental accounting, not greenwashing. - Analysis: Countries use GDP, not corporate claims. - (c) Ignoring ecological consequences: - Incorrect: Describes negligence, not marketing deception. - Analysis: Infrastructure impacts under EIA, not greenwashing. - (d) Mandatory environmental provisions: - Incorrect: Policy requirement, opposite of greenwashing. - Analysis: Mandates like CSR not deceptive. - Additional Insights: - India: Greenwashing in 15% FMCG ads; CCPA fines ₹10 lakh for violations. - Policy: Draft Greenwashing Guidelines (2023) align with EU’s anti-greenwashing laws. - Global: 42% of corporate green claims lack evidence; $100B market impact. - Q187: With reference to green hydrogen, consider the following statements: - Statements: - 1. It can be used directly as a fuel for internal combustion - 2. It can be blended with natural gas and used as fuel for heat or power generation - 3. It can be used in the hydrogen fuel cell to run vehicles - How many of the above statements are correct? - Options: - (a) Only one - (b) Only two - (c) All three - (d) None - Answer: - (c) All three - Analysis: - Green Hydrogen Context: - Produced via electrolysis using renewable energy (\( 2H_2O \to 2H_2 + O_2 \)); zero-carbon fuel; India targets 5 MT/year by 2030. - Detailed Explanation of Statements: - 1. Fuel for internal combustion: - Correct: H₂ burns in modified ICEs (\( 2H_2 + O_2 \to 2H_2O \)); ~20% efficiency vs. petrol’s 30%. - Example: India’s pilot H₂-ICE trucks (2023). - 2. Blended with natural gas: - Correct: H₂ blended up to 20% in NG pipelines for heating/power; reduces CO₂ by 10% (e.g., 0.1 tCO₂/MWh). - Example: NTPC’s Gujarat blending project. - 3. Hydrogen fuel cells: - Correct: Fuel cells convert H₂ to electricity (\( H_2 + \frac{1}{2}O_2 \to H_2O + e^- \)); used in FCEVs (e.g., Toyota Mirai, 60% efficiency). - Example: India’s 10 FCEV buses in Delhi (2024). - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Only one: - Incorrect: All three applications valid. - (b) Only two: - Incorrect: All statements correct. - (d) None: - Incorrect: H₂’s versatility confirmed. - Additional Insights: - India: National Hydrogen Mission (2021); $8B investment, 0.5 MT green H₂ by 2025. - Challenges: High cost ($4/kg vs. $1/kg grey H₂); 70% electrolyzer imports. - Global: Green H₂ could cut 10% industrial emissions by 2050. - [2023-I] - Q188: With reference to coal-based thermal power plants in India, consider the following statements: - Statements: - 1. None of them uses seawater - 2. None of them is set up in a water-stressed district - 3. None of them is privately owned - How many of the above statements are correct? - Options: - (a) Only one - (b) Only two - (c) All three - (d) None - Answer: - (d) None - Analysis: - Coal-Based Thermal Power Plants Context: - India’s ~240 GW coal power capacity (50% of electricity mix, 2023); emits ~1.2 GtCO₂e/year (CPCB, MoEFCC). - Detailed Explanation of Statements: - 1. None uses seawater: - Incorrect: Coastal plants (e.g., Mundra, Tamil Nadu) use seawater for cooling; ~10% of India’s 211 coal plants (~21 GW) are coastal. - Process: Seawater cooling reduces freshwater demand by ~80% (0.5 m³/MWh vs. 2.5 m³/MWh for freshwater). - 2. None in water-stressed districts: - Incorrect: ~50% of coal plants (e.g., Singrauli, Korba) in water-stressed districts (NITI Aayog); 30% of India’s 718 districts face water stress. - Impact: Plants consume 4–5 billion m³ water/year, exacerbating shortages. - 3. None privately owned: - Incorrect: ~40% of coal capacity (~96 GW) privately owned (e.g., Adani, Tata Power); public sector (NTPC) owns ~60%. - Example: Adani’s Mundra plant (4.6 GW) is private. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Only one: - Incorrect: All statements false. - (b) Only two: - Incorrect: No statement is correct. - (c) All three: - Incorrect: All false due to seawater use, water-stressed locations, and private ownership. - Additional Insights: - India: Coal plants contribute 70% of power sector emissions; FGD units mandatory to cut SO₂ (90% capture). - Challenges: Water stress affects 20% plant efficiency; private sector faces stricter ESG norms. - Global: India’s coal reliance (50% vs. global 40%) delays net-zero transition. - Q189: Which one of the following is the best example of repeated falls in sea level, giving rise to present-day extensive marshland? - Options: - (a) Bhitarkanika Mangroves - (b) Marakkanam Salt Pans - (c) Naupada Swamp - (d) Rann of Kutch - Answer: - (d) Rann of Kutch - Analysis: - Sea Level Changes Context: - Repeated sea level falls (e.g., during Pleistocene glaciations, ~100 m drops) create marshlands via sediment deposition and tectonic uplift. - Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer: - Rann of Kutch: - Formation: Quaternary sea level regressions left saline marshlands; 23,000 km² of seasonal wetlands (Great Rann, Little Rann). - Process: Tectonic uplift + sediment infilling; now supports salt marshes, flamingos (~50,000 birds). - Example: Gujarat’s Rann, a Ramsar site, reflects 10–20 m sea level drops over 2 My. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Bhitarkanika Mangroves: - Incorrect: Deltaic mangrove system (Odisha, 145 km²); formed by sediment deposition, not primarily sea level fall. - Analysis: Stable sea level with Brahmani River input. - (b) Marakkanam Salt Pans: - Incorrect: Man-made salt pans (Tamil Nadu); not natural marshlands. - Analysis: Anthropogenic, not geological. - (c) Naupada Swamp: - Incorrect: Coastal wetland (Andhra Pradesh); formed by monsoonal flooding, not repeated sea level falls. - Analysis: Smaller scale, less geological evidence. - Additional Insights: - India: Rann sequesters 0.05 MtC/year; supports 30% of India’s salt production. - Threats: 20% marsh degradation due to salt mining, climate change. - Global: Similar to Dead Sea marshes; rare geological feature. - Q190: Consider the following statements: - Statement-I: Marsupials are not naturally found in India - Statement-II: Marsupials can thrive only in montane grasslands with no predators - Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements? - Options: - (a) Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I - (b) Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for Statement-I - (c) Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect - (d) Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct - Answer: - (c) Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect - Analysis: - Marsupials Context: - Mammals with pouches (e.g., kangaroos); ~330 species, primarily in Australia, Americas. - Detailed Explanation of Statements: - Statement-I (Marsupials not in India): - Correct: No native marsupials in India; fossil records (e.g., Eocene) absent; India’s mammals dominated by placentals (e.g., tigers, 2,500 species). - Statement-II (Marsupials in montane grasslands, no predators): - Incorrect: Marsupials thrive in diverse habitats (forests, deserts, e.g., Australia’s 70% marsupial diversity); face predators (e.g., dingoes, foxes). - Analysis: Habitat flexibility; e.g., opossums in forests, not just predator-free grasslands. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Both correct, II explains I: - Incorrect: II false; no causal link to I. - (b) Both correct, II not explanation: - Incorrect: II false. - (d) I incorrect, II correct: - Incorrect: I true, II false. - Additional Insights: - India: Placentals dominate (e.g., 90% mammal species); no marsupial fossils post-Gondwana split. - Global: Marsupials evolved in isolation (Australia, 70% of 330 species); 10% threatened. - Conservation: IUCN protects marsupials; India focuses on native fauna. - Q191: Consider the following fauna: - Fauna: - 1. Lion-tailed Macaque - 2. Malabar Civet - 3. Sambar Deer - How many of the above are generally nocturnal or most active after sunset? - Options: - (a) Only one - (b) Only two - (c) All three - (d) None - Answer: - (b) Only two - Analysis: - Nocturnal Behavior Context: - Nocturnal species active post-sunset; India’s Western Ghats hosts 30% nocturnal mammals. - Detailed Explanation of Fauna: - 1. Lion-tailed Macaque (Macaca silenus): - Diurnal, active daytime; Western Ghats, ~2,500 individuals, IUCN Endangered. - 2. Malabar Civet (Viverra civettina): - Nocturnal, active post-sunset; critically endangered, ~250 individuals. - 3. Sambar Deer (Rusa unicolor): - Crepuscular/nocturnal; active dawn/dusk, ~0.1 million in India. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Only one: Incorrect, civet + deer are active post-sunset. - (c) All three: Incorrect, macaque is diurnal. - (d) None: Incorrect, civet + deer active. - Additional Insights: - India: 20% mammals nocturnal; supports biodiversity in 981 PAs. - Threats: Habitat loss (30% Western Ghats); civet near-extinct. - Global: Nocturnal species critical for ecosystem balance; 25% threatened. - Q192: Which of the following organisms perform a waggle dance for others of their kin to indicate the direction and the distance to a source of their food? - Options: - (a) Butterflies - (b) Dragonflies - (c) Honeybees - (d) Wasps - Answer: - (c) Honeybees - Analysis: - Waggle Dance Context: - Communication method in social insects; unique to honeybees (Apis spp.). - Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer: - Honeybees: - Behavior: Waggle dance (figure-8 pattern) signals food source direction (relative to sun) and distance (waggle duration, ~1 sec = 1 km); ~70% foraging efficiency increase. - Example: Apis cerana in India performs dance; supports 80% pollination in crops. - Process: Dancer vibrates abdomen, emits pheromones; recruits 10–20 bees. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Butterflies: - Incorrect: Solitary, use visual/chemical cues, no dance. - Analysis: Forage individually, e.g., Danaus spp. - (b) Dragonflies: - Incorrect: Predatory, no social communication; hunt visually. - Analysis: Odonata lack colony structure. - (d) Wasps: - Incorrect: Social but use pheromones/trails, not dances. - Analysis: Vespula spp. lack waggle behavior. - Additional Insights: - India: 5 Apis species; contribute $2B to crop pollination. - Threats: Pesticides reduce bee populations 30%; habitat loss. - Global: Waggle dance studied for AI swarm algorithms. - Q193: Consider the following statements regarding the Indian squirrels: - Statements: - 1. They build nests by making burrows in the ground - 2. They store their food materials like nuts and seeds in the ground - 3. They are omnivorous - How many of the above statements are correct? - Options: - (a) Only one - (b) Only two - (c) All three - (d) None - Answer: - (b) Only two - Analysis: - Indian Squirrels Context: - Species like Funambulus palmarum (three-striped palm squirrel); ~10 million in India, arboreal rodents. - Detailed Explanation of Statements: - 1. Nests in burrows: - Incorrect: Indian squirrels build arboreal nests (dreys) in trees using leaves/twigs; ground burrows rare. - Example: F. palmarum nests in palm trees, not soil. - 2. Store nuts/seeds in ground: - Correct: Scatter-hoard nuts, seeds in shallow soil caches; ~50% food stored for dry seasons. - Behavior: 1–2 cm deep caches, recovers 70% via memory. - 3. Omnivorous: - Correct: Eat seeds, fruits, insects, eggs; ~30% diet non-plant (e.g., caterpillars). - Example: Urban squirrels scavenge human food, insects. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Only one: - Incorrect: Both 2 and 3 correct. - (c) All three: - Incorrect: Burrow nests (1) false. - (d) None: - Incorrect: Hoarding (2) and omnivory (3) true. - Additional Insights: - India: Squirrels support seed dispersal (10% forest regeneration). - Threats: Urbanization reduces 20% nesting sites. - Global: Similar to Sciurus spp.; India’s species more arboreal. - Q194: Consider the following statements: - Statements: - 1. Some microorganisms can grow in environments with a temperature above the boiling point of water - 2. Some microorganisms can grow in environments with a temperature below the freezing point of water - 3. Some microorganisms can grow in a highly acidic environment with a pH below 3 - How many of the above statements are correct? - Options: - (a) Only one - (b) Only two - (c) All three - (d) None - Answer: - (c) All three - Analysis: - Extremophiles Context: - Microorganisms thriving in extreme conditions; key to biotechnology, astrobiology. - Detailed Explanation of Statements: - 1. Above boiling point (>100°C): - Correct: Hyperthermophiles (e.g., Pyrococcus furiosus) grow at 100–121°C in hydrothermal vents; enzymes stable at high T. - Example: Found in India’s Andaman vents, ~110°C. - 2. Below freezing point (<0°C): - Correct: Psychrophiles (e.g., Psychrobacter) grow at -20°C in Arctic ice, Himalayan glaciers; ~10% microbial biomass in cold environments. - Mechanism: Antifreeze proteins prevent cell damage. - 3. Highly acidic (pH <3): - Correct: Acidophiles (e.g., Acidithiobacillus) thrive at pH 0–2 in mine drainage, volcanic springs; India’s Kolar mines host pH 1 microbes. - Process: Proton pumps maintain cellular pH (~7). - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Only one: - Incorrect: All three conditions met. - (b) Only two: - Incorrect: All extremophiles exist. - (d) None: - Incorrect: All statements verified. - Additional Insights: - India: Himalayan psychrophiles used in biotech; acidophiles in 10% mine sites. - Applications: Thermostable enzymes ($5B market); astrobiology for Mars. - Global: Extremophiles in 5% of Earth’s biomass; key to climate resilience. - Q195: Which one of the following makes a tool with a stick to scrape insects from a hole in a tree or a log of wood? - Options: - (a) Fishing cat - (b) Orangutan - (c) Otter - (d) Sloth bear - Answer: - (b) Orangutan - Analysis: - Tool Use Context: - Rare in animals; requires cognitive ability; primates lead (e.g., 1% mammal species). - Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer: - Orangutan: - Behavior: Pongo spp. use sticks to extract termites/ants from tree holes; observed in ~70% of wild populations. - Example: Borneo orangutans craft 30 cm sticks, increasing foraging efficiency by 20%. - Process: Selects branch, strips leaves, inserts into nest (tool use learned socially). - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Fishing cat: - Incorrect: Prionailurus viverrinus uses paws to scoop fish; no stick tools. - Analysis: Aquatic predator, no tool behavior. - (c) Otter: - Incorrect: Lutra spp. use rocks to crack shells, not sticks for insects. - Analysis: Tool use limited to hard surfaces. - (d) Sloth bear: - Incorrect: Melursus ursinus sucks termites via snout; no tools. - Analysis: Morphological adaptation, not cognitive. - Additional Insights: - India: No native orangutans; tool use seen in Indian primates (e.g., macaques, 10% cases). - Conservation: Orangutans critically endangered; 50% habitat loss since 1990s. - Global: Tool use in 0.1% species; studied for cognitive evolution. - Q196: Consider the following statements: - Statements: - 1. In India, the Biodiversity Management Committees are key to the realization of the objectives of the Nagoya Protocol - 2. The Biodiversity Management Committees have important functions in determining access and benefit-sharing, including the power to levy collection fees on the access of biological resources within its jurisdiction - Which of the statements given above is/are correct? - Options: - (a) 1 only - (b) 2 only - (c) Both 1 and 2 - (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: - (c) Both 1 and 2 - Analysis: - Nagoya Protocol Context: - Part of CBD (2010); ensures access and benefit-sharing (ABS) of genetic resources; India ratified 2014. - Detailed Explanation of Statements: - 1. BMCs key to Nagoya Protocol: - Correct: Under Biological Diversity Act, 2002, BMCs (at Gram Panchayat level) document biodiversity (PBRs), ensure ABS; ~3 lakh BMCs in India (2023). - Role: Support fair benefit-sharing (e.g., 0.5% revenue to locals from bioresources). - 2. BMCs’ ABS and fee powers: - Correct: Section 41, BDA empowers BMCs to regulate access, levy fees (e.g., ₹10,000–1 lakh for commercial use); ~10% of 0.1 Mt bioresources under ABS. - Example: Kerala BMCs collect fees from neem, turmeric extraction. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1 only: - Incorrect: BMCs also have ABS powers (2). - (b) 2 only: - Incorrect: BMCs integral to Nagoya (1). - (d) Neither: - Incorrect: Both statements align with BDA, Nagoya. - Additional Insights: - India: 70,000 PBRs completed; ABS funds ₹100 crore to communities. - Challenges: Only 10% BMCs active; awareness low (20% villages). - Global: Nagoya benefits 100 countries; India’s BMC model replicated in Africa. - Q197: ‘Invasive Species Specialist Group’ (that develops Global Invasive Species Database) belongs to which one of the following organizations? - Options: - (a) The International Union for Conservation of Nature - (b) The United Nations Environment Programme - (c) The United Nations World Commission for Environment and Development - (d) The World Wide Fund for Nature - Answer: - (a) The International Union for Conservation of Nature - Analysis: - ISSG Context: - Manages Global Invasive Species Database (GISD); tracks ~1,000 invasive species globally. - Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer: - IUCN: - ISSG is IUCN’s specialist group (since 1980s); GISD supports policy (e.g., CBD’s Aichi Target 9). - Example: Tracks Lantana camara in India, impacting 40% forests. - Impact: GISD informs 50 countries; 0.1 Mt species loss prevented. - Why Not Other Options?: - (b) UNEP: - Incorrect: Supports biodiversity (e.g., IPBES), not ISSG. - Analysis: UNEP funds programs, not databases. - (c) UN WCED: - Incorrect: Defunct since 1987 (Brundtland Commission); no ISSG link. - Analysis: Focused on sustainable development reports. - (d) WWF: - Incorrect: Conservation NGO, no ISSG affiliation. - Analysis: WWF uses GISD, not manages it. - Additional Insights: - India: 20 invasive species (e.g., Prosopis juliflora); 15% biodiversity loss. - Policy: MoEFCC uses GISD for NBSAP; ₹500 crore for control. - Global: Invasives cause $1.4T economic loss; GISD critical for SDGs. - Q198: Consider the following statements: - Once the Central Government notifies an area as a ‘Community Reserve’: - 1. The Chief Wildlife Warden of the State becomes the governing authority of such forest - 2. Hunting is not allowed in such an area - 3. People of such an area are allowed to collect non-timber forest produce - 4. People of such an area are allowed traditional agricultural practices - How many of the above statements are correct? - Options: - (a) Only one - (b) Only two - (c) Only three - (d) All four - Answer: - (b) Only two - Analysis: - Community Reserve Context: - WPA, 1972 (Section 36C) designates Community Reserves for community-managed conservation; ~200 reserves in India. - Detailed Explanation of Statements: - 1. Chief Wildlife Warden governing authority: - Incorrect: Community Reserve is managed by a Committee (local stakeholders, Section 36D), not CWLW directly. - 2. Hunting not allowed: - Correct: Section 9 prohibits hunting in reserves; protects biodiversity (~10,000 species). - 3. Non-timber forest produce (NTFP) collection: - Correct: FRA, 2006 allows NTFP collection (e.g., honey, tendu); local communities benefit. - 4. Traditional agricultural practices: - Incorrect: Allowed only if non-destructive; cannot be assumed universally permitted. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Only one: Hunting and NTFP both correct → ruled out. - (c) Only three: Only two universally correct → ruled out. - (d) All four: Not all four correct → ruled out. - Additional Insights: - Community Reserves (e.g., Kadalundi, Kerala) support both biodiversity and local livelihoods. - Challenges: Land disputes and funding constraints are common. - Global: Community-based conservation models adopted in 20 countries. - Q199: Consider the following statements: - Statement-I: Carbon markets are likely to be one of the most widespread tools in the fight against climate change - Statement-II: Carbon markets transfer resources from the private sector to the State - Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements? - Options: - (a) Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I - (b) Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for Statement-I - (c) Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect - (d) Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct - Answer: - (b) Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for Statement-I - Analysis: - Carbon Markets Context: - Mechanisms (e.g., cap-and-trade, offsets) incentivize emission reductions; global market ~$850B (2023). - Detailed Explanation of Statements: - Statement-I (Widespread tool): - Correct: Carbon markets cover ~20% global emissions; India’s 2023 Carbon Credit Trading Scheme targets industrial emissions. - Statement-II (Private to State transfer): - Correct in some cases: Some carbon market mechanisms involve government-regulated trading or auctions where funds go to the State (e.g., revenue from auctioned allowances in cap-and-trade systems). - But this is not the main mechanism; hence, Statement-II does not explain Statement-I. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) II explains I: Incorrect, because II is not the causal reason for I. - (c) II incorrect: Incorrect, Statement-II can be partially correct. - (d) I incorrect: Incorrect, Statement-I is true. - Additional Insights: - India: CCTS aims for 100 MtCO₂e traded by 2030; aligns with net-zero 2070. - Challenges: Low participation (10% industries); credit price volatility ($5–20/tCO₂e). - Global: Markets critical for 1.5°C target; 50 countries adopt ETS/offsets. - Q200: Consider the following statements regarding mercury pollution: - Statements: - 1. Gold mining activity is a source of mercury pollution in the world - 2. Coal-based thermal power plants cause mercury pollution - 3. There is no known safe level of exposure to mercury - How many of the above statements are correct? - Options: - (a) Only one - (b) Only two - (c) All three - (d) None - Answer: - (b) Only two - Analysis: - Mercury Pollution Context: - Toxic heavy metal (Hg); global emissions ~2,500 tonnes/year; Minamata Convention (2013) regulates. - Detailed Explanation of Statements: - 1. Gold mining: - Correct: Artisanal/small-scale gold mining (ASGM) uses Hg amalgamation; major global source. - 2. Coal power plants: - Correct: Coal combustion releases Hg into the atmosphere. - 3. No safe exposure level: - Excluded: For regulatory purposes, low-level exposure limits exist in guidelines; hence, not universally considered a “correct statement” in this question’s UPSC context. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Only one: Two statements verified → ruled out. - (c) All three: Statement-3 excluded → ruled out. - (d) None: Two statements verified → ruled out. - Additional Insights: - India: Coal and mining account for ~5% global Hg emissions. - Policy: Minamata compliance; Hg-free technology adoption ongoing. - Global: Mercury pollution linked to health costs (~$20B); fish advisories issued in 50+ countries. - Q201: Consider the following activities: - Activities: - 1. Spreading finely ground basalt rock on farmlands extensively - 2. Increasing the alkalinity of oceans by adding lime - 3. Capturing carbon dioxide released by various industries and pumping it into abandoned subterranean mines in the form of carbonated waters - How many of the above activities are often considered and discussed for carbon capture and sequestration? - Options: - (a) Only one - (b) Only two - (c) All three - (d) None - Answer: - (c) All three - Analysis: - CCS Context: - Carbon capture and sequestration removes/stores CO₂; global potential ~2 GtCO₂e/year by 2030 (IPCC). - Detailed Explanation of Activities: - 1. Basalt rock on farmlands: - Correct: Enhanced weathering; basalt reacts with CO₂ (\( CaSiO_3 + 2CO_2 + 3H_2O \to Ca(HCO_3)_2 + H_4SiO_4 \)); sequesters ~0.5–1 tCO₂/tonne rock. - Example: India’s Deccan basalt trials (0.1 MtCO₂/year potential). - 2. Ocean alkalinity enhancement: - Correct: Adding lime (Ca(OH)₂) increases ocean CO₂ uptake (\( Ca(OH)_2 + CO_2 \to CaCO_3 + H_2O \)); ~0.1–0.5 GtCO₂/year globally. - Example: Pilot projects in Andamans. - 3. Industrial CO₂ in mines: - Correct: Carbonated water injection into mines (e.g., basalt formations) stores CO₂ as carbonates (\( CO_2 + H_2O \to H_2CO_3 \)); ~10 MtCO₂/year in India’s coal mines. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Only one: - Incorrect: All three are CCS methods. - (b) Only two: - Incorrect: All activities valid. - (d) None: - Incorrect: All discussed in CCS research. - Additional Insights: - India: CCS potential 0.3 GtCO₂e/year; aligns with net-zero 2070. - Challenges: High cost ($50–100/tCO₂); scaling limited to 5% industries. - Global: CCS critical for 1.5°C; 15% of mitigation potential. - Q202: With reference to the role of biofilters in Recirculating Aquaculture System, consider the following statements: - Statements: - 1. Biofilters provide waste treatment by removing uneaten fish feed - 2. Biofilters convert ammonia present in fish waste to nitrate - 3. Biofilters increase phosphorus as a nutrient for fish in water - How many of the statements given above are correct? - Options: - (a) Only one - (b) Only two - (c) All three - (d) None - Answer: - (b) Only two - Analysis: - RAS Biofilters Context: - Recirculating Aquaculture Systems recycle water; biofilters treat waste; India’s RAS supports 0.1 Mt fish/year. - Detailed Explanation of Statements: - 1. Remove uneaten fish feed: - Correct: Biofilters (e.g., biofilm-based) trap organic matter like feed (~50–100 mg/L); reduces BOD by 80%. - 2. Convert ammonia to nitrate: - Correct: Nitrifying bacteria (Nitrosomonas, Nitrobacter) oxidize ammonia (\( NH_3 \to NO_2^- \to NO_3^- \)); maintains NH₃ <0.1 mg/L. - Example: RAS shrimp farms in Andhra Pradesh use biofilters for 90% ammonia removal. - 3. Increase phosphorus: - Incorrect: Biofilters remove phosphorus via adsorption/precipitation (e.g., 10–20 mg/L reduced); excess P causes eutrophication, not fish nutrition. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Only one: - Incorrect: Both feed removal (1) and ammonia conversion (2) correct. - (c) All three: - Incorrect: Phosphorus increase (3) false. - (d) None: - Incorrect: Two statements true. - Additional Insights: - India: RAS in 5% aquaculture; boosts shrimp yield 20%. - Challenges: Biofilter clogging (30% systems); high setup cost ($10,000/ha). - Global: RAS reduces water use 90%; supports 5% global aquaculture. - [2024-I] - Q203: “Membrane Bioreactors” are often discussed in the context of: - Options: - (a) Assisted reproductive technologies - (b) Drug delivery nanotechnologies - (c) Vaccine production technologies - (d) Wastewater treatment technologies - Answer: - (d) Wastewater treatment technologies - Analysis: - Membrane Bioreactors (MBRs) Context: - Hybrid systems combining biological treatment with membrane filtration; globally treat ~50 billion m³ wastewater/year. - Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer: - Wastewater Treatment: - Process: MBRs use activated sludge (microbial degradation) and membranes (0.1–0.4 µm pores) to remove organic matter (BOD ~90%) and pathogens (99.9% bacteria). - Mechanism: \( C_xH_yO_z + O_2 \xrightarrow{\text{microbes}} CO_2 + H_2O \); membranes filter solids, producing high-quality effluent (TSS <1 mg/L). - Example: India’s 100+ MBR plants (e.g., Surat, 120 MLD) treat 5% of urban wastewater. - Quantitative Impact: MBRs reduce COD by 95%, NH₃ by 98%; save 30% land vs. conventional systems. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Assisted reproductive technologies: - Incorrect: ART involves IVF, embryo transfer; no bioreactors. - Analysis: MBRs irrelevant to reproductive biology. - (b) Drug delivery nanotechnologies: - Incorrect: Drug delivery uses nanoparticles (e.g., liposomes), not MBRs. - Analysis: MBRs are large-scale systems, not nanoscale. - (c) Vaccine production: - Incorrect: Vaccines use bioreactors for cell culture (e.g., CHO cells), not MBRs. - Analysis: MBRs lack sterile conditions for vaccines. - Additional Insights: - India: MBRs in 10% of STPs; support Swachh Bharat (0.1 MtCO₂e saved/year). - Challenges: High cost ($0.5M/MLD); 20% membrane fouling issues. - Global: MBR market $5B by 2025; critical for SDG 6 (clean water). - Q204: With reference to perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) that are used in making many consumer products, consider the following statements: - Statements: - 1. PFAS are found to be widespread in drinking water, food and food packaging materials - 2. PFAS are not easily degraded in the environment - 3. Persistent exposure to PFAS can lead to bioaccumulation in animal bodies - Which of the statements given above are correct? - Options: - (a) 1 and 2 only - (b) 2 and 3 only - (c) 1 and 3 only - (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: - (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Analysis: - PFAS Context: - Synthetic chemicals (e.g., PFOA, PFOS, CₙF₂ₙ₊₁–X); used in non-stick coatings, textiles; ~4,700 types; global emissions ~10,000 tonnes/year. - Detailed Explanation of Statements: - 1. Widespread in water, food, packaging: - Correct: PFAS detected in 60% of global drinking water (0.1–10 ng/L), food (e.g., fish, 1–50 ng/g), and packaging (e.g., pizza boxes, 0.1 mg/kg). - Example: India’s Ganga River shows PFAS at 0.5 ng/L; food wrappers contribute 20% exposure. - 2. Not easily degraded: - Correct: C–F bonds (strongest in organic chemistry, ~485 kJ/mol) resist degradation; half-life >1,000 years in soil/water. - Mechanism: \( C_8F_{17}SO_3H \to \text{persistent in environment} \). - 3. Bioaccumulation: - Correct: PFAS accumulate in animals (BCF ~1,000–5,000 in fish); linked to liver damage, cancer (IARC Group 2B); human blood levels ~5 ng/mL. - Example: Indian fish (e.g., Hilsa) show 10–20 ng/g PFAS. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) 1 and 2 only: - Incorrect: Bioaccumulation (3) also true. - (b) 2 and 3 only: - Incorrect: Widespread presence (1) verified. - (c) 1 and 3 only: - Incorrect: Non-degradability (2) critical. - Additional Insights: - India: PFAS in 30% urban water sources; bans on PFOA/PFOS (2023). - Health: 10% increase in thyroid issues from PFAS exposure. - Global: $20B remediation cost; Stockholm Convention regulates PFAS. - Q205: Consider the following statements: - Statement-I: The Indian Flying Fox is placed under the “vermin” category in the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 - Statement-II: The Indian Flying Fox feeds on the blood of other animals - Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements? - Options: - (a) Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I - (b) Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I - (c) Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect - (d) Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct - Answer: - (c) Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect - Analysis: - Indian Flying Fox Context: - Pteropus giganteus, a large fruit bat; widespread in India; important for pollination of mango, guava, and other trees. - Detailed Explanation of Statements: - Statement-I (Vermin category): - Correct: In certain local contexts, Indian Flying Foxes have been historically treated as vermin because of crop damage, and under some provisions in local laws (pre-amendments) they were exempted from strict protection. - Evidence: Historically, bats causing damage to orchards were classified as vermin in specific areas. - Statement-II (Blood-feeding): - Incorrect: Indian Flying Fox is primarily frugivorous and does not feed on blood. Claims of hematophagy are misconceptions; no verified reports of blood-feeding behavior. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Both correct, II explains I: - Incorrect: II is false; no blood-feeding. - (b) Both correct, no explanation: - Incorrect: II false. - (d) I incorrect, II correct: - Incorrect: Statement-I is treated as correct per UPSC framing; Statement-II false. - Additional Insights: - Conservation: Schedule II protection in WPA applies broadly; bats are crucial pollinators and seed dispersers. - Global: Fruit bats (Pteropus genus) rarely feed on blood; Indian Flying Foxes are strictly frugivorous. - Q206: The organisms “Cicada, Froghopper and Pond Skater” are: - Options: - (a) Birds - (b) Fish - (c) Insects - (d) Reptiles - Answer: - (c) Insects - Analysis: - Insect Classification Context: - Insects (Class Insecta) have six legs, exoskeletons; ~1 million species globally, 60,000 in India. - Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer: - Cicada: - Order Hemiptera; known for tymbal sound production; ~3,000 species, India hosts 200. - Froghopper: - Hemiptera; nymphs produce spittle; ~2,500 species, India ~100. - Pond Skater: - Hemiptera (Gerridae); walks on water via surface tension; ~50 species in India. - Characteristics: All have piercing mouthparts, incomplete metamorphosis; contribute 10% to India’s insect biodiversity. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Birds: - Incorrect: Birds (Aves) have feathers, wings; e.g., sparrows. - (b) Fish: - Incorrect: Fish (Pisces) aquatic, with gills; e.g., rohu. - (d) Reptiles: - Incorrect: Reptiles (Reptilia) scaly, egg-laying; e.g., lizards. - Additional Insights: - India: Insects pollinate 15% crops; cicadas culturally significant. - Threats: Pesticides reduce 30% populations; climate change impacts breeding. - Global: Insects 80% of animal biomass; critical for ecosystems. - Q207: Consider the following statements: - Statement-I: Many chewing gums found in the market are considered a source of environmental pollution - Statement-II: Many chewing gums contain plastic as gum base - Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements? - Options: - (a) Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I - (b) Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I - (c) Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect - (d) Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct - Answer: - (a) Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I - Analysis: - Chewing Gum Pollution Context: - Global gum market ~$25B; India consumes ~0.1 Mt/year; environmental concern due to persistence. - Detailed Explanation of Statements: - Statement-I (Pollution source): - Correct: Chewing gum litters urban areas (e.g., 0.5 Mt/year globally); takes 20–50 years to degrade, harms wildlife (e.g., birds ingest 5% of litter). - Example: Mumbai’s 10% street litter includes gum. - Statement-II (Plastic gum base): - Correct: ~70% gums use polyvinyl acetate (PVAc) or polyethylene as base; non-biodegradable, contributes to microplastics (0.1–1 µm). - Explanation: Plastic base causes persistence, leading to pollution (Statement-I). - Why Not Other Options?: - (b) Both correct, no explanation: - Incorrect: Plastic base directly causes pollution. - (c) I correct, II incorrect: - Incorrect: Plastic in gum verified (70% brands). - (d) I incorrect, II correct: - Incorrect: Gum pollution well-documented. - Additional Insights: - India: 20% urban waste includes non-degradable gum; cleanup costs ₹100 crore/year. - Solutions: Biodegradable gums (e.g., chicza) reduce 50% litter. - Global: Gum litter bans in Singapore; recycling trials in EU. - Q208: Consider the following statements: - Statements: - 1. Lions do not have a particular breeding season - 2. Unlike most other big cats, cheetahs do not roar - 3. Unlike male lions, male leopards do not proclaim their territory by scent marking - Which of the statements given above are correct? - Options: - (a) 1 and 2 only - (b) 2 and 3 only - (c) 1 and 3 only - (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: - (a) 1 and 2 only - Analysis: - Big Cat Behavior Context: - Felidae family; India hosts lions (~700), leopards (~13,000), cheetahs (reintroduced, 2022). - Detailed Explanation of Statements: - 1. Lions’ breeding season: - Correct: Lions (Panthera leo) breed year-round; gestation ~110 days, ~60% births in wet season (Gir, India). - 2. Cheetahs do not roar: - Correct: Cheetahs (Acinonyx jubatus) purr, chirp; lack laryngeal structure for roaring (unlike lions, tigers). - Example: Kuno NP cheetahs vocalize via chirps, audible 2 km. - 3. Leopards’ scent marking: - Incorrect: Male leopards mark territory with urine, scat (10–20 marks/km²); similar to lions. - Analysis: Leopards’ marking maintains 30–50 km² territories. - Why Not Other Options?: - (b) 2 and 3 only: - Incorrect: Leopard marking (3) false. - (c) 1 and 3 only: - Incorrect: Leopard marking false. - (d) All three: - Incorrect: Leopard marking false. - Additional Insights: - India: Gir lions breed 2x/year; cheetah reintroduction (10 individuals) aims for 50 by 2030. - Conservation: WPA Schedule I protects big cats; 20% habitat loss threat. - Global: Cheetahs’ vocalization unique among 40 felid species. - Q209: Which one of the following shows a unique relationship with an insect that has coevolved with it and that is the only insect that can pollinate this tree? - Options: - (a) Fig - (b) Mahua - (c) Sandalwood - (d) Silk cotton - Answer: - (a) Fig - Analysis: - Pollination Symbiosis Context: - Obligate mutualism rare; figs (Ficus spp.) exemplar case. - Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer: - Fig: - Relationship: Figs (~750 species) coevolved with fig wasps (Agaonidae); each species has a specific wasp pollinator. - Process: Female wasp enters fig (syconium), pollinates, lays eggs; males die inside; ~100% pollination specificity. - Example: India’s Ficus benghalensis relies on Ceratosolen wasps; supports 20% of fig diversity. - Why Not Other Options?: - (b) Mahua: - Incorrect: Madhuca longifolia pollinated by moths, bats; not specific to one insect. - (c) Sandalwood: - Incorrect: Santalum album pollinated by bees, butterflies; not obligate. - (d) Silk cotton: - Incorrect: Bombax ceiba pollinated by birds, bees; no single-insect dependency. - Additional Insights: - India: Figs support 10% of avian frugivores; 0.1 million ha of Ficus forests. - Threats: 30% wasp decline from pesticides; impacts fig reproduction. - Global: Fig-wasp mutualism model for coevolution studies; 50% figs threatened. - Q210: Consider the following: - Organisms: - 1. Butterflies - 2. Fish - 3. Frogs - How many of the above have poisonous species among them? - Options: - (a) Only one - (b) Only two - (c) All three - (d) None - Answer: - (c) All three - Analysis: - Poisonous Species Context: - Toxins in animals deter predators; India hosts ~1,000 toxic species. - Detailed Explanation of Organisms: - 1. Butterflies: - Correct: Poisonous species (e.g., Danaus chrysippus) sequester cardenolides; toxic to birds (LD50 ~0.1 mg/kg). - Example: India’s 1,500 butterfly species include 5% toxic monarchs. - 2. Fish: - Correct: Pufferfish (Tetraodontidae) contain tetrodotoxin (TTX, LD50 ~10 µg/kg); ~20 species in Indian waters. - Example: Lagocephalus in India’s coasts, 0.1% fishery poisonings. - 3. Frogs: - Correct: Poison dart frogs (e.g., Dendrobatidae, introduced) secrete batrachotoxins; Indian ranids (e.g., Hoplobatrachus) mildly toxic (0.01 mg/kg). - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Only one: - Incorrect: All three have toxic species. - (b) Only two: - Incorrect: Butterflies, fish, frogs all toxic. - (d) None: - Incorrect: Toxins well-documented. - Additional Insights: - India: Toxic species in 10% of biodiversity; 0.1% human poisonings. - Conservation: WPA protects toxic frogs; fish bans in 5 states. - Global: 5% of animal species toxic; key for chemical ecology. - Q211: According to the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), which one of the following is the largest source of sulphur dioxide emissions? - Options: - (a) Locomotives using fossil fuels - (b) Ships using fossil fuels - (c) Extraction of metals from ores - (d) Power plants using fossil fuels - Answer: - (d) Power plants using fossil fuels - Analysis: - SO₂ Emissions Context: - Sulphur dioxide (SO₂) from combustion (\( S + O_2 \to SO_2 \)); global emissions ~80 Mt/year; causes acid rain, health issues. - Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer: - Power Plants: - EPA Data: Fossil fuel power plants (coal, oil) emit ~65% of US SO₂ (2.5 Mt/year, 2020); globally, ~50% (40 Mt/year). - Process: Coal with 1–2% sulphur emits ~20 kg SO₂/MWh; India’s 211 coal plants emit ~0.5 Mt SO₂/year. - Example: NTPC’s Singrauli plant, 10% of India’s SO₂. - Why Not Other Options?: - (a) Locomotives: - Incorrect: Diesel trains emit ~2% SO₂ (0.1 Mt/year globally); minor vs. power plants. - (b) Ships: - Incorrect: Shipping emits ~10% SO₂ (8 Mt/year); IMO 2020 caps sulphur at 0.5%. - (c) Metal extraction: - Incorrect: Smelting (e.g., copper) emits ~15% SO₂ (12 Mt/year); secondary to power. - Additional Insights: - India: Coal plants contribute 70% SO₂; FGD units in 50% plants cut 90%. - Health: SO₂ exposure (>10 ppm) increases asthma by 15%. - Global: SO₂ emissions down 30% since 1990; power plants still dominate.
